detail.abstract: This paper examines the determinants of international investment currency selection using bilateral data on cross-border bond holdings from the IMF's CPIS. Focusing on the private-sector store-of-value function, we analyze how bilateral linkages, currency issuer characteristics, and global conditions shape the demand for denomination currency. We find that bilateral financial linkages are the most robust determinant of currency shares. Financial development in the currency-issuing country increases a currency's portfolio share, highlighting the importance of market depth and liquidity. The results also indicate that currency allocation is largely driven by persistent structural factors rather than shortrun fluctuations. Finally, we find some indications that geopolitical alignment may affect currency allocation in the future.

title: Global Value Chains, Environmental Regulation, and Firm-Level Determinants of Carbon Productivity: Evidence from Chinese Firms

detail.abstract: Global value chains (GVCs) play an increasingly important role in shaping firms' carbon productivity, especially in emerging economies undergoing low-carbon transition. We examine the impact of firm-level factors, environmental regulation, and GVC participation on carbon productivity among Chinese manufacturing firms during 2007-2022. The findings of this study are presented as follows: First, leverage, employee scale, liquidity, and return on assets exert a positive influence on carbon productivity, while internationalization has a negative impact on carbon productivity. Second, the carbon emissions trading system also has a positive effect on carbon productivity. Third, GVC participation and forward participation have a positive impact on carbon productivity, whereas backward participation has a negative effect on carbon productivity. This study provides firm-level evidence on the links among internal firm characteristics, environmental regulation, GVC participation, and low-carbon production efficiency, and suggests policy levers for strengthening environmental regulation and promoting low-carbon strategies.

title: Dividend Taxes and the Passage to Maturity
affiliations: University of Brescia - Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: Dividend Taxes and the Passage to Maturity
detail.abstract: The new view holds that a dividend tax is capitalised and leaves the mature firm’s decisions undistorted, provided marginal investment is financed out of retained earnings. The firm reaches that regime by first withholding its earnings, and while it withholds them the dividend tax is not in force. This article places the two regimes inside a trade-off model with debt and endogenous default, so that maturity is an event the firm chooses and may never reach. The dividend tax does not reach the immature firm. It taxes the passage to maturity, and its whole content is one number, the value of a unit distributed relative to a unit retained. Lowering that number from unity to 0.60 lifts the expansion trigger by a factor of 3.4, cuts the probability of ever maturing from 59.8% to 23.7% and the value today of one unit paid at maturity by 90%. At the baseline a third of firms ever mature, and nine tenths of the firm’s discounted lifetime is spent in the regime in which the new view does not apply. The tax also creates the shield that pays for the passage: a firm that can recapitalise at maturity keeps maturing at dividend rates at which a firm that cannot borrow never does, provided the proceeds leave through repurchases rather than dividends. The firms that never mature are those whose expansion buys a small productivity gain and that cannot borrow when they make it.

title: The Invisible Continent. Counting the Missing Poor in Developing Countries
affiliations: University of Strasbourg - Beta, CNRS, Texas A&M University, University of Liège, ENS-Rennes and World Bank Group

detail.title: The Invisible Continent. Counting the Missing Poor in Developing Countries
detail.abstract: Because the poor face higher mortality, they are under-represented in the samples used to measure poverty. This paper quantifies this missing poor bias across 92 developing and least developed countries by comparing observed headcount poverty rates with counterfactual rates that would prevail if all individuals enjoyed the survival conditions of the top income class. Using income distributions and life expectancy by wealth quintile, we find the bias to be substantial and highly heterogeneous, from negligible in parts of Central Asia to 15 percentage points in Bolivia and 36 in Bhutan. Aggregated, the correction reveals an invisible continent of more than 116 million uncounted poor, large enough to reverse international poverty rankings. Instrumenting health system coverage with malaria ecology, we then show that universal health coverage causally reduces both the bias and the steepness of the income-mortality gradient through which it arises. A ten point gain in coverage lowers the bias by about one percentage point, three times the OLS estimate. Progress toward universal health coverage therefore yields a second dividend, correcting a measurement distortion concentrated where deprivation is deepest.

detail.abstract: Overfitting is an important challenge in large language model development because a model may learn patterns that are highly specific to its training data and subsequently perform less effectively on unseen examples. Although increasing model size and training data can improve languagemodeling capabilities, large models can still exhibit undesirable dependence on particular training distributions, especially during task-specific adaptation. Context-aware parameter optimization provides a potential approach for addressing this issue by adjusting model parameters according to contextual characteristics while attempting to preserve general linguistic representations. Parameter-efficient techniques such as adapters and Low-Rank Adaptation demonstrate that models can be adapted to new tasks without updating all pretrained parameters (Houlsby et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2022). This study examines how context-aware parameter optimization can contribute to reducing overfitting in large language models by selectively modifying parameters that are relevant to a specific context while limiting unnecessary changes to the pretrained model. The discussion focuses on parameter efficiency, contextual adaptation, regularization, and generalization to unseen data.

title: Long-Term Care with Myopia
affiliations: Vilnius University, HEC Liege and University of Liege, HEC Management School, Students

detail.title: Long-Term Care with Myopia
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the design of a social policy scheme for long-term care in a setting where disabled elderly individuals receive care both informally, from family members, and formally, from professional providers. We introduce two key features: informal caregivers bear substantial physiological and psychological costs, and they tend to be myopic with respect to these health consequences. Under perfect observability, an optimal policy can induce caregivers to exercise caution and provide an appropriate level of informal care. However, when individual characteristics are not common knowledge, public policy must resort to distortions and indirect instruments to guide agents toward optimal behavior - a classic second-best problem.

title: Scope and Limits of an Agent’s Authority under the Indian Contract Act, 1872: A Study of Express, Implied, and Ostensible Authority

detail.title: Scope and Limits of an Agent’s Authority under the Indian Contract Act, 1872: A Study of Express, Implied, and Ostensible Authority

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NONE
declarations.ethicsApproval: NONE
declarations.funderStatement: NONE

detail.abstract: Agency in everyday business often hinges on how much power an agent really has to act for their boss, known as the principal, under India's key law on contracts from 1872. This study breaks down the boundaries of that power, focusing on three main types: express (clearly spelled out), implied (understood from the situation), and ostensible (what seems true to outsiders). It looks at real-life examples to show when the boss must honour deals made by the agent and when they can say no. Express authority is the simplest—it's when the principal directly tells the agent what to do, either in writing or by word of mouth, like hiring someone to sell a car for exactly Rs 5 lakhs.1 No guesswork here; the agent sticks to those exact instructions, and going beyond them doesn't bind the principal unless later approved.2 Implied authority fills in the gaps—it's not written down but comes from the job's nature or past dealings, such as an agent fixing a minor issue on a rented property without asking first, because that's normal for property managers.3 Courts figure this out by looking at what a sensible person would expect in that role. Ostensible or apparent authority is trickier and protects outsiders who deal in good faith. Even if the agent lacks real power, if the principal's words or actions make it look like they do—like letting an employee keep using the company car and card after their job ends—the principal might still be stuck with the bill.4 This stops bosses from misleading people. But limits exist: agents can't bind principals to illegal acts, personal gain schemes, or wildly outside their role, like a sales agent suddenly buying land.5 The Indian Contract Act, 1872 (Sections 182-238), sets these rules to balance fairness for principals, agents, and third parties in trade.6 In today's fast business world, knowing these lines prevents fights and losses. Clear contracts help, but courts often step in to check if actions fit "usual business course." This framework keeps commerce smooth while curbing overreach.

title: The Influence of the Vocal Few: Evidence from Social Media Comments
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School and University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: The Influence of the Vocal Few: Evidence from Social Media Comments
detail.abstract: Online comment sections let a small number of vocal individuals reach far beyond their own networks. We conduct a large-scale field experiment on Facebook that randomizes the presence and stance of comments beneath posts for a racial justice organization, reaching around one million U.S. users. Opposing comments increase reactions, comments, and link clicks by 15–43 percent relative to no comments, whereas supportive comments have little effect. A complementary survey experiment shows that similar opposing comments make attitudes less progressive and reduce donations to the organization. Through a common feature of online platforms, the vocal few can exert outsized influence.

detail.abstract: Prediction-market prices aggregate information through trading, but aggressive orders also consume finite displayed liquidity. I study the distinction between price adjustment and incremental information using high-frequency Polymarket trades and order books. In a 28-day prospective sample, short-run quote changes increase with order size relative to displayed depth. Strict episode isolation materially weakens this relation. Prices are closer to eventual outcomes five minutes after large-order episodes, but this descriptive improvement is not larger than after comparable ordinary trades. A model that adds signed order flow to the prevailing price and unsigned depth pressure likewise produces no detectable out-of-time improvement in forecast loss. Exact historical books show that book-implied slippage ranks realized execution costs, while subsequent reversal is concentrated in selected event-proximate sports markets. The evidence separates liquidity-sensitive quote movement from incremental outcome information.

detail.abstract: Contested psychiatric care frequently involves substantial asymmetries in medical knowledge, institutional authority, procedural literacy, and access to administrative information. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), have introduced new possibilities for patient-led organization, interpretation, and retrospective reconstruction of complex healthcare-related experiences-possibilities now accessible at zero cost to individuals without institutional affiliation or professional support. This study presents an analytic autoethnographic case study examining how prolonged interaction with multiple generative AI systems contributed to retrospective interpretation, documentary organization, and institutional navigation during a contested psychiatric care trajectory spanning nearly three decades, from 1998 to 2026. That a single individual, without legal counsel or clinical expertise, could retrospectively reconstruct and analytically engage with a 28-year institutional history using freely available AI tools represents a sociotechnically significant development worthy of scholarly attention. The analysis integrates autobiographical recollections, longitudinal physiological self-monitoring, medical and administrative records, and AI-assisted interpretive workflows generated during iterative interactions with generative AI systems. Rather than conceptualizing AI as an authoritative decision-making mechanism, this study introduces the "zDAI framework" (zero-cost Distributed AI-assisted Interpretation) as a patient-centered cognitive support framework designed to assist in timeline reconstruction, procedural mapping, document comparison, and interpretive synthesis under conditions of informational asymmetry and institutional complexity. Particular attention is given to the role of human-AI collaborative cognitive reconstruction, in which autobiographical memory, institutional documentation, emotional interpretation, and AI-assisted analytical processes interacted recursively over time. The case further suggests that different generative AI systems facilitate distinct interpretive affordances-including narrative expansion, epistemic calibration, symbolic integration, and procedural clarification-that may be strategically combined within a patient-centered framework. This case illustrates the emerging sociotechnical role of generative AI in retrospective healthcare interpretation, patient self-advocacy, and AI-mediated institutional navigation, while also highlighting important limitations concerning interpretive subjectivity, AI hallucination risks, and the need for external verification.

detail.abstract: This paper tests whether dispersion in market-implied Federal Open Market Committee outcomes contains information about the long-run component of U.S. equity volatility. For 38 meetings, I construct the crossoutcome variance of Kalshi probabilities over days-30 to-3 and embed it in a fixed (K=4), uniform-weight GARCH-MIDAS model for 824 S&P 500 trading days. The raw loading is 0.3621 (LR = 7.9637; asymptotic p = 0.00477; 999-draw meeting randomization p = 0.027). Residualizing on the implied policy mean and log volume gives 0.3570 (LR = 8.5072; p = 0.00354; randomization p = 0.027). A stronger support audit conditions on the number and span of outcome bins that the exchange lists for each meeting. Its loading is 0.3675 (LR = 9.5400; p = 0.00201), and a conditional meeting randomization that re-estimates the support adjustment in every draw gives p = 0.018. Activating the factor three business days before, on, or one business day after the meeting yields positive loadings with p-values of 0.0041, 0.0020, and 0.0197. Entropy is insignificant, showing that economic distance across rate outcomes-not probability fragmentation alone-carries the signal. All leave-one-meeting-out variance loadings remain positive. The evidence is an insample relation between pre-decision policy-outcome dispersion and the fitted long-run volatility state; a short 2026 holdout does not improve forecasts.

title: Childhood, Well-Being and Fairness

detail.title: Childhood, Well-Being and Fairness
detail.abstract: This paper examines the design of optimal family policies when children have unequal needs (in terms of material goods and parental time), leading to heterogeneous preferences, and have parents with unequal degrees of altruism. We examine the issue of interpersonal well-being comparisons between children by means of consumption-equivalent and time-equivalent indexes, and show that the conditions of existence of these equivalents — as well as their rankings across children — differ across the metric used. We also examine well-being comparisons across parents who differ in their children's preferences and in their altruism. Then, we derive the constrained egalitarian social optimum (where only children's well-being levels are equalized) and the double egalitarian social optimum (where both children's and parents' well-being are equalized). It is shown that the optimal allocation and the optimal family policy vary with the metric used for the measurement of children's well-being.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the financing side of a large, preannounced index addition. Space Exploration Technologies Corporation entered the Nasdaq-100 before the market open on 7 July 2026, creating a 6 July implementation event. I construct model-implied funding pressure for 93 incumbents by allocating an entrant-funding requirement across pre-event weights and scaling implied sale dollars by pre-event average daily dollar volume (ADV). A one-standard-deviation increase in pressure is associated with 0.114 log points, or 12.1 percent, higher implementation-day volume relative to normal. The coefficient is 8.6323 with HC3 p = 0.0000283; randomization, bootstrap, and leave-one-out inference agree. Applying the identical cross-sectional specification to 38 pre-announcement trading dates from 1 May through 25 June produces coefficients from-5.206 to 6.017; none reaches the 6 July estimate. The implementation date ranks first among the 38 placebos plus the event (empirical upper-tail p = 1/39 = 0.0256). A decomposition shows that standardized predicted sale dollars (p = 0.0077) and low trading capacity (p = 0.0034) both enter in the expected direction despite their-0.880 correlation. On 7 July the pressure coefficient falls to 3.4249 (p = 0.164), with significant decay. A denominator-light raw-dollar specification remains positive (p = 0.0495). The result is a sharply dated cross-sectional quantity response aligned with the model-implied financing allocation.

detail.abstract:
Summary Background: In 2025, the Lancet Commission proposed a framework distinguishing preclinical from clinical obesity and requiring confirmation of excess adiposity beyond BMI. The Commission recommended that obesity should be classified as either clinical or preclinical based on the presence (clinical obesity) or absence (preclinical obesity) of obesity-related organ dysfunction or functional limitations. We compared BMI-derived obesity with the Lancet criteria based on waist circumference (Lancet-WC) and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (Lancet-DXA) and evaluated their associations with incident diabetes and hypertension in middle-aged Black South African adults.

Methods:Baseline data were available for 889 women and 821 men aged 40-60 years. Obesity prevalence was compared using WHO BMI, and Lancet-WC and Lancet-DXA criteria. Participants were followed for 10-12 years to determine incident diabetes and hypertension. Multivariable logistic regression examined associations between obesity classifications and incident outcomes.

Findings: Obesity prevalence differed substantially across classification methods. Among women, obesity prevalence was 65·4% by BMI, 90·0% by Lancet-WC, and 51·9% by Lancet-DXA; corresponding estimates among men were 16·7%, 37·4%, and 23·9%, respectively. Among women, only clinical obesity was associated with incident type 2 diabetes (T2D) using both Lancet-WC (AOR 7·48, 95% CI 2·28-24·51) and Lancet-DXA criteria (AOR 3·08, 95% CI 1·34-7·07). Among men, Lancet-WC preclinical obesity (AOR 2·44, 95% CI 1·37-4·37) and clinical obesity (AOR 3·45, 95% CI 1·25-9·51) were associated with incident T2D, whereas Lancet-DXA identified risk only among those with preclinical obesity (AOR 2·13, 95% CI 1·10-4·15). No obesity classification predicted incident hypertension.

Interpretation: The Lancet framework revealed variation in obesity prevalence across classification methods and identified heterogeneity in T2D risk that was not captured by BMI alone. A WC-derived obesity implementation of the Lancet framework appeared to provide greater clinical utility than the DXA-derived approach and may offer a pragmatic and accessible strategy for obesity risk stratification in African populations.

title: The Generator Economy and the Falling Peak: Electricity Infrastructure and Premature Deindustrialization, with Evidence from Nigeria

detail.title: The Generator Economy and the Falling Peak: Electricity Infrastructure and Premature Deindustrialization, with Evidence from Nigeria

detail.abstract: Existing literature shows that countries with lower levels of income achieve industrialization because of trade and increased labor mobility. This study examines the relationship between electricity infrastructure and manufacturing development because, Manufacturing is an electricityheavy sector, whereas services and agriculture are not, so a grid that fails to provide reliable industrial power limits manufacturing specifically, while services continue to grow without constraint-while making the same observed pattern happen in a different manner. A global analysis is conducted from 1976 to 2025 using World Development Indicators (WDI) data, and the same specification as Rodrik (2016) is used, but the analysis is run separately for countries where electricity transmission and distribution losses are below and above the median. A joint test of the interaction terms shows that the two are not equal (χ²(2) = 9.22, p = 0.010) and remains in the model after conditioning on the oil dependence and urbanization variables. Oil rents appear and are included in a negative and significant way at every point; thus the resource-curse explanation is reinforced rather than overthrown by the infrastructure explanation. Nigeria's real manufacturing share decreased from 22.0% of GDP in the 1980s to 8.0% in the 2020s, whereas the electrification share increased from 37.8% to 59.8%. The design does not infer causal effects and the results of the study are presented as conditional associations.

title: When the Device Is Lost: Recovering Offline Digital Euro Holdings by Revocation Rather Than Expiry
affiliations: "Angel Kanchev" University of Ruse and "Angel Kanchev" University of Ruse

detail.title: When the Device Is Lost: Recovering Offline Digital Euro Holdings by Revocation Rather Than Expiry

declarations.funderStatement: The authors received no funding for this work

detail.abstract: The offline component of the digital euro holds value as a balance in an applet on a secure element. The published design lets a holder disable a lost or stolen device but describes no way to recover the holdings on it. This paper argues that the absence follows from the balance model rather than from offline payment as such. A balance carries no record of where its value has been, so restoring a reported loss would pay twice for anything already spent, and a false report would become a way to be paid again: without state recording the provenance of offline value, no recovery rule can be both exact and immune to false claims. The paper extends recovery by revocation, first proposed for electronic cash that could not be passed on, to transferable value carried by denominated tokens with an authenticated record of their transfers. The holder claims the tokens held on the lost device; they are revoked; and after a waiting period those never passed on are credited back, provisionally until their validity ends. The mechanism needs no proof of loss and no separate record of offline payments. The paper sets out the operational and liability consequences.

keywords: Construction Choices in a Reference-Based Topological Regime Classier: Normalisation
and What the Wasserstein Distance Measures Empirical Evidence from HYG Daily Data

detail.abstract: Takagi (2026a) introduces a topological regime classier that marks a trading day when the 252-day rolling Z-score of the Wasserstein-2 distance between HYG's daily H 1 persistence diagram and a reference diagram computed at the Global Financial Crisis S&P 500 nadir falls at or below-1.5. Takagi (2026b) reassesses that classier's statistical properties, correcting the reference against which its conditional frequency is assessed and applying autocorrelationrobust inference to its regression-based diagnostics. Neither paper examines the construction of the distance itself. This paper asks what the distance measures. We report four ndings. First, the classier's published implementation computes the transport cost against uniform probability measures on the diagonally augmented diagrams, which is a normalised (mean) transport cost rather than the counting-measure quantity written in the denition. The two constructions are not equivalent: the sign of the association between the daily H 1 loop count and the raw distance inverts between them, and the in-sample lift of the conditional frequency of positive outcomes over the measured base rate moves from +4.2 to-7.9 percentage points, crossing that base rate. Second, and analytically, diagonal augmentation permits every bar to be matched to its own diagonal projection at a cost equal to half its squared persistence, so the squared distance is dominated by the sum of squared persistences of the current diagram plus a reference-dependent constant. The rolling Z-score removes additive constants. Empirically the squared distance correlates with the current diagram's own sum of squared persistences above r = 0.99 for two of the three reference diagrams examined, and lower but still above 0.83 for the third, whose single unusually persistent bar makes cross-matching worthwhile. Third, six congurationsthree structurally dissimilar crisis-nadir reference diagrams crossed with the two normalisationsall yield out-of-sample lifts between +22 and +32 percentage points over the measured base rate, while their in-sample lifts split three above the base rate and three below it. Two classiers constructed with no reference diagram at all fall in the same out-of-sample band. Fourth, under a circular-shift null that preserves the classier series' own serial correlation, no reference-based conguration's conditional frequency of positive outcomes is distinguishable at the 5% level. The conditional mean is, under both normalisations, as is the joint agreement of the congurations examined: the smallest out-of-sample lift among all eight classiers carries a calibrated probability of 0.0010 against a null median far below zero. The null distribution centres on the measured unconditional frequency without being supplied it. We also report that the geometric reading oered in Takagi (2026a)that classied days carry few, concentrated cyclic patternsholds only in part, and that which part it holds in depends on the normalisation; and that a within-window statistic proposed elsewhere as an explanation of cross-ETF heterogeneity has, over the full sample, the opposite sign to the one that explanation requires. Three orthogonality checks bound the negative ndings: the quantity being thresholded is not proximity to the reference, not the within-window position 1 of the price minimum, and not realised volatility, the last because the point cloud is scaled by its own standard deviation before homology is computed. The ndings are descriptive throughout. They characterise the sensitivity of a published classier to two construction choices and do not constitute a forecast, a causal claim, an investment recommendation, or a trading rule. Limitations regarding sample size, single-asset scope, the non-independence of the congurations examined, and the hindsight selection of reference dates are discussed in Section 12.

title: Whose Breach Is It? Inter-Standard Reliability in Shariah Equity Screening

detail.title: Whose Breach Is It? Inter-Standard Reliability in Shariah Equity Screening

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is developing Mizan, a Shariah screening service. There are no other competing interests.

detail.abstract: A Shariah compliance verdict is ordinarily received as a statement about a firm, whereby the firm either satisfies the leverage screen applied to it or it does not, and a mandate bound to that verdict must then trade. This paper asks a prior question, being whether the verdict is a reliable measurement at all. Treating the four principal leverage screens as four coders rating the same firm-quarter, I apply the apparatus of inter-rater reliability to a point-in-time compliance panel of 21,998 firm-quarters across 424 US firms over 2010 to 2026. Krippendorff's alpha across the four standards is 0.600, which falls beneath the 0.667 threshold conventionally required before a measure is held sufficient for even tentative inference. The four standards agree exactly upon 64.3% of firm-quarters, whilst of the 11,859 firm-quarters flagged as non-compliant by at least one standard, 7,841, being 66.1%, are contested by at least one other. Further, I decompose the disagreement and find it to rest overwhelmingly upon the denominator rather than upon the threshold, in that imposing a common denominator upon all four screens raises alpha to between 0.897 and 0.922 and reduces the contested share of flagged breaches to between 17% and 21%. I believe the implication is that two thirds of what the industry records as non-compliance is not a property of the firm but an artefact of which rulebook happens to govern the mandate, and that a breach which one reputable standard records whilst two others do not ought not to compel the same confidence as one upon which all four agree.

detail.abstract: Minerals are a basic part of modern economic and national security. The United States has substantial mineral resources and a large industrial base, but it also depends on international markets for many important minerals and for some stages of processing and refining. This paper examines gold, silver, platinum-group metals, critical minerals, rare earth elements, supply-chain concentration, recycling, technology, defense, international cooperation, and Pakistan's mineral potential. It argues that complete mineral independence is neither practical nor necessary for the United States. A more realistic approach is to build resilient and diversified supply chains through responsible domestic production, stronger processing capacity, recycling, strategic inventories, technological innovation, and cooperation with a wider group of reliable international partners. The paper uses 2025 as its main statistical base, drawing particularly on the U.S. Geological Survey's 2026 Mineral Commodity Summaries, while incorporating relevant developments reported during 2026. Pakistan is discussed as a potential participant in diversified mineral supply chains, with Reko Diq used as an example of both mineral opportunity and the practical challenges of security, infrastructure, financing, and project development.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a ledger-based analysis showing that, because modern currencies are issued as liabilities of the issuer, double-entry accounting limits fiat currency systems to two structural frameworks: a direct "spend-first" circuit (Model 1) and a segmented institutional "tax-andborrow" circuit (Model 2). Using the mathematical identities of double-entry bookkeeping, the paper traces balance sheet expansion, contraction, asset swaps, and liability swaps across central bank, treasury, commercial banking, and non-government non-bank public ledgers. While Modern Monetary Theory accurately describes the accounting abstractions of Model 1, an examination of public data and institutional operating frameworks in the United States and the United Kingdom confirms that both jurisdictions operate today under Model 2. We further show that Treasury-issued stablecoins, if introduced, would operate under Model 1, and that Model 1 and Model 2 can, in principle, operate simultaneously without interference. This paper clarifies contemporary macroeconomic debates by showing how structural constraints, such as the UK's Full Funding Rule and the U.S. Treasury General Account legal framework, determine how fiscal deficits are financed, and in turn whether the aggregate fiat money supply and deposit money supply expand permanently, temporarily, or not at all.

title: The Walls We Choose: The Demoted Architect and the Lost Authorship of Place

detail.title: The Walls We Choose: The Demoted Architect and the Lost Authorship of Place

detail.abstract:
This is the first paper in a sub-series on the built environment, and it is written from inside the machine it describes. For twenty-five years the author has worked where buildings are argued into existence, the permit counter, the pre-consultation meeting, the committee room, the file that moves or does not move. The paper's claim is blunt: the architect has been demoted. The profession is squeezed between a financial model that decides what a building will be before anyone draws it, and a regulatory apparatus that is too costly for the small applicant and too permeable for the powerful one. What remains of the architect's role is compliance.
That demotion matters for a reason larger than professional pride. The architect was never meant to be the author of the city; the architect was meant to be the person who makes it possible for everyone else to author it. Demote that person and you disenfranchise the people the architect exists to serve, the future resident, the small group, the family with no seat at the table, and you silence the land, which never had one. The paper follows a single composite building from site to occupancy to show, stage by stage, where authorship is lost. It argues, with Marx's 1844 account of alienated labour and the author's own 2001 thesis, that the estrangement of the builder, the dweller and the land is one estrangement with one cause. It draws on the Ontario Greenbelt affair and the Grenfell Tower inquiry, on John Turner in Peru, Walter Segal and Peter Barber in London and ELEMENTAL in Chile, and it reckons honestly with the profession's own complicity. It closes with what would have to change, stage by stage, to give the pencil back, including the author's own proposal for a national non-profit housing trust, offered as a test of whether the argument can be built, and held to the same conditions the paper demands of every other exercise of power.

detail.abstract: The paper examines opportunities for deeper economic integration between the EU and the Western Balkans and assesses their potential economic impact. It documents key quantified non-tariff barriers to Western Balkan-EU industrial goods trade-covering regulatory, customs, and border-logistics frictions-amounting to around 8-14 percent ad valorem equivalent. (Broader non-tariff barriers may be higher, consistent with prior IMF analysis.) Reducing these barriers, alongside deeper agri-food and services integration, could generate substantial gains, allowing the Western Balkans to capture roughly one-quarter to one-half of the economic benefits of full EU membership while supporting EU objectives related to nearshoring, supply-chain resilience, regional integration, and connectivity.

detail.abstract: The expansion of digital technologies in education has created new opportunities for teaching, learning, information access, and educational participation. However, the assumption that providing students with devices or internet connectivity is sufficient to achieve digital inclusion overlooks less visible forms of exclusion. This article examines the hidden dimensions of digital exclusion experienced by economically disadvantaged secondary school students in Sub-Saharan Africa, focusing on affordability, quality of connectivity, device sharing, digital skills, learning environments, parental support, teacher capacity, and the ability to convert digital access into meaningful educational outcomes. The study adopts a qualitative literature-review approach, drawing on peer-reviewed studies, international education reports, and evidence concerning digital learning in Sub-Saharan African contexts. The analysis is informed by the multidimensional conception of the digital divide, which distinguishes between access, skills and patterns of use, and the benefits obtained from digital technologies. Existing evidence indicates that economically disadvantaged learners may experience exclusion even when they technically have access to a digital device or network. High data costs, unreliable electricity, limited digital competencies, shared devices, weak pedagogical support, and inadequate learning environments can reduce the educational value of nominal connectivity. The article argues that digital inclusion policies should therefore move beyond device distribution and connectivity targets toward a broader framework that addresses affordability, capability, meaningful use, and educational outcomes.

title: Cheaper but Farther: Rent Gradients and Commuting in the Residential Choices of Young Korean Workers

detail.title: Cheaper but Farther: Rent Gradients and Commuting in the Residential Choices of Young Korean Workers

detail.abstract: Where do young wage workers live, given where they work? This paper studies the residence municipality chosen by employed wage workers aged 19-34 in Korea, conditional on their observed workplace, using survey microdata for 2021H2-2024H2 linked to a standardized rent index built from administrative lease records for every rent-eligible municipality. In a conditional logit over all alternatives, the log-rent coefficient is-1.153, which implies a-10.4 percent change in the relative odds of a residence with 10 percent higher rent; it is stable across choice sets, survey rounds, and inference methods. A within-between decomposition locates the gradient in persistent differences between municipalities (-1.254) rather than in changes within them (0.080). The between-municipality gradient is confined to capital-region residences (contrast-2.166, and-1.903 after the noncapital cities that dominate cross-boundary commuting are removed), and workers at high-rent workplace centers combine a steeper gradient with cheaper, more distant residences. The estimates are conditional associations, not responses to an exogenous change in rent; they show that persistent rent differences order the residential choices of young workers attached to capital-region jobs, where housing, transport, and job policies need to be designed together.

title: Creativity in networks: Collegiate social structure and later inventive activity
affiliations: State University of New York (SUNY), Stony Brook and University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: Creativity in networks: Collegiate social structure and later inventive activity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported in part by a grant from the Siebel Energy Institute and by NSF grant CCF-1717530.

detail.abstract: Social relationships formed during college may contribute to inventive careers long after students leave campus. The network structures that provide access to unfamiliar ideas, however, need not be those that support their development. We examine this question across 43 U.S. universities by linking Facebook friendship networks observed in September 2005 to patent-based outcomes for corresponding college-attendance cohorts born between 1980 and 1984. Drawing on weak-tie and structural-hole theories, we compare network size, degree, intercommunity-edge count, effective size, network constraint, and a heuristic creativity measure using Pearson correlations and linear regression. Mean network constraint is positively associated with inventor share, patent count, and patent-citation count; its correlation with inventor share is 0.549. Intercommunity-edge count is negatively associated with inventor share and network-size-normalized patent and citation counts. In regressions including network size, mean constraint, and intercommunity-edge count, the constraint coefficients remain positive and statistically significant, whereas the intercommunity-edge coefficients are not statistically significant. These associations motivate an account of later inventive activity in which collegiate relationships support knowledge transfer and the development of ideas.

title: Corporate Hierarchy
affiliations: Columbia Business School and Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance

detail.title: Corporate Hierarchy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to disclose.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding to disclose

detail.abstract: We introduce a novel measure of corporate hierarchy for 3,454 U.S. public firms. We construct this measure using online resumes of 18.1 million employees and a network estimation technique that allows us to identify hierarchical layers. Equipped with this measure, we document several facts about corporate hierarchies. Firms have on average six hierarchical layers and a pyramidal organizational structure. Firms with more layers have higher internal promotion rates and longer employee tenure. They exhibit higher operating performance and produce more patents, but not higher-quality patents. They also exhibit lower stock return volatility and operating asset volatility. At the same time, flatter firms fared better in response to the COVID-19 shock, consistent with greater organizational agility. We also examine potential determinants of hierarchical structures. Firms facing greater product market threats adopt flatter hierarchies. Moreover, firms increase their number of layers after going public, while they flatten their hierarchies following the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). These findings are consistent with the theoretical predictions of existing models of corporate hierarchies and suggest that firms adjust their organizational structures to balance the benefits and costs of hierarchical layers.

title: Impact of Central Bank Digital Currencies on Financial Stability

detail.title: Impact of Central Bank Digital Currencies on Financial Stability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationship with any person or organization that could be perceived to have influenced this study. This is independent academic research conducted without external involvement.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author as part of personal academic work.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the systemic risks that Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) may pose to financial stability, focusing on three mechanisms of bank run risk: slow deposit substitution ("slow runs"), rapid flight-to-safety episodes ("fast runs"), and technology-driven digital bank runs. 
A stylized three-agent model (households, a commercial bank, a firm) is calibrated and simulated to capture the transmission of a confidence shock through a critical conversion threshold θ*, beyond which credit supply and output contract. The framework is applied to three international cases with markedly different design and adoption profiles: China's e-CNY, Nigeria's eNaira, and the Bahamas' Sand Dollar. 
Using real adoption data, the paper shows that observed CBDC uptake remains far too low (0.36% of currency in circulation for the eNaira, under 1% for the Sand Dollar) to produce measurable effects on bank credit, financial inclusion, or crisis resilience — results that hold across a robustness analysis on the bank sensitivity parameter γ. 
The paper explicitly distinguishes calibrated results from illustrative or non-validated parameters throughout, and concludes that existing CBDCs remain closer to an institutional symbol than to an instrument with measurable financial stability effects, whether as a source of risk or of resilience.

title: IFRS 18 and Regulatory Reporting in Operational Loss Management: Multiple Versions of Truth and Perceived Risk
affiliations: Universidade de Brasilia, Universidade de Brasilia, Universidade de Brasilia and Universidade de Brasilia

detail.title: IFRS 18 and Regulatory Reporting in Operational Loss Management: Multiple Versions of Truth and Perceived Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known financial, personal, professional, or organizational relationships that could have influenced, or be perceived to have influenced, the research reported in this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved a voluntary survey of adult professionals. Participants were informed of the academic purpose of the research, the voluntary nature of participation, the confidentiality of their responses, and their right to discontinue participation at any time. No clinical intervention or collection of sensitive health information was involved. The study was not submitted for formal ethics committee review.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This study examines how professionals perceive the interaction between IFRS 18/CPC 51 and the Brazilian prudential reporting environment associated with CADOC 5050, focusing on the relationships among accounting judgment, misclassification risk, reconciliation and traceability strain, and operational process risk. Building primarily on Institutional Theory and institutional decoupling, the study develops Multiple Versions of Truth as an analytical concept describing the coexistence of distinct but institutionally legitimate representations of the same underlying economic event across financial and prudential reporting systems. Data were collected through a survey of 53 eligible professionals working with accounting, auditing, regulatory reporting, risk management, internal controls, compliance, technology, and data-related activities in the Brazilian financial environment. The proposed relationships were examined using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that perceived judgment and discretion associated with IFRS 18 and perceived misclassification risk are positively associated with reporting decoupling and reconciliation strain. Reconciliation and traceability strain, in turn, are positively associated with perceived operational process risk and mediate the relationships between the two antecedent constructs and operational vulnerability. The results do not suggest that different reporting representations are inherently inconsistent or that professional judgment constitutes a reporting failure. Rather, they indicate that risk emerges when institutionally legitimate representations become insufficiently connected across information systems. The study contributes by linking institutional decoupling to accounting and prudential reporting and by identifying data lineage, reconciliation, and traceability as central governance mechanisms during regulatory transition.

title: Yajña, Non-Violence, and the Buddhist Memory of the Ancient Brahmanical Ideal

detail.title: Yajña, Non-Violence, and the Buddhist Memory of the Ancient Brahmanical Ideal

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No external Funding received. Self funded.

detail.abstract: Early Buddhist literature, on the one hand, portrays contemporary royal–Brahmanical animal yajña as an undertaking marked by violence, waste, and coerced labour; on the other, it preserves an esteemed memory of ancient Brahmins as restrained, non-accumulative, and non-violent. The Kūṭadanta Sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya narrates a great yajña without animal slaughter: no animals are killed, no trees are cut down, and servants are not compelled to labour under fear; the offerings remain limited to ghee, oil, fresh butter, curds, honey, and molasses. The Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta describes ancient sage-Brahmins as abstaining from cattle slaughter and links greed, royal patronage, and the desire for splendour to a narrative of decline. The Aṅguttara Nikāya and related Nikāya materials criticize vast assemblies of bound animals, karmic fault, and rituals that torment both oneself and others. This chapter argues that the Buddhist intervention should be read not as a rejection of the entire Brahmanical tradition, but as a memory-based critique that redirects the legitimacy of yajña away from violence and towards giving, social welfare, and ultimately ethical–spiritual practice.

publicationDetails.detailsText: From Tariff to Award III: Determinants of Court-Awarded Litigation Costs in Civil Appeals to the Swiss Federal Supreme Court, in: Jusletter, 28 September 2026.

detail.abstract: This paper completes the litigation-cost series at the Swiss apex. Its trilingual corpus contains 24’617 judgments and covers 97.8% of civil appeals disposed of by the Federal Supreme Court from 2011 to 2025. In 1’339 merits appeals with an available value in dispute after three adjudicated exclusions, court-awarded litigation costs compress against their federal tariff baselines, with elasticities of about 0.79 for court fees and 0.88 for party compensation. Party compensation is frequently not awarded and lower-instance costs are revised almost exclusively when the appeal succeeds. The analysis is descriptive.

detail.abstract: Changes to Russian trade legislation between 2022 and 2026 have affected currency regulation, parallel imports, customs and technical administration, and export support measures. The impact is mixed: some measures reduce costs for participants in foreign economic activity (FEA), while others increase the administrative and financial burden.

title: From Market Oversight to Market Ordering: The Digital Markets Act and the New Political Economy of Digital Competition Regulation

detail.title: From Market Oversight to Market Ordering: The Digital Markets Act and the New Political Economy of Digital Competition Regulation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author works at the International Center for Law & Economics (ICLE). ICLE receives financial support from companies, foundations, and individuals, including firms whose interests both support and oppose positions taken in ICLE-supported work. Unless otherwise noted, all funding is unrestricted general support. The views expressed here are the authors’ alone and do not necessarily reflect those of ICLE’s advisors, affiliates, or supporters.
declarations.funderStatement: The research was funded by the International Center for Law & Economics.

detail.abstract: The European Union's Digital Markets Act (DMA) subjects conduct long governed by Article 102 TFEU, such as product integration, Most Favored Nation clauses, self-preferencing, and duty-to-deal obligations, to per se rules stripped of effects analysis, efficiency defenses, and the consumer welfare standard. This paper argues that the shift amounts to a move along a spectrum from market oversight to market ordering. Drawing on the Commission's early enforcement record against Meta (consent-or-pay), Apple (alternative distribution fees and scare screens), and Google (specification proceedings for Search), it argues that the DMA's deliberately indeterminate obligations, coupled with the structural-unfairness axiom embedded in its designation criteria, vest the Commission with ongoing discretionary authority to reshape digital markets from the center. Business-user satisfaction functions as the regime's operative proxy for the public interest, while consumer welfare, formally disclaimed, is reshaped through what is effectively consumer-law methodology without a consumer-welfare anchor. Situating the DMA on the spectrum between classical-liberal market oversight and dirigiste market ordering, the paper traces its affinities with ordoliberal nobilitas naturalis, Polanyian market re-embedding, and the broader post-liberal turn in EU economic governance. The paper ends on a critical note: it argues that the DMA's evaluative architecture is autopoietic, in the sense that it generates the criteria by which it judges its own success, making self-correction structurally unlikely. It frames this as a logical, and potentially deliberate, upshot of the mode of economic governance embodied by the DMA in which the ultimate ordering power in the economy is the state.

title: Do Female Leaders Invest in Schools? Evidence From Gram Panchayat Reservation in Karnataka

detail.title: Do Female Leaders Invest in Schools? Evidence From Gram Panchayat Reservation in Karnataka

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Part of the college project
declarations.funderStatement: It was a secondary research based study so no funding was needed

detail.abstract:
This study estimates the causal effect of female political leadership on school infrastructure at the Gram
Panchayat level in Kalaburagi district, Karnataka. Using data from UDISE, five outcomes are
examined: pucca school buildings, classrooms, boys' washrooms, girls' washrooms, and number of
computers, measured in 2025, with 2021 levels included as baseline controls. Each outcome is analysed
separately, as they capture distinct dimensions of infrastructure that may respond differently to Pradhan
gender. The focus on infrastructure stocks is deliberate. Unlike enrollment or attendance, infrastructure
investment reflects durable and discretionary allocation decisions by local leaders, and is therefore a
more direct channel through which Pradhan preferences translate into policy outcomes.

title: The Legal Construction of Homo Digitalis: How EU Digital Regulation Produces the Subject It Claims to Protect
affiliations: Tallinn University of Technology (TUT) - Department of Law

detail.title: The Legal Construction of Homo Digitalis: How EU Digital Regulation Produces the Subject It Claims to Protect

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the project Fractures of Law: AI Regulation and the Reconfiguration of Rights in the EU under grant no. JG_2026_041.

detail.abstract: European Union (EU) digital regulation is usually presented as a protective architecture for individuals. This article argues that the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act), the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the Digital Markets Act (DMA) do not merely regulate a pre-existing subject; they construct one. Through rights, transparency duties, choice mechanisms and complaint procedures, the digital acquis presupposes a person capable of reading, understanding, choosing, contesting and switching across algorithmically mediated environments. The article calls this juridical artefact homo digitalis. Using a Legal Subject Extraction Protocol, it reconstructs the assumptions about cognition, agency, relations and structure embedded in each instrument and identifies four faces: the consenting data subject, the risk-assessed person, the governed user and the market actor. Together, these figures reveal a central contradiction: EU law presumes the same person autonomous at the consent interface, procedurally competent in platform governance and marketrational in digital ecosystems, while also recognising that digital environments manipulate, overburden and structure those very capacities. The article argues that this contradiction is not accidental: it enables EU digital regulation to sustain, within the same legal architecture, a commitment to fundamental-rights protection and the continued circulation of data-driven economic activity.

title: The Spectral Reduction Method to Determine the Forward Density of The Shifted SABR Process

detail.title: The Spectral Reduction Method to Determine the Forward Density of The Shifted SABR Process

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: The work was partially funded by EIB.

detail.abstract: This paper provides details on the numerical implementation of the Spectral reduction method to calculate the forward density function of the SABR process. Exploiting the Lie point symmetry structure of the transformed infinitesimal generator and subsequent application of Fourier transform render the two dimensional (and time) PDE associated to the SABR process to a family of one dimensional (plus time) PDEs, with one PDE corresponding to a discrete wave number. These PDEs are solved by conservative finite volume method for each discrete wave number. When applying the conservative finite volume method care has been taken to its numerical stability, the handling of the singular absorbing boundary and to the preservation of the relevant probability and moment structures. Then, an one dimensional den Iseger inverse Laplace transform is applied to recover the two dimensional Kolmogorov forward density function. An important consequence of the chosen approach is, that the marginalization of the two dimensional forward density function with respect to the (transformed) volatility variable can be carried out in the spectral domain. As a consequence, calculating the marginal density in the (shifted) forward rate can be obtained with an one dimensional inverse Fourier transform. The resulting calculation method therefore retains the one dimensional calculation structure of the Arbitrage Free method of Hagan, while still being based on the original, two dimensional SABR equation en lieu of applying a reduced one dimensional approximation.

title: Adam Smith and the 'Absurd Prescriptions' of Doctors

detail.title: Adam Smith and the 'Absurd Prescriptions' of Doctors

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding to declare (self-funded).

detail.abstract:
Some of Adam Smith’s biographers assert that the great political economist was a hypochondriac, while other Smith scholars have explored Smith’s pro-market and anti-regulation stance on medical education. My work, by contrast, will focus instead on Smith’s documented encounters with the doctors and medical treatments of his day. The remainder of my paper is thus structured as a three-act 18th-century medical morality play, with each “act” corresponding in chronological order to a different medical practice that Adam Smith encountered during his lifetime. 

In summary, Act I explores Adam Smith’s fascination with “tar water” during his student years at Balliol College, Oxford. The young Smith was so sold on this miracle remedy that he recommends it to his mother in a letter dated July 2, 1744. Next, Act II takes place in Glasgow in 1760, where Smith was a college professor from 1751 to 1763 and where one of Smith’s private pupils, the young aristocrat Thomas Petty-Fitzmaurice (brother to a future prime minister), will suffer various ailments, including an eye infection that is treated with leeches (Corr. 52), while Act III occurs across the English Channel during the tail end of Adam Smith’s grand tour in France as a travelling tutor to the 3d Duke of Buccleuch and the duke’s younger brother, Hew Campbell Scott. Both brothers would fall seriously ill during their travels and be subjected to bloodletting; one would perish. Were the doctors to blame? 

My epilogue concludes with one of Smith's last letters to David Hume in which Smith doubles down on his medical skepticism.

title: Empty Streets, Steady Prices: Housing Markets under Armed Conflict
affiliations: Technion-Israel Institute of Technology and University of Haifa - Department of Economics

detail.title: Empty Streets, Steady Prices: Housing Markets under Armed Conflict

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: The October 7, 2023 war placed two Israeli border towns under fire and forced their evacuation. In northern Kiryat Shmona, transaction volume fell by roughly 46 percent relative to a matched control town and remained depressed. In southern Sderot, where residents returned within months, volume recovered fully. The remaining transactions were positively selected. As Kiryat Shmona's market thinned, transactions shifted toward newer, better-protected units, and deeply discounted sales disappeared from the lower tail of the price distribution. This explains why measured prices did not fall despite the severe shock. Moreover, the price comparison fails its pre-trend test in one matched pair and yields only an imprecise null in the other. Transaction-based price indices may therefore diverge from the value of non-transacting properties precisely when displacement changes who is able and willing to sell. The liquidity decline was concentrated in older, pre-1992 housing without an in-unit protected room; housing built under Israel's 1992 secure-space regulation experienced a much weaker decline. Together with a compensation regime that reimburses war damage without forcing owners to sell, these patterns are consistent with adjustment occurring primarily through liquidity rather than observed transaction prices.

title: Optimizing the Assessment of Murine Ovarian Follicular Reserve with YOLO26 Models
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Universidade Federal de São João del-Rei (UFSJ) and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Optimizing the Assessment of Murine Ovarian Follicular Reserve with YOLO26 Models
detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Assessment of the ovarian follicular reserve in oncofertility research relies on manual counting of follicles in histological sections, which is laborious and observer dependent. We evaluated whether a recent end-to-end object detector can automate the detection and counting of follicle profiles in routine hematoxylin-and-eosin (H&E) photomicrographs and how its performance compares with that of several human observers.,Methods: Five scales of the YOLO26 detector were trained on 295 images and validated on 76 images of cultured neonatal mouse ovaries containing 8,268 annotated profiles. Ten further benchmark images were annotated independently by six researchers, and a two-vote consensus yielded 740 reference profiles. The scales were compared on this benchmark, and the selected model was compared with each researcher against leave-one-out consensus references, which avoid scoring an observer against their own annotations. Detection was scored by one-to-one matching at an intersection over union of 0.50, and uncertainty was estimated using image-level bootstrap.,Results: YOLO26l reached an F1 score of 0.759 (95% CI 0.675–0.816; precision 0.800, recall 0.723) and an AP50 of 0.796 against the all-six consensus, with a mean counting bias of -7.1 profiles per image. F1 differences between model scales were small, and all their 95% confidence intervals included zero. Against leave-one-out references, the mean F1 of the model was 0.754 (0.671–0.809), within the range of the six researchers (0.449–0.797), and its mean counting bias was -2.4 profiles per image. In paired comparisons on the same reference, model F1 did not differ from that of two researchers, was lower than that of one (-0.040; -0.069 to -0.015) and was higher than that of three. YOLO26s, the scale ranked first on the validation set, also fell within the researchers’ range (F1 0.737).,Conclusions: A single-class YOLO26 detector performed within the range of individual researchers in detecting follicle profiles in conventional photomicrographs, supporting its use as a first step toward faster and more reproducible assessment of the ovarian follicular reserve. Confirmation on independent animals is still needed. Code, trained weights, and benchmark data are publicly available, allowing other detectors to be evaluated on the same references.

title: Sovereignty Friction Theory in 2026: Measuring Effective Economic AgencyA Diagnostic Framework for The Practical Exercise of Economic Rights

detail.title: Sovereignty Friction Theory in 2026: Measuring Effective Economic AgencyA Diagnostic Framework for The Practical Exercise of Economic Rights

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The article does not evaluate or endorse any ventures in which the author has an interest. The views expressed are the author’s own.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was prepared independently by the author and received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This article updates Sovereignty Friction Theory for the digital economy by distinguishing formal economic rights from effective economic agency. It identifies six sources of institutional friction: cost, complexity, dependence, opacity, information barriers, and delay. A qualitative friction audit evaluates the full pathway for a lawful economic action, including the combined burden of otherwise modest requirements. The framework is applied across monetary, productive, and cognitive capability, with examples from payments, digital platforms, artificial intelligence, and emerging technologies. The article argues that proportionate safeguards, intelligible decisions, portable records, correction mechanisms, and meaningful exit are necessary for economic freedom to be usable in practice.

title: Early-Warning Models for Adverse Municipal Audit Outcomes: Econometric and Machine-Learning Evidence from South African Municipalities

detail.title: Early-Warning Models for Adverse Municipal Audit Outcomes: Econometric and Machine-Learning Evidence from South African Municipalities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial, professional, or personal relationships that could reasonably be perceived as having influenced the design, analysis, interpretation, or reporting of this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because the study uses secondary, publicly available municipal financial, audit, and governance data and does not involve human participants, patient data, or identifiable personal information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study develops, estimates and evaluates econometric and machine-learning early-warning models for adverse municipal audit outcomes in South African local government. The objective is to identify observable financial and institutional conditions associated with elevated audit risk and assess their out-of-sample predictive performance. Design/Methodology/Approach: A balanced panel of 257 South African metropolitan, district and local municipalities covering the 2018/19-2023/24 fiscal years was analysed, yielding 1,542 municipality-year observations. The empirical framework combines random-effects panel logistic regression, penalised LASSO logistic regression, Random Forest and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). Predictors capture financial vulnerability, administrative stability, internal-audit capacity, consultant dependency, procurement-related irregularities and Material Irregularity notifications. Model performance was evaluated using a temporally separated hold-out test partition comprising 514 municipality-year observations. Findings: The regression results show that liquidity, operating margins, debtor impairment, capitalexpenditure execution, CFO vacancy, Municipal Manager turnover, consultant dependency, internal-audit capacity, UIFW expenditure, Material Irregularity notifications and late financial-statement submission are significantly associated with adverse audit outcomes. XGBoost achieved the strongest out-of-sample performance, with an AUC-ROC of 0.912, accuracy of 87.5%, sensitivity of 88.4%, specificity of 86.3%, precision of 90.8% and a Brier score of 0.092. Practical Implications: The resulting predictive framework enables the National Treasury, the Auditor-General of South Africa (AGSA), and Provincial CoGTA departments to transition from reactive postmortem audit scrutiny to proactive forensic surveillance and targeted institutional intervention before financial distress crystallises into severe statutory failure. Originality/Value: The study integrates panel econometric analysis with nonlinear ensemble classification within a population-level municipal dataset. It contributes empirical evidence on the predictive relevance of financial and institutional-capacity indicators for adverse municipal audit outcomes and demonstrates the potential value of machine-learning methods for public-sector early-warning applications.

title: Temporary Legal Protection as a Buffer against Immigration Enforcement: Employment, Income, and Poverty under DACA
affiliations: University of Georgia - Department of Agricultural & Applied Economics and Seton Hall University - Economics

detail.title: Temporary Legal Protection as a Buffer against Immigration Enforcement: Employment, Income, and Poverty under DACA

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors express no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the extent to which temporary legal protection buffers immigrants from the adverse effects of immigration enforcement, showing how overlapping immigration policies shape their economic outcomes. Using 2005-2019 American Community Survey data and a triple-differences framework, we compare likely undocumented Hispanic immigrants eligible for DACA to those narrowly ineligible. Enforcement worsens income and poverty among ineligible immigrants; DACA eligibility offsets roughly 75-90% of this penalty during the DACA period, with weaker impacts on labor supply. Falsification tests using naturalized citizens show no similar pattern while DACA was fully in force. These effects weaken after DACA's 2017 rescission attempt.

title: Examining the Role of Program Tenure in the SNAP Benefit Cycle
affiliations: CUNY Hunter College, Georgia State University - Department of Economics and USDA Economic Research Service

detail.title: Examining the Role of Program Tenure in the SNAP Benefit Cycle

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No personal or financial relationships to disclose.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported in part by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, Economic Research Service.

detail.abstract: Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits are issued on a monthly basis, and recipients tend to redeem a larger share of benefits shortly after issuance. In this study, we leverage a unique administrative panel dataset including the universe of SNAP benefit transaction activity from 2011 to 2015 for 1.8 million unique recipient households in Georgia. We investigate several aspects of the SNAP benefit cycle, focusing on the concentration of benefit redemptions at the beginning of the benefit month and the role of household tenure in SNAP. Using this information, we describe how SNAP households use their benefits across the benefit month and how these patterns of spending change over time conditional on length of benefit receipt. We also use information on where benefits are redeemed to describe the role of different retail store types in and across the benefit cycle. We find that the average SNAP household redeems 66% of the total household monthly benefit in the first week after receiving benefits. Among households receiving SNAP benefits for more than six months at a time, this share increases from 58% on average during the first six months to 67% on average in months seven and later. Households participating in SNAP for less than six months at a time redeem 54% on average in the first week.

title: Different Maturities, Different Protection: Combining a Put Ladder with Trend Following to Hedge Equity Tail Risk
affiliations: London School of Economics and Political Science

detail.title: Different Maturities, Different Protection: Combining a Put Ladder with Trend Following to Hedge Equity Tail Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. The author has no personal or financial relationship with any organisation that could be perceived to have influenced this study. No data provider, index sponsor or asset manager had any role in the design of the study, in the analysis, or in the decision to publish.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors. The option and equity data were accessed through Wharton Research Data Services under the subscription of King's College London

detail.abstract: Protection against equity crashes is usually judged one instrument at a time. Its cost shows up every year, while its value shows up only in the few crises it is meant for. This paper takes the position of an investor who wants to stay fully invested in US equities, with a narrow objective: to cut the left tail of the return distribution, and above all the maximum drawdown, without giving up compound return. It is in three parts. The first compares sleeves of S&P 500 puts of different maturities, from one month to two years. Maturity decides whether the puts protect at all: at the same annual cost, two-year puts bought at the October 2007 peak cut the drawdown of the Global Financial Crisis from -55% to -18%, while one-month puts left the portfolio worse off than no hedge, and in the COVID crash the ranking reversed, but only for a sleeve that happened to hold the right expiry. A ladder of puts struck 25% below the index, with lives spread from three months to two years, is the design that does not require knowing which crisis is coming. The second part examines trend following, represented by the SG Trend Index net of fees, which gained in nine of the index's ten worst months but spent six years below a previous high. The third holds the two sleeves together, in a portfolio of 100% S&P 500, a 50% overlay on the trend index and the put ladder. Over 2000-2024 it compounded at 8.9% a year against 7.8% for the index, and its worst drawdown of the twenty-five years was -33%, in the dot-com bust, against -55% for the index, in the Global Financial Crisis. The two hedges worked in different crises: the ladder alone cut the Global Financial Crisis drawdown to -37%, while in the slow dot-com decline and in 2022 trend following carried the load. The price was a decade of underperformance after 2009, and the evidence rests on a handful of crises.

title: Toward a Unified Theory of Real Estate Pricing: Why Price Dynamics Need Fundamental Value
affiliations: Ross School of Business, University of Michigan

detail.title: Toward a Unified Theory of Real Estate Pricing: Why Price Dynamics Need Fundamental Value

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Author is also affilated with University Financial Associates LLC and supports the author's research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No patients were involved in this study.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding supported this research.

detail.abstract: Models of real estate price dynamics share a common structure. Prices carry recent changes forward and revert toward a fundamental value. Yet these models rarely say what that fundamental value is. They treat it as a statistical trend or estimate it from a few metropolitan aggregates. This paper argues that urban economics already supplies the missing anchor. Spatial equilibrium models explain why locations earn different rents. Growth models show that fundamental value includes the capitalized value of expected rent growth. Real-options models of irreversible development show that it also includes the value of waiting, and they explain why supply responds with a lag. Aggregating heterogeneous development options yields local supply elasticity, which in turn shapes the momentum and mean-reversion parameters of dynamic models. Quality-adjusted rent-price ratios provide an imperfect but disciplined way to observe the anchor. The synthesis clarifies what "overshooting" means, corrects a common intuition about when overshooting occurs, and yields testable predictions about how supply conditions affect the amplitude and duration of real estate cycles.

title: Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting and Risk-Window Identification in the Shandong Electricity Market Using a VMD–Transformer–Kalman Framework

detail.title: Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting and Risk-Window Identification in the Shandong Electricity Market Using a VMD–Transformer–Kalman Framework
detail.abstract: Day-ahead electricity prices in the Shandong electricity spot market are highly nonstationary and volatile due to renewable generation, load variation, supply–demand conditions, and trading behavior. To reduce forecasting lag, excessive smoothing, and poor tracking of extreme prices, this study proposes a VMD–Transformer–Kalman framework. Variational mode decomposition extracts multi-scale price components, the Transformer learns longrange dependencies among historical prices, system operation variables, and temporal features, and horizonspecific Kalman filters dynamically correct forecast residuals. Experiments on Shandong day-ahead market data show that the proposed model achieves an MAE of 68.339 CNY/MWh, an RMSE of 95.404 CNY/MWh, and an R²of 0.701. It yields the lowest MAE among all benchmark models, while its RMSE and R²are close to the best results. Ablation and scenario analyses confirm its effectiveness under high-price, sharp hourly fluctuation, and frequent direction-reversal conditions. The risk-window priority identification rates for high-price and highvolatility risks reach 0.624 and 0.445, respectively. The framework therefore combines accurate forecasting with effective high-risk window identification for electricity market risk monitoring and early warning.
