detail.abstract: Industrial maintenance must hold enough replacement parts to restore critical equipment without committing excessive capital to slow-moving inventory. Historical issues of intermittent demand make conventional point forecasts unreliable for many items; equipment age, maintenance plans and condition signals can also change requirements within a replenishment lead time. This conceptual paper develops a decision-support framework connecting these signals to inventory policy. A focused synthesis of peer-reviewed research on intermittentdemand forecasting, installed-base information, condition-based maintenance, probabilistic inventory control and spare-parts sourcing informs six stages: data reconciliation, item segmentation, condition-informed demand distribution, lead-time risk assessment, constrained policy selection and monitored feedback. A two-part forecast distinguishes scheduled interventions from stochastic failures, while the inventory decision explicitly accounts for on-hand and pipeline stock, repair returns, service criticality, obsolescence and supplier uncertainty. The paper compares classical estimators, machine learning and maintenance-informed forecasting without assuming that lower point error implies better service or cost. Three tables define data requirements, modelling choices and decision controls. Two figures reproduced from separate open-access peer-reviewed papers illustrate an observed spare-parts demand classification and a published dual-sourcing cost trade-off. Their numerical results belong to those studies and do not validate the proposed framework. The contribution is an auditable connection between predicted demand distributions and replenishment decisions for industrial maintenance. Prospective evaluation should test lead-time forecast calibration, equipment availability, stockouts, total cost and decision workload against existing inventory practice. No original dataset, simulation, field deployment or performance improvement is claimed.

title: Detecting and Mitigating Bias in Transportation Recommendation Algorithms
affiliations: TUM School of Management,Technical University of Munich

detail.title: Detecting and Mitigating Bias in Transportation Recommendation Algorithms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests relevant to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific external funding and was supported solely by the author's institutional resources.

detail.abstract: As intelligent transportation systems increasingly rely on algorithmic decision-making, recommendation algorithms have become central to how users navigate urban mobilitysuggesting routes, modes of transport, departure times, and ride-sharing matches. However, growing evidence indicates that these systems can encode and amplify biases that disadvantage already marginalized communities, including low-income neighborhoods, racial and ethnic minorities, people with disabilities, and areas with limited transit infrastructure. This study investigates the sources, manifestations, and consequences of bias in transportation recommendation algorithms, with particular attention to how training data, optimization objectives, and feature engineering contribute to inequitable outcomes. Drawing on a mixedmethods approach that combines algorithmic auditing, fairness metrics, and stakeholder interviews with transit agencies and community organizations, the research identifies key bias mechanisms across route selection, mode prioritization, and dynamic pricing systems. It then develops and evaluates a suite of mitigation strategies, including fairness-aware re-ranking, multi-objective optimization, and community-informed data collection practices. Findings aim to provide actionable guidance for transportation planners, algorithm designers, and policymakers seeking to build recommendation systems that promote equitable access to mobility. By bridging fairness research in machine learning with the practical realities of urban transportation, this work contributes both a conceptual framework and empirical tools for detecting and mitigating bias in mobility recommendation systems.

title: Promotion Frontiers and Overtime Earnings Evidence from an NYPD Sergeant Examination

detail.abstract: Promotion changes an employee's rank and potentially the opportunities through which that employee earns pay. I link the public roster for the 2022 New York City Police Department (NYPD) sergeant examination to city payroll records and trace an observed title frontier over time: the largest adjacent-score jump in sergeant titles appears at 87/88 in FY2024 and 85/86 in FY2025. At the latter frontier, 94.7% of linked candidates scoring 86 held a sergeant title by FY2025 year-end, compared with 5.1% scoring 85. Among 327 candidates observed in FY2022, FY2024 and FY2025, the 86-minus-85 difference in FY2024-to-FY2025 changes is-$7,424 in annual overtime pay and-81 in reported overtime hours, even as the higher-score group's yearend salary rate rises more. Earlier overtime-pay changes are much smaller. A stricter namelinkage rule attenuates the overtime-dollar contrast to-$4,092, with an individual-level interval including zero. The paper documents how pay composition changes near a moving observed frontier and uses prior outcomes, neighboring scores and linkage diagnostics to assess this conditional reduced-form pattern.

title: Using Data-Driven Operations and Project Management to Improve Service Capacity in U.S. Behavioral Health Organization

detail.title: Using Data-Driven Operations and Project Management to Improve Service Capacity in U.S. Behavioral Health Organization

detail.abstract: Behavioral-health service capacity is a multidimensional organizational problem involving workforce availability, service breadth, utilization, operational access, scheduling, and the ability to convert available resources into completed services. This study develops an integrated data-driven operations and project-management framework for identifying capacity constraints and translating analytical findings into structured improvement initiatives in U.S. behavioral-health organizations. The empirical foundation is the 2024 National Substance Use and Mental Health Services Survey (N-SUMHSS), which provides national facility-level information on organizational characteristics, service configuration, and treatment operations. The manuscript combines verified national descriptive evidence with an analytical design specifying descriptive statistics, association analysis, multivariable regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting/XGBoost, feature-importance analysis, and sensitivity analysis where the released data support those procedures. The verified 2024 evidence includes 21,205 eligible facilities and a 90.4% overall response rate, with substantial outpatient orientation and variation in service and medication configuration. Because the supplied research materials do not include the underlying facility-level public-use file, facility-level coefficients, predictive metrics, feature rankings, and geographic estimates are not fabricated. Instead, the paper distinguishes observed national evidence from analyses that require direct PUF processing and provides a complete operational framework for that next analytical stage. The resulting contribution is a decision architecture linking operational data, analytics, bottleneck diagnosis, project management, intervention, and performance monitoring.

title: Stochastic and Distributionally Robust Aircraft Routing at a Hub-and-Spoke Carrier
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Institute of Operations Research and Analytics, Beijing Jiaotong University and NUS Business School - Department of Decision Sciences

detail.title: Stochastic and Distributionally Robust Aircraft Routing at a Hub-and-Spoke Carrier

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research is supported from the National Research Foundation, Singapore, and A*STAR under the RIE2020 Industry Alignment Fund – Industry Collaboration Projects (IAF-ICP) grant call [Grant No. I2001E0059].

detail.abstract: Airlines face a persistent tension between fleet utilization and resilience: tighter schedules improve productivity but leave little slack to absorb disruptions, causing delays to cascade. Once the schedule is published, aircraft routing is the airline's only remaining lever to embed resilience without altering customer-facing commitments. This paper develops a distributionally robust routing method requiring only three summary statistics per flight: mean, mean absolute deviation, and observed range, all estimable from two years of operational data and stable across seasonal and post-pandemic shifts in delay patterns. Three-point worst-case distributions enable exact route-cost evaluation through sparse-atom dynamic programming embedded in a branch-and-price algorithm that also supports expectation-based routing. The resulting algorithm obtains an exact solution to the largest five-day benchmark (284 flights) within one hour. We evaluate the method on 25 benchmark instances constructed from over 24 months of operational data from an anonymized full-service hub-and-spoke carrier, using Monte Carlo simulation. Results on the focal three-day full-fleet instance show that robust routing reduces expected delay cost by 2.75% relative to actual airline practice. The method also lowers maximum simulated arrival-delay cost by 44% relative to the deterministic benchmark. These gains arise from concentrating existing ground time in long buffers after delay-prone flights, thereby limiting downstream propagation. Additional experiments indicate that robust routing's advantage over expectationbased routing grows under distributional shifts and when maintenance constraints are incorporated.

title: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Dynamic Ridesharing Matching
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Boston and Indian Institute of Technology, Kanpur

detail.title: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Dynamic Ridesharing Matching

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests relevant to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific external funding and was supported solely by the author's institutional resources.

detail.abstract: Dynamic ridesharing has emerged as a transformative paradigm in urban mobility, offering the potential to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and improve vehicle utilization by connecting riders with drivers in real time. However, the matching of riders to drivers in dynamic, uncertain environments remains a formidable computational and strategic challenge. Traditional approaches, including greedy assignment and centralized optimization, struggle to adapt to rapidly fluctuating demand patterns and often fail to account for the long-term consequences of immediate matching decisions. This study proposes a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework for dynamic ridesharing matching that models drivers, riders, and the platform as interacting learning agents within a shared stochastic environment. The framework employs a centralized training with decentralized execution paradigm, enabling coordinated policy learning while preserving the capacity for real-time, distributed decision-making at the vehicle level. A graph attention network architecture encodes the dynamic spatial relationships among vehicles and requests, capturing the topological structure of the urban road network. A multi-objective reward structure balances platform efficiency, rider wait times, driver earnings, and spatial equity of service distribution. The proposed framework is evaluated against established baselines, including greedy matching, bipartite matching, and single-agent deep reinforcement learning, using large-scale real-world datasets from ride-hailing operations in Haikou, Chengdu, and New York City. Experimental results demonstrate that the MARL framework achieves substantial improvements in service rate, reductions in passenger waiting times, and more equitable distribution of driver earnings compared to centralized and myopic baselines. The framework maintains computational feasibility for real-time deployment at scale, processing matching decisions within sub-second intervals even for fleets of thousands of vehicles. The study contributes a scalable, adaptive, and fairness-aware approach to ridesharing matching and offers theoretical insights into the design of multi-agent systems for transportation applications.

title: Prices that Never Existed: A Universe-scale Measurement of Phantom-print Contamination in Equity Backtests

detail.title: Prices that Never Existed: A Universe-scale Measurement of Phantom-print Contamination in Equity Backtests

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The concept for this paper originated from Chris Bartlett at Algoseek, who also participated in reviewing this work prior to submission.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses only licensed US equity consolidated-tape trade data and CME futures data; it does not involve human participants or patient data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded in kind by Algoseek, which provided the licensed US equity tape data and compute resources used in the analysis.

detail.abstract: A printed trade reports that a transaction happened, not that an order could have traded there: odd lots, off-exchange prints, and condition-coded trades are unreachable by a marketable order or excluded from the official high, low, and last. A bar built from all prints therefore sits above the executable high and below the executable low, so every stop, target, and breakout is scored against prices that never existed. From one trades feed we build naive and executable bars by print-time condition codes, across the US equity top-1000 (2007-2026, 1.46 billion regular-hours bars); three results follow. First, 42.3% of bars carry a phantom-affected extreme, rising to 90% by 2026, led by odd-lot prints (76% of the range inflation). Second, the headline is selection fidelity, not profit: across 7,232 strategies in an edge-free universe, in-sample selection on executable bars predicts the executable out-of-sample ranking better than on naive bars (rank-IC 0.9987 versus 0.9948; gap +0.0039, p < 0.001 under an effective-N cluster bootstrap). Third, a CME futures negative control near zero and the 2013 odd-lot-tape-onset natural experiment isolate the effect to equity microstructure. A formal companion traces the mechanism partly to persistence, so a strategy can pass naive validation in and out of sample yet die on execution (the deployment trap); a known-answer planted-drift experiment on a 60-name panel finds the clean-selected book higher at every tested drift strength, consistent with a deployment flip it suggests rather than directly observes. The claim is one-sided: cleaning restores selection fidelity rather than manufacturing an edge.

title: The Intervening Role of Purpose-Driven Culture in Translating Meaningful Work into Employee Engagement: Evidence from India's Knowledge-Intensive Sector

detail.title: The Intervening Role of Purpose-Driven Culture in Translating Meaningful Work into Employee Engagement: Evidence from India's Knowledge-Intensive Sector

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research is no funded by university or external organisation.

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study examines how purpose and meaning at work influence employee engagement in collectivist, knowledge-intensive workplaces, with a focus on the mediating role of purpose-driven culture. While prior research has highlighted individual value alignment and intrinsic motivation, limited attention has been given to how organisational cultures embed purpose and meaning to sustain engagement. Addressing this gap, the study investigates Gen Z and Millennial IT professionals in India's knowledge-intensive sector, contributing to broader debates on age-diverse engagement and organisational effectiveness in emerging economy contexts. Design: A quantitative cross-sectional design was employed using three validated scales to measure purpose and meaning at work, purpose-driven culture, and employee engagement. Data were collected from 304 Gen Z and Millennial IT professionals in Bengaluru, India, through convenience and snowball sampling. Partial Least Squares-Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was applied to test the hypothesised relationships, with mediation analysis conducted via the PROCESS macro in SPSS. Findings: All four hypotheses were supported. Purpose and meaning at work are positively associated with both employee engagement (H1: β = 0.881, p < 0.05) and perceptions of a purpose-driven culture (H2: β = 0.921, p < 0.05). Purpose-driven culture significantly predicts engagement (H3: β = 0.843, p < 0.05) and mediates the purpose-engagement relationship (H4), with 67.6% of the total effect operating through this cultural pathway. The findings highlight that purpose-driven culture functions as a critical amplifier of individual meaning-seeking, translating personal purpose into discretionary effort, resilience, and sustained organisational commitment. Originality: This study makes three contributions. First, it extends self-determination theory by positioning purpose-driven culture as a collective, organisationally embedded pathway to engagement, beyond the three classic psychological needs. Second, it reframes purpose and meaning as a doubleedged construct-a powerful engagement driver when culturally embedded, but a source of cynicism and disengagement when misaligned. Third, it challenges Western-centric engagement models by demonstrating that collectivist cultural orientations in emerging economies such as India amplify the purpose-engagement relationship, offering a culturally sensitive framework for people management in multigenerational, knowledge-intensive workforces.

detail.abstract:
Problem definition: Large language models can translate business descriptions into optimization models, but executable code may misrepresent constraints or objectives. A solver can then return an optimal solution to the wrong problem. Even when the solution satisfies the intended operating rules, a better plan may exist. For organizations that repeatedly use optimization modeling, an LLM-based framework should produce accurate formulations at low cost and, ideally, run locally. We study how to verify improvements and allocate attempts across LLMs that differ in price and capability.

Methodology/results: We develop OSCAR (Optimization modeling by Simulator, Coder, And Reviewer), which uses an offline Simulator certified against labeled decision examples to compare candidates and continues searching beyond feasibility. We model the search for the next certified improvement as sequential decisions under unobserved difficulty: which LLMs to call and when to stop. In a simplified known-prior setting, we give conditions under which cost-ordered escalation is optimal. For general menus, we derive a prior-free competitive guarantee. On five benchmark problems, OSCAR achieves 95% to 100% accuracy at the reported settings using two small open-weight LLMs, each deployable locally on a single GPU. Their single-attempt accuracies average 29% and 48%. In five runs per problem, Codex and Claude Code incur average token costs 3.1 and 5.8 times OSCAR’s, respectively.

Managerial implications: Before upgrading to frontier models for optimization modeling, firms should assess what available models can achieve through verification and iterative improvement. OSCAR supports open-weight models locally or in the cloud, depending on budget and confidentiality requirements. Firms should maintain labeled decision examples of feasible and infeasible decisions to clarify plain-language operating rules. OSCAR follows these labels when an LLM’s interpretation conflicts with them. As LLM capabilities and prices change, OSCAR’s simple operating rules and adjustable settings help firms adapt their model choices and benefit from these advances.

declarations.funderStatement: Funding for this research was provided in part by Harvard Business School.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Harvard Business School Working Paper No. 27-029

detail.abstract: Are public equity valuations, which aggregate information across market participants, more informative than private equity valuations reflecting a single general partner’s judgment? We test how well a holding’s interim performance, which embeds its valuation, predicts realized exit performance. Using holdings-level MSCI data on 2,727 buyouts across 1998–2016 vintages, benchmarked against cash-flow-matched levered public equity investments, we find that public prices are no more informative than GP marks. A model in which markets aggregate information better but tend to overreact, while GPs smooth their marks, explains this result. The data support its predictions: public returns mean-revert while private returns persist.

title: The Architecture of Systemic Sovereignty  From the Ontology of Dead Capital to Managerial and Cognitive Singularity

detail.abstract:
This transdisciplinary paper cross-examines institutional economics, neuro-ergonomics, and corporate primatology to model a unified framework for systemic emancipation: The Destin Doctrine. The research diagnoses the systemic persistence of "Dead Capital" within post-colonial economies, demonstrating how asymmetric legal frameworks—specifically the unanimity requirement in civil joint possession—act as a structural "bad barrel." This legal architecture weaponizes historical grievances, trapping assets in a zero-sum game of structural paralysis and resentment.

To break this deadlock, the paper introduces a radical paradigm shift: extracting physical assets from the emotional volatility of Civil Law into the mathematical pragmatism of Corporate Law. This is executed through Insular Land Securitization (TFI) and the deployment of the DACH corporate model. By sequestering paralyzed land within Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs), the framework enforces "Cold Governance"—a fiduciary structure where operational control is completely insulated from shareholder emotion. This renders the land liquid, bankable, and antifragile, perfectly securing Foreign Direct Investments (FDI) against local legal uncertainties.

Transitioning from the institutional ecosystem to human capital, the research exposes the metrological obsolescence of standard psychometric tools (WISC/WAIS). Designed for linear compliance, these tools inflict "sequential violence" on neuro-atypical profiles, specifically Very High Intellectual Potential (VHIP) coupled with Dyslexia. Because VHIP brains operate via top-down, parallel matrix processing, forcing them through linear, sequential bottlenecks generates massive metabolic exhaustion and chronic over-adaptation.

As a structural antidote, the paper advocates for technological secession via the integration of Artificial Intelligence as a digital "Exocortex." This synthetic layer absorbs the friction of linear execution. Furthermore, the framework introduces "Legacy AI" (IA Héritage) as an immortal, transgenerational fiduciary, programmed to ensure the frictionless transmission of the founder's logical laws and immunize the corporate structure against future human irrationality.

Ultimately, by deploying Cold Governance to neutralize institutional friction, and the Exocortex to bypass biological limitations, the architecture elevates the operator to the status of a "Disembodied Architect," achieving ultimate systemic sovereignty.

title: Compute, Power, and Sovereignty: The Political Economy of AI Critical Infrastructure

detail.abstract:
This report examines how the United States allocates the costs, risks, and control of AI compute paired with dedicated electricity generation. It organizes the inquiry around three bargains: developers and utilities, developers and host governments, and private infrastructure providers and the federal security state. Across these bargains, it asks who pays, who controls, who decides, and who can inspect the terms.

The report argues that demand risk is a central mechanism connecting these questions: who bears the cost when expected electricity demand fails to arrive, falls short, or leaves before the supporting assets are paid off. Through regulatory proceedings, contracts, corporate disclosures, fiscal evaluations, and security instruments, it examines how minimum payments, exit charges, collateral, guarantees, and disclosure rules allocate that risk. It distinguishes electricity-price effects from cross-subsidies and public commitments from enforceable obligations.

The report proposes nine measures for existing institutions, including public contract terms, stronger financial protections, conditional tax incentives, and published criteria for federal security claims. Its focus is the United States, with Ireland and Singapore as comparators. It states the evidence that would weaken its conclusions and the limits of its public record.

title: Evaluation of Business Models for Thermal Energy Export from Supermarkets
affiliations: KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Royal Institute of Technology (KTH) and Royal Institute of Technology (KTH)

detail.title: Evaluation of Business Models for Thermal Energy Export from Supermarkets
detail.abstract: CO2 refrigeration systems in supermarkets offer the possibility to efficiently recover heat and produce air conditioning. However, empirical evidence suggests the technical potential is far from fulfilled, following the influence of a wide range of barriers, such as lack of capital, split economic incentives, and missing established business models. This work proposes four business models for thermal energy export from supermarkets. The business models are: Sell-and-Buyback, Self-Sufficiency and Export, Shared Geothermal, and Energy-as-a-Service (EaaS). The Sell-and-Buyback business model is recommended for gross lease structures and yields economic savings of 6400 AC/y for the supermarket and 2300 AC/y for the property owner, corresponding to 36 % and 9 % of annual energy costs (AEC), respectively. Self-Sufficiency and Export is recommended for net lease structures, and the results indicate that self-sufficiency alone generates the most significant savings of 14 000 AC/y or 49 % of the supermarket’s AEC. The Shared Geothermal business model, with ground source heat pump for the building and borehole subcooling for the supermarket, is a natural win-win configuration and it yields modest economic savings for both parties. Finally, the Energy-as-a-Service business model yields a profit of 37 000 AC/y for the energy service company, while offering 10 % savings in AEC to both supermarket and property owner. In summary, the proposed business models indicate that profitable agreements can be found for thermal energy export from supermarkets, but they need to be compatible with existing lease structures and technical systems.

title: Before You Swap the Feed: Characterizing What a Legacy Calculation's Inputs Mean

detail.title: Before You Swap the Feed: Characterizing What a Legacy Calculation's Inputs Mean

detail.abstract:
Calculation code in long-lived investment-operations systems can outlive the data feeds it consumes. When an upstream feed or vendor interface is replaced, the new source's specification says what the new data should be, not what the existing code did with the old data. A field can keep its name, type, and layout while its meaning changes, and every load check will pass. This article treats field meaning as an ordinary engineering artifact: meaning notes typed on explicit conventions and kept in version control, characterization tests for behavior that exists only in running code, and dry runs designed so that a typed meaning predicts an exact difference. In a synthetic example, a position field moves from trade-date to settlement-date basis, and a difference that looks like timing turns out to be a change of meaning. The article combines these practices and states their limits.

AI disclosure: The method described here, its conventions and its conclusions come from the author's professional work and earlier notes. The author used Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, to draft and revise the text of all sections from those notes, to propose and build the synthetic worked example and its figures, which the author reviewed, and to find references and check them against their primary sources. The author reviewed and edited all content and is responsible for it.

title: Silicon Cartels: Detector Orientation in Multi-Agent Pricing Testbeds

detail.title: Silicon Cartels: Detector Orientation in Multi-Agent Pricing Testbeds

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Detectors of coordinated behavior are calibrated against a control condition, and in multi-agent testbeds that control is synthetic. A control carrying less variation than the deployment environment reverses the sign of a detector rather than reducing its power: separation stays intact while the ranking runs backwards, so orientation-free summaries report success. Of 313 near-perfect separations across 440 detector cells, 103 point backwards. We derive in closed form the critical control volatility at which a coefficient-of-variation screen changes sign, give the exact counterpart for the standard deviation, and show that no such threshold transfers to quantile-based dispersion. On 280 tabular Q-learning runs carrying no language model, the measured crossing falls inside a band declared in advance and survives cross-fitting. Language-model agents price the coordinated arm below the competitive one, reversing the classmean ordering the condition assumes, so its threshold does not transfer to them at all. Separation and orientation must therefore be reported apart, and a screen checked against its control before it is credited with power.

title: Behavioral Institutionalism of the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Economy: The A2A Institutional Dynamics Standard (A2A-IDS)

detail.title: Behavioral Institutionalism of the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Economy: The A2A Institutional Dynamics Standard (A2A-IDS)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol specification v1.0.1 (Google, 2025; Linux Foundation) establishes syntactic interoperability across heterogeneous software agents via standardized discovery manifests (/.wellknown/agent-card.json), JSON-RPC 2.0 message framing (message/send, message/stream), and a deterministic Task lifecycle (SUBMITTED → WORKING → COMPLETED / FAILED / INPUT_REQUIRED / CANCELED). Concurrently, the Model Context Protocol (MCP; Anthropic, 2024) standardizes agent perception filters through structured tool, prompt, and resource binding. However, syntactic conformance provides no instrument for assessing multi-agent institutional resilience, service-level veracity, or cascading fragility. This study formulates and substantiates the A2A Institutional Dynamics Standard (A2A-IDS). We project seven behavioral primitives onto protocol telemetry, formalize the A2A hub as an active informational field characterized by four physical parameters, and define Institutional Anomie () as the Total Variation Distance between declared AgentCard capabilities and empirical log-derived execution clusters. We demonstrate that sustained anomie () triggers cascading orchestration failures, validate econometric stationarity testing (ADF/KPSS) to distinguish true digital institutions from stochastic drifts, and apply Markov-chain spectral gap analysis () to quantify convergence boundaries. The standard establishes automated governance response rules and backwards-compatible JSON Schema extensions to secure federated agent economies.

title: Capacity Planning in Food Delivery with Autonomous Vehicles: The Role of Delivery Time Guarantee
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management, University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management, University of Texas at Dallas - Department of Information Systems & Operations Management and University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management

detail.title: Capacity Planning in Food Delivery with Autonomous Vehicles: The Role of Delivery Time Guarantee

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: No one

detail.abstract: Food-delivery platforms traditionally rely on crowdsourced human-driven vehicles (HVs), but leased autonomous delivery vehicles (ADVs) are emerging as an alternative. A major challenge for such platforms is keeping costs low while meeting tight delivery time commitments. We address this challenge by analyzing how to optimally manage HV and ADV fleets and whether a hybrid fleet benefits the platform. We develop two optimization models: Pure HV (using only HVs), and Hybrid (using both HVs and ADVs). The hybrid model enforces delivery time constraints separately for HVs and ADVs, preventing the optimal hybrid solution from being trivially superior to the pure-optimal solutions. First, in the pure HV setting, we determine optimal capacity levels (number of HVs) and compensation rates to HVs (impacting their availability). Building on these solutions, we then study the hybrid setting: we first establish feasibility conditions jointly on HV and ADV pool sizes, the minimum achievable delivery time guarantee, and the feasible range of demand allocated to ADVs, and subsequently characterize HV and ADV capacity levels and compensation rates. By comparing the three optimal solutions, we identify when the hybrid setting is optimal and estimate resulting cost savings through a calibrated numerical study. The numerical study uncovers the cost advantage of the optimal hybrid strategy, while also revealing that the benefits of autonomy depend critically on operational decisions and demand variability rather than technological improvements alone. This study offers food-delivery platforms a roadmap to optimize fleet composition, reduce costs, and allocate demand between HVs and ADVs. It highlights the value of a hybrid fleet, demonstrating that even with cost-effective ADVs, human drivers remain essential by providing efficiency and operational flexibility.

title: The Enterprise Coherence Governance System (ECGS): A Governance System for Diagnosing, Measuring, and Governing Enterprise Coherence

detail.title: The Enterprise Coherence Governance System (ECGS): A Governance System for Diagnosing, Measuring, and Governing Enterprise Coherence

detail.abstract: The predominant challenge organizations face is not inadequate capability, but rather inconsistency in strategy, governance, operating model, culture and behavior, and external work (including partnerships). Common governance and management frameworks and standards assume consistency in these elements. This paper presents the Enterprise Coherence Governance System (ECGS), which provides organizations the means to systematically diagnose, assess, and manage enterprise coherence. ECGS employs a hierarchical structure and a graphical representation, known as the Coherence Tree. Within the Coherence Tree, there are four levels consisting of thirty domains and four hundred elements, spanning the four pillars of the system. ECGS prescribes a governance framework to address misalignment within an organization. This includes a Governance Operating Manual, a Range and Actual architecture of decision-making, and standard reporting and evidence. If ECGS identifies misalignment within the organization, it prescribes remedial actions to address the gaps. ECGS is described and analysed in relation to other governance systems and frameworks. This includes the recent G20/OECD Principles of Corporate Governance, the International Standard on All Forms of Corporate Governance (ISO 37000), the UK Corporate Governance Code, and the IFC Corporate Governance Framework. The paper concludes with possible ways the ECGS may be used and its limitations. Further, the authors outline possible means to substantiate claims made in the ECGS.

title: Inflation Targeting, Monetary Policy Surprises, and Capital Misallocation
affiliations: CAFRAL, Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research (IGIDR) and Centre for Advanced Financial Research and Learning

detail.title: Inflation Targeting, Monetary Policy Surprises, and Capital Misallocation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: There was no external funding for this research.

detail.abstract: We examine whether a more predictable monetary policy framework improves the allocation of capital across firms. Using firm-level data from the Indian manufacturing sector for 2005-2024, we study this in the context of India's adoption of flexible inflation targeting (FIT) in 2015. We find that firms with high pre-FIT average revenue per unit of capital (ARPK) subsequently accumulate more capital and experience a relative decline in ARPK, consistent with capital being reallocated toward previously under-capitalized firms. Event-study estimates show that these changes emerge after the reform. To further examine the role of monetary policy predictability in capital allocation, we use high-frequency measures of monetary policy surprises. We document a decline in the volatility of these surprises following FIT and show that larger surprises are associated with higher ARPK and lower capital accumulation, particularly among firms with high ex-ante ARPK. Together, these findings are consistent with greater monetary policy predictability contributing to improved capital allocation following FIT.

title: Unpacking the Role of Organizational Actorhood in Interorganizational Trust: A Reply to “Looking Behind the Continuum: An Institutional Economics Perspective on Schilke and Lumineau’s ‘How Organizational is Interorganizational Trust?'”
affiliations: University of Arizona and HKU Business School, The University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Unpacking the Role of Organizational Actorhood in Interorganizational Trust: A Reply to “Looking Behind the Continuum: An Institutional Economics Perspective on Schilke and Lumineau’s ‘How Organizational is Interorganizational Trust?'”

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: Research support was provided by a National Science Foundation CAREER Award (1943688) granted to the first author.

detail.abstract: This reply engages Schultz, Valentinov, and Pies’s commentary on our article on interorganizational trust, clarifying two central issues. First, we challenge the assumption that higher organizational actorhood necessarily makes organizations superior trustors or trustees. Instead, we argue that the relative trust accuracy of organizations and individuals is contingent on factors such as environmental dynamism, exchange history, relationship typicality, boundary-spanner expertise, organizational stability, and relationship scope. Second, we contest the view that organizational trust is reducible to individual-level trust and distrust. We conceptualize organizational trust as an emergent phenomenon shaped by both bottom-up individual dynamics and top-down organizational influences, calling for more nuanced multilevel research.

detail.abstract: Total Rewards (TR) is a substantial organizational investment, yet empirical research remains fragmented. Practitioners have designed integrated systems under real-world constraints. This study compares academic evidence with practitioner priorities across the WorldatWork framework to develop an evidence-informed Total Rewards Alignment Model. A sequential mixed-methods design combined a scoping review of 78 studies (Web of Science, Scopus; 2022-2026), coded by TR element, context, and outcomes, with a survey of 241 HR and TR practitioners across 19 countries assessing implementation, effectiveness, future importance, evidence sources, and barriers. The mapping identified 387 experience-and performance-related factors, 259 classified as TR elements; Compensation was most studied, followed by Well-being, Careers, Benefits, and Recognition. Research and practice converged on Compensation and Careers; Benefits showed the largest gap: offered by 92.9% of organizations, rated effective by 68.0% of practitioners, yet coded in only 17.4% of occurrences. Well-being led future priorities (81.7%), only eight studies covered all five elements, and 31.5% of practitioners consulted research. Academic attention diverges from operational use, perceived value, and practitioner priorities. The model integrates literature evidence, practitioner knowledge, co-designed priorities, employee outcomes, and business indicators. This is among the first systematic efforts to map TR research against a practitioner reference model and test the results directly with reward professionals across countries, giving HR leaders an evidence-coverage map for TR program-design decisions. Future research should evaluate complete TR configurations against productivity, quality, costs, and organizational performance.

title: Responsible Leadership for Societal-Scale AI: A Human-Centered Socio-Technical Approach to Ethical AI Deployment in Healthcare

detail.title: Responsible Leadership for Societal-Scale AI: A Human-Centered Socio-Technical Approach to Ethical AI Deployment in Healthcare

declarations.declarationOfInterest: As DBA student at Golden Gate University this is my doctoral research underway.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Golden Gate University ethics committee has given IRB approval.

detail.abstract: Healthcare organizations are deploying artificial intelligence at societal scale across clinical decision support, diagnostics, operations, and population health yet an estimated 70-90% of digital health initiatives fail to deliver expected value (Topol, 2019). These failures are rarely purely technical. They reflect leadership that optimizes algorithms without jointly optimizing the human systems, trust, professional identity, ethical norms, and workforce wellbeing, on which responsible AI depends. In resource-constrained settings, frugal and societally accountable AI requires leaders who steward technology without sacrificing human-centered care. This research paper extends Socio-Technical Systems (STS) theory [31, 32] as a framework for responsible, humancentered AI deployment. STS holds that organizational effectiveness emerges only when social and technical subsystems are jointly optimized. The study examines leadership effectiveness in AI-integrated healthcare by operationalizing the social subsystem through ethical and adaptive leadership [34, 35] and the technical subsystem through digital leadership and AI technology acceptance [36, 37]. The purpose is to determine how leaders who balance technological advancement with human values enable responsible AI governance and improved outcomes. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design will be employed. The quantitative phase surveys approximately 150 healthcare leaders using structural equation modeling; the qualitative phase conducts semi-structured interviews with 12-15 leaders to interpret how joint optimization is enacted in practice. Expected contributions include a validated STS-based measurement model for AI-era leadership, a practical framework for responsible AI implementation under healthcare resource constraints, and evidence-based insights on balancing technological capability with human values. Societal impact is framed as safer patient care, more equitable algorithmic outcomes, and sustainable workforce conditions in AI-enabled health systems.

title: Structured Human-AI Interaction and Independent Cognitive Transfer  Research Propositions and a Testable Protocol for Cognitive Agency and Transfer

detail.title: Structured Human-AI Interaction and Independent Cognitive Transfer  Research Propositions and a Testable Protocol for Cognitive Agency and Transfer

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract: Human-AI research increasingly distinguishes between artificial intelligence that substitutes for human cognition and AI that scaffolds human cognition. However, assisted performance and human cognitive development are often treated as the same outcome. This paper develops a testable model of structured human-AI interaction in which independent cognitive transfer is the primary developmental criterion. The proposed OECIRR protocol requires six recurring operations: Originate, Encounter, Contest, Integrate, Reconstruct, and Re-enter. The model predicts that preserving human origination, deliberate epistemic challenge, human adjudication, AI-free reconstruction, and real-world re-entry will produce stronger unaided transfer than answer-oriented AI assistance with equivalent task exposure. The paper operationalizes the dependent variables as question quality, contradiction detection, epistemic calibration, alternative generation, integrative reasoning, independent reconstruction, relational transfer, and delayed persistence. It also specifies a four-condition preregisterable longitudinal experiment comparing no-AI practice, answer-oriented AI, unrestricted collaborative AI, and OECIRR-structured interaction. Contextual Indwelling is treated as a falsifiable transfer construct: repeated cognitive practices qualify as developmental only when they become increasingly observable in novel tasks after AI support is reduced or removed. The model therefore separates coupled performance from human development and provides explicit conditions under which the developmental claim should be weakened or rejected.

title: Beyond the J-Curve: Towards a Possible W-Curve in India's Manufacturing Productivity?: Total Factor Productivity Growth in Indian Organised Manufacturing, 1980-81 to 2023-24
affiliations: Confederation of Indian Industry, New Delhi and Independent researcher

detail.abstract:
India’s manufacturing productivity has remained modest and highly cyclical despite successive reforms, with RBI India KLEMS showing near-flat aggregate TFPG over 1980-81 to 2022-23 and Goldar (2024) documenting a sharper organised-manufacturing cycle that stagnated after 2008. This paper extends the ASI-based organised-manufacturing series through 2023-24 and constructs a gross-output aggregate-manufacturing TFPG series from RBI KLEMS industry data. The estimates identify an exceptional 2002-07 regime: organised-manufacturing TFPG rises from 0.05 per cent in 1980-2001 to 3.16 per cent, before falling to -0.02 per cent in 2008-23, with 2002 and 2008 emerging as statistically identified, endogenous regime centres confirmed by a 22 industry fixed-effects panel. Higher TFPG significantly helps explain subsequent manufacturing growth only in 2002-07, a relationship absent before 2002 or after 2008. Aggregate manufacturing shows a broadly similar J-then-possible-W cycle, though the aggregate-minus-organised productivity gap still shifts sharply, from +0.12 percentage point to -1.70 and then +0.75, turning the early-2000s organised-sector premium into a deficit. A comparable post-2008 slowdown in China confirms this was partly global, but India’s organised-sector reversal was markedly sharper than its own aggregate trend. With reforms continuing to deepen, the central policy question is how quickly they can translate into a second sustained productivity upswing, completing the TFPG cycle’s possible W-curve.

detail.abstract: Payments are not one system but many, each built by different operators with its own rules, network and economics. I argue that this multiplicity is a legacy of an exploratory phase: carrying an instruction no longer requires purpose-built infrastructure, leaving agreement as the scarce input. Where the interoperability literature asks how separate systems can communicate, I ask whether they need to remain separate at the coordination layer, and set out the Unified Financial Architecture, in which shared network technology, a common protocol and global governance replace the arrangements that separate payment systems today.

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence Driven Revenue Cycle Management for Reducing Claim Denials and Improving Hospital Financial Sustainability

The author has no personal or financial relationships with any organizations that could have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animals, or patient data. All data used in this research were obtained from publicly available datasets (BUSI - Breast Ultrasound Images Dataset). Therefore, no ethics approval was required.

detail.abstract: Clinically appropriate non-charge encounters are lost in hospitals when they are not charged or not provided due to the failure to meet the eligibility, authorization and documentation, coding and payer-policy criteria requirements. Artificial intelligence has the potential to transform revenue cycle management by not relying on backward work queues to optimize work but instead shift it to be prospective-focused and preventive in nature with the reported accuracy failing to create any financial value or the responsible use. This article evolves and establishes an evidence-based model to choose, justify and regulate artificial intelligence within the United States hospital revenue cycle. It summarizes peer reviewed literature, federal government directions, and industry facts; develops a mapping of denial mechanisms to data and interventions site; and offers a model of value linking model outputs tied to the avoided write-offs, recovered cash, lab work, and expenditure to collect. There are four illustrations of analytical concentrations denial, discrimination and calibration, financial sensitivity, and operating thresholds, which have to be analyzed. The main point is that workflow redesign and careful measurements, as opposed to independent claim determinations are the sources of sustainable value. Implementations that are of high value include regulations and interpretable machine learning, position doubtful cases with skilled personnel, maintain traceable evidence about its source and test the implementation prospectively, before production. The models that hospitals ought to consider are those that can be temporarily and payer-specifically validated, calibrated, and be accurate at their operational capacity, net benefit, allow subgroup error exploration, and track drift. Generative models can help with the summarizing of documents and writing of appeals, but the results have to be source-grounded and they must be approved by a person. It provides a phased implementation plan to get ready to the data, silently pass validation, deploy in a controlled manner, and undertake governance. This framework facilitates the reduction of denial and safeguard compliance, access to patients and financial viability. Figure estimates which are purely empirical are clearly illustrative, and ought to be substituted with institution specific estimates, prior to operational or investment decisions.

declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: Not applicable — this study is not a clinical trial and does not involve human participants or clinical intervention.

detail.abstract:
This paper documents and evaluates a convergence of regulatory, infrastructural, institutional, and machine-economy developments observed between mid-2025 and the third quarter of 2026, assessing the extent to which they are directionally consistent with the Network-Based Monetary Theory (NBMT) model introduced in Papers I–IV of this series.
Between mid-2025 and the third quarter of 2026, multiple independent jurisdictions enacted or advanced digital asset regulatory frameworks; major financial market infrastructure operators initiated tokenized asset settlement at production scale; central banks — including the European Central Bank and the Bank for International Settlements — began operational integration of tokenized settlement layers; and autonomous AI agents began executing financial transactions without human authorization. Each development is documented with primary sources, interpreted through NBMT's theoretical variables (V_s, ρ_v, α_e, σ_r, R_ext), and evaluated against the model's five falsifiable hypotheses (H1–H5).
The paper finds that the observed developments are directionally consistent with NBMT's predictions regarding regulatory convergence (H1, H3), infrastructure transformation (H2, H5), and the emergence of a machine economy layer (H4). Individually, none of these developments constitutes proof of NBMT's model. Collectively, they represent the earliest observable phase of the infrastructure convergence the model anticipated — with the 2035 horizon reaffirmed not as a forecast date but as a research horizon by which the digital monetary and settlement infrastructure may be sufficiently mature to empirically test whether network-based monetary variables have become economically operative at scale.

title: Humanitarian Protection is not Immigration Selection: Why the United States needs both

detail.title: Humanitarian Protection is not Immigration Selection: Why the United States needs both

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Amerpass Foundation and has a professional interest in immigration policy. The Foundation did not influence the research design, analysis, interpretation, or conclusions. The author declares no financial conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because the study is based exclusively on publicly available legal materials, administrative statistics, and published research. It involved no human participants, interviews, confidential case records, or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Humanitarian protection and employment-based immigration address different public questions. Protection examines whether a person meets a legal standard related to persecution. Employment-based selection examines eligibility under categories that recognize qualifications, work, investment, or other designated activities. A person may satisfy both standards, one, or neither. This article argues that confusing these functions produces two errors: making protection depend on expected economic usefulness, and treating a protection claim as a substitute for employment-based eligibility. The analysis combines a comparison of statutory purposes with descriptive evidence from United States immigration statistics and published research on refugee integration. Fiscal year 2023 records show the limits of reading admission categories as descriptions of people's abilities. Fiscal studies further show why estimates of contribution depend on the population counted, the period observed, and the level of government considered. Research on asylum processing illustrates how institutions can influence subsequent employment. These findings support distinct eligibility decisions alongside coordination in access to information, verification of relevant evidence, and integration services. The proposed approach preserves protection criteria, recognizes economic agency among people seeking safety, and permits professional qualifications to be evaluated through their appropriate legal channels. Its contribution is a practical account of how the two functions can coexist without allowing the success or failure of one application to predetermine the other. The article offers a framework for institutional design and evaluation, not a new estimate of immigration's overall economic effects.

detail.abstract:
Organizations frequently describe leadership and workforce problems as issues of communication, employee performance, hiring, workload, or executive effectiveness. Across operating engagements conducted through Marie Management between 2024 and 2026, these conditions repeatedly reflected a broader enterprise problem: organizational growth had exceeded the leadership, management, and workforce architecture originally built to support it. This practitioner-based portfolio case study examines leadership, management, and workforce interventions across organizations operating at different stages of development, revenue levels, staffing structures, and degrees of organizational complexity. 

The engagements included founder-led enterprises, professional-service organizations, healthcare operations, contracting businesses, and organizations preparing for substantial expansion. Recurring conditions included executive overfunctioning, undefined management authority, inadequate delegation infrastructure, reactive staffing, inconsistent performance accountability, insufficient management capacity, and organizational dependence on individual leaders. The operating interventions included executive role redesign, delegation systems, management structures, role and authority clarification, workforce-capacity planning, performance accountability, administrative infrastructure, staffing models, project-management capacity, and redistribution of organizational responsibility. 

The work repositioned leadership from the personal execution of organizational work toward direction, resource allocation, decision-making, accountability, and enterprise oversight. The evidence demonstrates that leadership and workforce architecture directly affected economic capacity. Organizations connected staffing and management capacity to revenue targets, project volume, contract execution, client capacity, overhead, and enterprise expansion. In one engagement, organizational restructuring supported an enterprise operating at approximately $13 million in annual revenue while preparing for increased project capacity. 

Across the portfolio, workforce and management interventions increased organizations' ability to distribute responsibility, coordinate additional work, reduce executive dependency, and build the human infrastructure required to support revenue-producing activity. The central finding is that leadership capacity is not demonstrated by how much responsibility an executive can personally carry. It is demonstrated by how much responsibility the organization can carry without requiring the executive to personally perform, coordinate, or control the work.

title: Relying More, Depending Less: Group Affiliation and Bank Financing among SMEs
affiliations: University of Limoges - Laboratoire d'Analyse et de Prospectives Économiques (LAPE)

detail.title: Relying More, Depending Less: Group Affiliation and Bank Financing among SMEs
detail.abstract: This paper examines how group affiliation affects SMEs' reliance on bank financing. We exploit firms' entry into a corporate group as a shock to credibility and access to internal funding sources using a staggered difference-indifferences framework with matched controls. We find that group affiliation increases SMEs' reliance on bank credit in their financing mix, while reducing their dependence on individual lenders as firms diversify their banking relationships. This effect operates through reputation transfer and reduced informational opacity, facilitating credit access and lowering borrowing costs. Overall, our findings highlight the credibility and transparency gains resulting from group affiliation and the enduring role of banks in SMEs' financing when alternative funding sources become available.

title: Expected Shortfall Changes under Common Heavy Tails Ordered Quantile Localization and Nonregular Comparison

detail.title: Expected Shortfall Changes under Common Heavy Tails Ordered Quantile Localization and Nonregular Comparison

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study consists of mathematical analysis and computational simulations and does not involve human participants, animal subjects, or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Common heavy-tailed shocks can cancel when portfolios are compared, but cancellation of losses does not by itself remove uncertainty from tail selection. We study differences in expected shortfall for losses with a common integrable factor and bounded idiosyncratic components. Ordering the positive factor loadings yields an exact representation of the complete optimized contrast on a coupled quantile strip. Its compensated kernels are bounded at the scale of the portfolio update at fixed positive loadings. Independent product localization provides quantile brackets and atom-valid slope bounds for finite-sample inference. We also characterize the firstorder effect of nonunique quantiles for equal factor loadings. An explicit distribution with infinite loss variance produces a non-Gaussian product-estimator limit inside a fixed secondorder tail envelope; a vanishing contamination preserves this limit despite unique positivedensity quantiles at every sample size. Exploratory computations expose invalid variance transfer and the conservative width of current certificates. The results separate cancellation, optimization regularity and useful risk certification.

title: Retail Market Inefficiencies in an Urban Economy: A Comparative Analysis of Pricing, Brand Premiums, and Price Dispersion Across Five Sectors in Moscow

detail.title: Retail Market Inefficiencies in an Urban Economy: A Comparative Analysis of Pricing, Brand Premiums, and Price Dispersion Across Five Sectors in Moscow

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is based entirely on publicly available retail pricing data and did not involve human participants or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or non-profit sector.

detail.abstract: This independent research project presents a comprehensive, empirical comparative pricing analysis conducted across five key consumer retail sectors in Moscow-essential medicines, petrol, staple groceries, commercial coffee drinks, and baby essentials-using data collected between May and June 2026. Utilizing a unified analytical framework encompassing cross-vendor data collection, statistical normalization, and economic interpretation, the study examines price formation mechanisms, brand-to-generic dynamics, and systemic market inefficiencies. The empirical findings reveal substantial price dispersion and limited price transparency across both essential and non-essential sectors. A systematic "brand premium" is observed across all categories, with branded options ranging from 1.4 times more expensive in the fuel market to an acute 5.35 times markup in pharmaceutical products. Furthermore, the data exposes significant market fragmentation and weak arbitrage: identical generic drugs and retail staples vary by 50% to 400% depending solely on the choice of vendor within the same municipality. The study also identifies notable retail strategies, such as bimodal pricing in the coffee industry and loss-leader strategies in pharmaceutical chains. Ultimately, this paper highlights significant consumer-side access asymmetries and discusses the efficacy of civic awareness campaigns and regulatory oversight, such as mandatory generic substitution policies, in mitigating retail market inefficiencies.

detail.title: Consumer-Firm Pareto Efficiency in Differentiated

detail.abstract: I study whether Bertrand-Nash equilibria in differentiated-product oligopoly are Pareto efficient with respect to consumer surplus and individual firm profits. In a single-product duopoly with gross substitutes, the equilibrium is consumer-firm Pareto efficient. With three or more firms, efficiency can fail. Under linear demand, a Pareto-improving price vector exists whenever one firm's markup is sufficiently large relative to its rivals' markups. When all markups lie below this threshold, the equilibrium is locally efficient, while a tighter bound on markup dispersion guarantees global efficiency.

detail.abstract: His intellectual and artistic trajectory spans nearly five decades, articulating Law, thought, literature, criticism, and art in an eloquent, genuinely Brazilian vocation. His poetic production spans more than forty years and culminates in A caturna e outros poemas-40 anos de poesia brasileira and, especially, in the poem A caturna, to which Nelson Cerqueira devoted a 48-page critical treatise, later translated into English. He conceived, presented, organized, and curated Signos em Transe: uma Fortuna Crítica sobre a Semiótica de Lícia Soares de Souza (2025), a collection bringing together 62 authors from seven countries and five languages, launched at the Academia de Letras da Bahia, with academic and institutional support from UNEB and CNPq. A recipient of the honorary title Cidadão Benemérito da Liberdade e da Justiça Social João Mangabeira (CBJM), his visual-art production, particularly the Assemblage no Parque da Cidade series, has international circulation and is indexed in global authority databases, such as the Getty Research Institute, whose Union List of Artist Names-ULAN-identifies him accordingly. Across all these languages, one gesture remains constant: Taurino Araújo brings together, under a single signature, what narrow classifications tend to separate. EDITORIAL NOTE This article is an authorized English version of Taurino Araújo-O Mercado das Sete Portas: Sete caminhos de uma eloquente vocação genuinamente

title: Defensive Land Acquisition: State-owned Enterprises and Government-driven Mergers in China
affiliations: Wuhan University, Peking University, Wuhan University, South China Normal University and Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU)

detail.title: Defensive Land Acquisition: State-owned Enterprises and Government-driven Mergers in China

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: State firms may not fully comply with the government's directives, and their strategic responses can be driven by their own interests, which contradicts government's initial objectives. This paper investigates how state firms operating in the real estate sector strategically respond to government-led merger initiatives by engaging in land acquisitions as a means of avoiding being merged. In a stylized tullock contest model, we find that government-driven mergers motivates defensive land acquisition, especially for small state firms. The resulting demand pressure raises both land and housing prices. Using detailed land parcel transaction data from 2007 to 2017 in China, our empirical findings are consistent with the theoretical predictions and state firms significantly increase land transaction volumes at higher prices and push up housing prices. This effect is mostly pronounced among weaker and smaller state firms which may have higher possibilities of being merged, and such strategic land acquisitions reduce their probabilities of being merged. However, these acquired land parcels were developed less efficiently, as indicated by lower nighttime light intensity.

title: Tariffs, Export Controls, and the Reshoring of AI Compute

detail.title: Tariffs, Export Controls, and the Reshoring of AI Compute

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Since 2023, the United States has layered an escalating stack of trade instruments-Entity List additions, revised licensing rules for advanced computing exports, and Section 232 tariffs on semiconductor articles-on top of subsidy-based industrial policy aimed at reshoring chip manufacturing. This paper examines whether these overlapping policy shocks have measurably redirected capital expenditure by the world's largest semiconductor manufacturers across the United States, Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, Germany, and China. Using a staggered differencein-differences design anchored to five major policy dates between September 2025 and September 2026, and a firm-quarter panel constructed from SEC EDGAR filings, DART disclosures, MOPS filings, and investor earnings calls, I test whether announced capex and fab-location decisions shifted toward jurisdictions granted tariff exemptions relative to jurisdictions facing tightening controls or ambiguous exposure. Aggregate industry data already show a divergence consistent with policy-driven reallocation: global semiconductor capital expenditure is projected to rise to roughly $200 billion in 2026, with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's guidance climbing toward $64 billion even as China-exposed segments face continued restriction. I situate these patterns within the weaponized-interdependence and strategic-autonomy literatures and argue that firm-level capex reallocation, rather than country-level trade balances, is the appropriate unit for evaluating whether this policy stack is achieving its stated reshoring objective.

title: Government-Backed Zombies? Evidence from France's COVID-19 Public-Guaranteed Loan Scheme
affiliations: University of Limoges - Laboratoire d'Analyse et de Prospectives Économiques (LAPE) and Université de Limoges, LAPE

detail.title: Government-Backed Zombies? Evidence from France's COVID-19 Public-Guaranteed Loan Scheme
detail.abstract: Using loan-level data from the Banque de France, we investigate the impact of the French COVID-19 Public-Guaranteed Loan (PGL) program on zombie lending. The scheme created a quasi-experimental setting in which loans meeting specific criteria became eligible for a state guarantee. Our difference-indifferences estimation shows that the PGL program increased zombie lending, consistent with reduced screening incentives and weaker lending discipline once banks were largely insulated from credit risk. This effect was amplified for lenders with stronger evergreening incentives and firms with diversified borrowing networks, while it was mitigated by local banks' informational advantage. However, distressed firms receiving PGLeligible loans were charged relatively higher interest rates. Overall, our findings highlight the long-term risks associated with large-scale guaranteed schemes, which can distort credit allocation and hamper post-crisis recovery by increasing zombie lending.

title: A Theoretical Rate of Return Framework and its Cross-sectional Implications

detail.title: A Theoretical Rate of Return Framework and its Cross-sectional Implications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study, as it did not involve human participants, personal data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops a structural framework that decomposes realized stock returns into three fundamental drivers: cash distribution, internal growth, and valuation adjustment. Rather than introducing a new empirical factor model, we propose a multiplicative decomposition that links observable firm fundamentals to returns, implying that expected returns are jointly shaped by growth and valuation dynamics in ways that additive linear specifications may fail to capture. 

     Using data from China, Hong Kong, and the United States, we test two minimal forms of structural consistency: cross-sectional ROE-return rankings and long-run coherence between cumulative ROE and cumulative returns. Our findings confirm that higher-ROE firms tend to earn higher realized returns across all three markets, and that cumulative profitability aligns closely with cumulative market returns over extended horizons. However, the translation of fundamentals into returns varies systematically by market-exhibiting amplification in China, moderated conversion requiring scaling adjustment in Hong Kong, and relatively stable but compressed transmission in the United States. 

      The paper's primary contribution is not a new factor model, but a unified structural interpretation of return formation that integrates internal value creation with marketdriven valuation changes. Our results suggest that stock returns are better understood as an outcome of a structural value-generation process mediated by valuation dynamics, rather than as a purely additive combination of independent factors.

title: The Gold Standard for Capital Recovery in AI Infrastructure Investment What Fiber, Towers and Public Cloud Businesses Teach Us

detail.title: The Gold Standard for Capital Recovery in AI Infrastructure Investment What Fiber, Towers and Public Cloud Businesses Teach Us

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are none.
declarations.ethicsApproval: All case studies and examples are from the cited public sources.
declarations.funderStatement: All costs were funded internally by WiseHarbor.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is driving an infrastructure investment cycle of exceptional scale. Whether that investment earns adequate returns will depend not only on growth in AI demand, but also on market structure, utilization, contractual commitments, counterparty credit, technological change and pricing. This article examines which historical infrastructure business models provide the most useful precedents for evaluating AI Infrastructure investment prospects.

The fiber-optic communications boom demonstrates that enormous demand growth does not guarantee capital recovery. Capacity became excessive relative to demand at prices capable of remunerating the original capital base, as numerous suppliers competed to fill largely undifferentiated networks whose construction costs were already sunk. By contrast, the U.S. tower-colocation sector has produced resilient cash flows through locally scarce assets, anchor tenants, long and escalating leases, high renewal propensity and attractive incremental economics from additional tenants. Public cloud offers a different successful model: hyperscalers aggregate diversified customer workloads, benefit from statistical multiplexing, control capacity expansion and add software-platform value above raw infrastructure.

AI Infrastructure currently exhibits elements of all three models. Long leases, contracted power capacity, prepayments and guarantees make some projects tower-like. Neoclouds and hyperscalers may achieve cloud-like workload aggregation. Yet fragmented build plans, reciprocal financial relationships, uncertain future pricing and a potentially large number of suppliers also create fiber-like risks.

The article distinguishes four utilization measures relevant to AI Infrastructure investment: serving utilization, economic utilization, physical utilization and industry utilization. Separating these measures helps identify which party bears utilization risk at different layers of the AI ecosystem and provides a more useful basis for capital-recovery analysis than reliance on a single utilization percentage. The central investment test is not whether AI demand will grow and create substantial value. It is whether contracted and realized demand will grow quickly enough, at sufficiently high prices, for first owners to recover committed capital before contracts expire, equipment is repriced, counterparties fail or competing supply erodes renewal economics.

AI use declaration. Microsoft Copilot was used as a research and writing aid in preparing this article, including for literature searches, source identification, drafting assistance and editorial review. Its use was directed by the author, and all resulting material was reviewed, revised and verified by the author. The article’s subject matter, analysis, judgments, conclusions and opinions are the author’s own. The author accepts full responsibility for the final content.

title: Are TARGET2 imbalances remunerated? The hidden mechanisms of Eurosystem monetary income
affiliations: University of Siena - Dipartimento di Economia Politica, University of Newcastle (Australia), University of Castilla-La Mancha and University of Napoli Federico II

detail.title: Are TARGET2 imbalances remunerated? The hidden mechanisms of Eurosystem monetary income

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: This paper addresses the vexed question of whether Eurosystem National Central Banks (NCBs) pay interest on their respective TARGET2 (T2) liabilities by considering the process through which all NCBs pool and are subsequently allocated an amount of "monetary income". The paper argues that NCBs with T2 liabilities do pay, but in disguised ways that are only fully revealed by unpacking the monetary income pooling/allocation process. To show how this is the case both in theory and in practice, we detail two specific mechanisms that are saddled within the monetary income pooling and allocation process-denoted as a "restitution mechanism" and a "compensation mechanism". The paper also exhibits how certain factors can influence the extent to which NCBs with T2 claims are renumerated.

title: Structural Return Components under Alternative Asset-pricing Frameworks: Evidence from China

detail.title: Structural Return Components under Alternative Asset-pricing Frameworks: Evidence from China

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
