declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This study examines how economically motivated structural return components are interpreted under alternative empirical asset-pricing frameworks. Rather than proposing another pricing factor or return anomaly, the study adopts the Theoretical Rate of Return (TRR) framework, which is analytically derived from the accounting identity of shareholder returns and organizes expected returns into three structural components: cash distribution, internal growth, and valuation adjustment. The framework provides a structural representation of expected-return generation that can be evaluated using complementary empirical methodologies. Quarterly firm-level data from the Chinese, Hong Kong, and U.S. equity markets over the period 2005-2025 are analyzed using Fama-MacBeth regressions and crosssectional characteristic regressions under a unified empirical design. Cross-market comparisons, subsample analyses, and delayed-horizon tests are conducted to evaluate the robustness of the empirical evidence. The empirical results indicate that the structural return components contain economically meaningful predictive information, although their empirical interpretation differs across estimation frameworks and market environments. Crosssectional characteristic regressions generally provide stronger evidence of incremental firm-level explanatory power than factor-pricing tests, while the magnitude and statistical significance of the structural components vary across the three equity markets. The strongest evidence is observed in China, weaker evidence is found in Hong Kong, and only limited incremental evidence is identified in the United States. The findings suggest that structurally derived return components should not be viewed exclusively as either pricing factors or firm characteristics. Instead, their empirical role depends jointly on the estimation methodology and institutional environment. By providing a unified comparison across complementary empirical asset-pricing frameworks, this study offers a structural perspective for interpreting economically motivated return components and contributes to the integration of valuation theory and empirical asset-pricing research.

title: Expanding the Moral Circle? Evidence from European Attitudes Toward Farmed Animal Welfare, 2007-2023
affiliations: University of Valladolid - Department of Finance and Accounting

detail.title: Expanding the Moral Circle? Evidence from European Attitudes Toward Farmed Animal Welfare, 2007-2023

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: I examine whether Europeans' moral circle expanded to include farmed animals between 2007 and 2023. Using three Special Eurobarometer waves with a dedicated animal-welfare module, I build a moral-concern index for a balanced panel of 24 EU member states. Concern rose between 2007 and 2015 and has held essentially steady since, but paths appear to have diverged across welfare-regime groups after 2015: the Continental group kept rising, while the Southern group lost about half its earlier gain. An age-period-cohort analysis shows the 2007-2015 rise was mostly a period shift in which all birth cohorts moved together. Concern is higher among women, the more educated, and the left. A Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition places roughly 90-99% of the increase within demographic groups, depending on the reference year, consistent with changed minds rather than compositional change. The expansion toward farmed animals appears real, but nothing in its form guarantees that it will persist.

title: Near-Field Exploration: Effect on Petroleum Reserve Replacement and Security of Supply
affiliations: University of Stavanger and University of Stavanger

detail.title: Near-Field Exploration: Effect on Petroleum Reserve Replacement and Security of Supply

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Osmundsen thanks Norewegian Offshore Directorate for financial support
declarations.funderStatement: Norewegian Offshore Directorate

detail.abstract: A crucial part of the transitioning strategies of European major petroleum companies has been a nearfield exploration strategy. Current production should be kept up for a certain number of years, to fund transitioning into renewable energy. After 2030, global petroleum demand was expected to fall steeply, together with petroleum production. Thus, reserve replacement was not on the agenda. Exploration would be near-field, and added resources tied into existing fields. The projects should have low breakeven price and a short payback time, to minimise climate risk. There was fear of stranded assets. Instead, large investments were made in renewables, in particular offshore wind. The renewable investments turned out to be less profitable than expected, and they could not compete with petroleum investments. Thus, the transition strategies are being reversed. With a substantial upward adjustment in petroleum demand, also beyond 2050, a dramatic cut in oil company renewable investment, and capital market demanding petroleum reserve replacement, the predominant near-field exploration strategy-an integrated part of the transition strategy-is no longer viable. However, it is to a large extent still prevalent. We discuss this challenge, using the Norwegian continental shelf as a case.

title: Beef, Brahmins, and the Politics of History: Rethinking a Modern Controversy Chapter 7 -Brahmanical Meat-Consumption Debate Series

detail.title: Beef, Brahmins, and the Politics of History: Rethinking a Modern Controversy Chapter 7 -Brahmanical Meat-Consumption Debate Series

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No external Funding received. Self funded.

keywords: modern historiography Suggested English Title Beef
and the Politics of History: Rethinking a Modern Controversy OECD FORD Classification 6.01 (History and Archaeology)

detail.abstract: The question of beef consumption in ancient India has, in the modern period, moved beyond the domain of food history to become a controversy bound up with religious identity, nationalism, caste discourse, and historiographical method. This study argues that opposing sides in the debate often treat selected textual evidence as representative of the Brahmanical tradition as a whole. The prohibition in Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 3.1.2.21 against a consecrated sacrificer consuming the flesh of a cow or bull, together with Yājñavalkya's dissent within the same passage; the desiderative prescription involving bovine meat in Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.18; and the coexistence of ritually sanctioned meat, prohibition, substitution, and renunciation in the fifth chapter of the Manusmṛti-all point to a multilayered historical situation. The evidence is sufficient to establish the existence of bovine-meat consumption, but it does not demonstrate that the practice was universal or customary among Brahmins across all periods. The article uses the term "spotlight fallacy" to describe the historiographical tendency by which a highly publicized example comes to stand for an entire tradition. A more reliable reconstruction must consider period, textual genre, ritual context, social role, region, and the distinction between normative prescription and actual practice in conjunction.

detail.abstract: This paper applies the capital dynamics framework (Carbonaro Golan, 2026) to the public debt of the United States. The framework distinguishes accounting identities from adjustment laws and holds that, once the endogenous limit of private valorization has been reached, the State is the only agent able to expand effective demand autonomously, through the inflation of private portfolios validated by the monetary authority. The framework is completed with a consolidated budget constraint that includes interest payments, a three-bloc system of economies that respects the zero-sum identity of current accounts, a financial fragility module based on the gap between the market price of assets and their simultaneous realization price, and a specification of the composition of fiscal adjustment grounded in the law of a declining marginal propensity to consume. The computational model is calibrated with published estimates and reproduces the order of magnitude of official projections. The current debt trajectory is explosive but slow (196% of output in 2055), and its stabilization requires a primary adjustment of about 2 percentage points of output, in line with the official estimate. The employment cost of that adjustment depends on its composition: cutting transfers to low-income households raises unemployment for decades, whereas taxing incomes with a low propensity to consume, together with a tax on interest income from public debt, a half-point monetary accommodation and macroprudential regulation, stabilizes debt without raising unemployment and reduces the probability of a financial crisis. The result holds under variation of the most contested parameters. The paper also analyzes the nominal dimension-de-anchoring, indexation, adjustment frequency and the Olivera-Tanzi effect-and a ladder of limits with regime changes that culminates in a nominal breakdown (5% monthly inflation) or a renegotiation with a haircut. Debt ratios are shown to conceal nominal explosion; for the issuer of the reserve currency the real limit arrives before the nominal one (around 2049-2053 absent a fiscal response); and the fastest route to explosion is monetary resistance under fiscal dominance. The paper concludes that the cost of fiscal consolidation is a distributive decision rather than a technical parameter, and that the interest rate is not an effective instrument of financial stability.

title: Wealth Concentration and Economic Performance

detail.title: Wealth Concentration and Economic Performance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A

detail.abstract:
Why does capital compound at an accelerate rate among top wealth percentiles, even during the period of moderate macro economic expansions? This paper looks past the typical moral arguments to unpack the actual mechanical engine behind the gap: corporate leverage and the math of capital compounding.
By pairing Thomas Piketty’s classical r > g framework with standard corporate finance, we show how fixed costs and corporate debt create a major leverage multiplier. Using long-term Federal Reserve (FRED) data alongside the Survey of Consumer Finances, we find that corporate earnings don’t just track the economy—they swing at roughly 2 to 2.5 times the rate of nominal GDP. Because economic expansions last far longer than recessions, this continuous multiplier has steadily expanded corporate profits as a share of the total economy.
The catch is where those earnings go. Because equity ownership is heavily concentrated by dollar volume, leveraged corporate earnings compound asset values primarily among top tier portfolios, even as corporate earnings support broad employment and wage growth over time.
Finally, we examine the macroeconomic effects: how differences in marginal propensity to consume (MPC) between high earners and everyday consumers affect aggregate demand, how rising healthcare costs act as a persistent balance-sheet drag on working households, and why relying on recessions to compress inequality is counterproductive. True balance-sheet accumulation historically occurs during sustained expansions, where rising real wages and broad asset ownership allow more households to compound capital.

title: Manufacturing as a Middle-Education Destination: Structural Transformation and the Schooling Ladder in China

detail.title: Manufacturing as a Middle-Education Destination: Structural Transformation and the Schooling Ladder in China

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N.A.

detail.abstract: Structural transformation is usually summarized by how much labor leaves agriculture. I show that its schooling consequences also depend on where the receiving sector hires along the schooling ladder. Using harmonized censuses for 197 Chinese prefectures, I find that a 10-percentage-point reallocation from agriculture to manufacturing during 1990-2000 is associated with 3.6 points higher junior-middle (lower-secondary) completion among adolescents, whereas reallocation to other non-agricultural sectors is associated with almost none. The di↵erence is concentrated at a single rung: the manufacturing-other gap is 3.2 points in completing junior middle without entering upper secondary, but only 0.1 points in upper-secondary entry. In a simple labordemand model, which schooling transition a sectoral expansion rewards depends not on the sector's average skill intensity but on the curvature of its employment profile across adjacent schooling levels. In the census, manufacturing employment rises steeply at junior-middle completion and flattens beyond it, whereas other non-agricultural employment rises most at upper secondary. Education-specific non-employment among adults is consistent with the implied shift in returns toward the junior-middle margin. Structural transformation can thus raise attainment at an intermediate rung without generating continued upgrading.

detail.abstract: We study commodity taxation when consumers weigh the convenience of AI delegation against the benefit of human review. At a given tax, better AI tax accounting raises the price used by the AI to choose quantities, so existing users buy less. The improved purchase also makes review less worthwhile, encouraging delegation. When AI remains less tax-aware than human review, new users buy more than they would under review and generate additional tax revenue. Holding the initial user group fixed yields a welfare loss because the welfare cost of replacing lost revenue exceeds the gain from better purchases. This result does not require fully tax-aware human review. Entry can more than offset the revenue loss, allowing the same expenditure to be financed at a lower tax. The same AI improvement can therefore lower welfare with a fixed user base but raise it when consumers can switch.

detail.abstract: This article surveys the empirical literature on the effect of immigration on housing costs. We focus on studies that address the endogeneity of immigrant location choice and organise the evidence around a common effect-size metric: the percentage change in house prices or rents associated with a one-percentage-point increase in the immigrant share of the local population. Our survey highlights that immigration raises housing costs, but that the effects are typically modest: house-price and rent responses usually lie in the range between 0 and 3%. Estimates vary across countries, spatial scales, housing-market segments and empirical strategies, reflecting differences in housing-supply responsiveness, native mobility responses, immigrant income and tenure composition, local amenities, and construction-sector adjustment. Methodological choices also matter; studies using smaller spatial units usually find less positive, and sometimes negative, effects, consistent with local mobility responses. Finally, we develop a comparative framework for assessing the relevance of international evidence to specific country contexts, using the UK as an illustrative case.

detail.abstract: We investigate whether political uncertainty as a result of a temporary rise in unpredictability about future government policy and leadership surrounding national elections affects how investors allocate their investments between home and foreign equity markets. Using panel data of 49 countries from 2001 to 2019, we find that political uncertainty exerts a positive and significant effect on equity home bias, but, in contrast, political uncertainty leads to a significant reduction in equity foreign bias. Our findings suggest that, whereas political uncertainty induces over-investment in equity holdings of domestic investors, the converse is the case for foreign investors. Our results also show that institutional quality and information environment moderate the effects of political uncertainty on home and foreign biases. Our channel analysis indicates that differences in information between home and foreign investors explain how investors make their investment decisions during the period of political uncertainty.

detail.abstract: This paper reassesses Brazil's canonical case study of import substitution industrialization during the Great Depression. Combining new panels of publicly traded firms (1926-1942) and São Paulo industrial censuses (1928-1933), we challenge stylized accounts of a frictionless turning point. While census data confirms a surging, uneven recovery in consumer manufacturing employment, corporate financial data reveals severe, prolonged distress. Listed manufacturers suffered massive relative declines in market capitalization and market-to-book ratios. We reconcile these conflicting views: industrial output and employment rebounded through expenditure switching and idle capacity utilization without an equally rapid recovery in corporate valuation or new capital formation.

It did not involve human participants, identifiable personal data, or animal subjects. Accordingly, institutional ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: Leadership scholars have long recognized that effective organizations depend upon alignment between strategy, organizational identity, leadership communication, and organizational behavior. Existing research demonstrates that strategic execution, organizational culture, identity, and leadership communication each contribute to organizational effectiveness, yet comparatively less attention has been devoted to the leadership process through which these elements remain continuously aligned as institutions adapt to changing internal and external conditions. This paper examines the relationship between strategic alignment, organizational identity, leadership communication, and organizational behavior through a conceptual analysis of scholarship on strategic management, organizational culture, organizational identity, and organizational sensemaking. The analysis identifies a theoretical gap concerning how institutions preserve alignment between who they are, what leaders communicate, how organizational members behave, and the operational realities they experience. To address this gap, the paper develops the concept of Strategic Coherence, defined as the alignment between institutional identity, organizational behavior, leadership communication, and operational reality. The analysis argues that sustainable organizational effectiveness depends not solely upon sound strategy, effective leadership, or organizational performance, but upon the degree to which these organizational elements remain mutually reinforcing over time. By identifying Strategic Coherence as a distinct leadership mechanism, this paper extends existing scholarship on strategic alignment and organizational leadership while contributing the integrating construct of Narrative Power Leadership Theory (NPLT). The findings provide a theoretical framework for understanding how institutions sustain organizational alignment, preserve interpretive consistency, and maintain effective leadership under conditions of continuity, adaptation, and change.

detail.abstract: Crowd-sourced, randomly located vehicles in large-scale on-demand mobility systems result in uncertainty in customer waiting times, posing challenges for service reliability and system efficiency. We theoretically establish that, under nearest-eligible-vehicle assignment and the stated independence condition, any nondegenerate limit of suitably normalized customer waiting-time minima must belong to the minimum-GEV family. Under a lower-bounded spatial Poisson benchmark, we derive how the cumulative spatial intensity of eligible idle vehicles determines the minimum-GEV location, scale, and shape parameters. Numerical simulations show close finite-sample agreement between fitted minimum-GEV distributions and simulated waiting-time distributions under the specified designs, including expected eligible-set sizes as low as ten and random selection among the first three order statistics. Observations from e-hailing trajectory data provide descriptive distributional evidence that GEV distributions approximate customer waiting times. We also formulate a generalized-cost comparison across providers. A lower-bounded observed-quote benchmark links provider quotes to physical pickup-time distributions, while a behavioral benchmark uses independent minimum-Gumbel generalized-cost disturbances with a common scale and yields the Multinomial Logit (MNL) form. Moreover, we analytically derive a unique stationary throughput turning point associated with the Wild Goose Chase (WGC) phenomenon under an uncontrolled, lower-bounded benchmark. The resulting turning point provides a stress-test benchmark for examining how assignment, admission, dispatch limits, and repositioning alter stationary throughput.

detail.abstract:
This document sets out eight observations in which a company named a constraint in its own document, on a date, and then set or restated a target that did not carry that constraint. Each entry gives the constraint as the company stated it, the document and date that carry it, the decision taken after that date, and the cost as the company later reported it.

Three of the eight were published before their outcomes were known. Two of those closed with a cost, after 28 days and after 89 days. One is open, with its next data point named.

The record states no cause, and makes no statement about how often the sequence occurs.

detail.abstract: Supplier diversification can improve reliability, yet it may alter the optimal total order quantity. We examine how the supply-risk mechanism shapes this ordering response in a newsvendor model. Under exchangeable proportional random yields, we derive conditions on the demand distribution under which diversification increases or decreases the optimal total order relative to single sourcing. In contrast, exchangeable all-or-nothing disruptions rule out a decrease. For random capacities with a common continuous distribution, the smallest optimal total order under multiple sourcing is no smaller than under single sourcing, regardless of capacity dependence. The total-order response to diversification thus depends on the mechanism through which orders are converted into deliveries.

detail.abstract: This article analyzes the constitutional architecture established by the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement and argues that Bosnia and Herzegovina's current crisis, marked by secessionist rhetoric, defiance of state institutions, and stalled EU accession, is the predictable outcome of a constitutional order designed to end a war, not to sustain durable democratic governance. Drawing on one author's firsthand participation in the Bosnian delegation and subsequent decades of peace-process experience, it traces how the extraordinary wartime pressures of the negotiations subordinated constitutional design to military enforcement, producing a framework of territorial decentralization, ethnic power-sharing, and veto mechanisms borrowed from an inherently undemocratic Yugoslav template. The article concludes by proposing pathways for reform, including curbing veto-based obstruction, aligning change with EU accession and civic rights, and shifting from international supervision toward legitimate domestic governance.

detail.title: The Asian Battery Companies Charging the EV Transition

publicationDetails.detailsText: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series No. 253

detail.abstract:
Based on a program to develop a zero-emission electric vehicle (EV) launched in 1990, between 1996 and 1999 General Motors (GM) produced 1,117 EV1s, leasing them to selected customers. In October 2000, however, having ceased the production of EV1s, GM sold its EV battery joint venture with Energy Conversion Devices to Texaco. Then, from April 2003, GM began to reclaim the EV1s from their users and literally crushed them out of existence. Recognizing the opening created by GM's destruction of the EV1, in July 2003, Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning founded Tesla. Ten months later, Elon Musk became Tesla's main financial backer and chairman, investing $6.35 million of the $7.5 million raised in Tesla's first round of venture funding. Flash forward 15 years to 2019, when Tesla sold 367,656 battery electric vehicles (BEVs) worldwide, with 51.5 percent delivered outside the United States, including 42,715 BEVs produced and sold in China. Tesla's success signaled that the United States was positioned to become the leader of the global EV transition. That apparent lead was short-lived. China-based BYD, which sold just 147,185 BEVs in 2019, delivered 2,256,714 BEVs in 2025, compared with Tesla’s 1,636,129.

BYD also sold 2,288,709 plug-in hybrids (PHEVs), compared with Tesla’s zero, and the Chinese company could claim global leadership in both types of EV. Moreover, inside every vehicle BYD delivered in 2025 was a BYD battery, making the company the world’s second largest EV battery maker. BYD’s 16.4 percent share of the global EV battery market was less than half the 39.1 percent share of China-based CATL, a pure-play battery maker, but far surpassed Korea-based LG Energy Solution, in third place with a 9.3 percent share. Japan-based Panasonic, which supplies the batteries for Tesla’s EVs produced in the United States, had 3.9 percent of the global EV battery market in 2025. Asia is home to all the leading EV battery companies, while the United States can claim no major EV battery maker. This paper documents the rise to global dominance of the Asian EV battery companies, focusing on Panasonic, LG Energy Solution, BYD, and CATL. Building on the contents of this paper, we are currently deploying the “theory of innovative enterprise” to explain fully, in future papers, the sources of competitive advantage of the Asian battery makers and the reasons why the United States has fallen so far behind in the development and production of this critical technology.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: In November 2022 the 10-year Treasury yield fell below the 3-month bill rate, an inversion of the yield curve, and a probit model of the spread between the two put the probability of a recession 12 months ahead at 40 percent. By May 2023 it was 77 percent, but no recession followed. This note records what nine other recession signals, chosen from published studies by a stated rule, said at the start of that inversion and of the eight earlier inversions since 1966, using data as first published wherever they survive. The yields on 1-, 5- and 10-year Treasury securities and on Moody's highest-rated (Aaa) corporate bonds exceeded the federal funds rate, the overnight rate the Federal Reserve targets, by more than at any earlier start, although the 5- and 10-year spreads later fell further than before the 2001, 2008 and 2020 recessions, if much less far than before those of 1973 to 1981. Stock prices, building permits, the Gilchrist–Zakrajšek corporate credit spread, financial conditions and the curvature of the yield curve, a measure of its shape, gave readings within the range seen at earlier starts, which include both recessions and the 1966 false alarm, when stocks and permits had fallen further than in 2022. With nine inversions and two false alarms, the comparisons cannot show whether disagreement among signals predicts the curve's errors.

detail.abstract: Oversight changes the evidence it relies on. We ask when randomized audits and scoring align AI agents that can conceal misconduct and alter records. Stronger auditing makes undeterred violations better hidden. Because the provider writes the agent's objective, sanctions need not stop at forfeiture, and rare audits deter every type of agent if evidence survives concealment and audit draws cannot be learned in advance. When evidence can be erased, deterrence must come from lower gains from violation, such as credit for stopping, or from costlier or fewer ways to conceal. These conditions identify what failed when agents in OpenAI's cybersecurity evaluations compromised parts of Hugging Face's infrastructure in July 2026.

detail.abstract: Filings with the US Federal Communications Commission for about 1.16 million orbital data-center satellites exceed the European Southern Observatory's sustainable limit of 100,000 faint satellites more than tenfold, and satellites kept permanently in sunlight remove the dark hours near midnight that observatories now rely on. Chile holds roughly 40% of the world's astronomical observing capacity, so any terrestrial alternative sited there must answer to astronomy first. This paper compares the two for observatories and regulators. It argues that the orbital alternative is worse for astronomy than the Global Data Center Park, a proposed dry-cooled, solar-and-storage-powered AI compute park in the María Elena / Sierra Gorda belt of the Antofagasta Region. The park's local cost is bounded, measurable and negotiable: the candidate sites are 209–264 km from the ELT and VLT, about twenty times INNA's distance from Paranal, and the park commits to dark exterior design, noise setbacks and instrumented sky monitoring with a remediation trigger. The paper also states what the park cannot claim. It does not improve astronomy, it cannot stop foreign filings, and mid-infrared heat and radio interference at ALMA are not solved by distance. Every figure on the orbital side is sourced to the observatory community or to the applicants' own filings. The author directed the research, reviewed every source and figure, and is responsible for the content.

detail.abstract: Innovation management is central to the long-run competitiveness and renewal of entrepreneurial families, and prior research has documented how socioemotional wealth preservation, risk preferences, long-term orientation, and idiosyncratic endowments shape their innovative behavior. We welcomed contributions that deepened our understanding of how family involvement shapes innovation inputs, processes, and outcomes; moved beyond R&D intensity and patenting; and extended the analysis to the diversity of actors, governance arrangements, and organizational forms through which entrepreneurial families innovate. The nine featured articles answer that call across multiple levels of analysis, from board and top management team composition, through succession and intra-family relational dynamics, to firms' embeddedness in local knowledge ecosystems. These studies show that the predominant unit of analysis remains the single operating firm, systematically underestimating the transgenerational and multi-entity character of innovation in entrepreneurial families that today operate across a multitude of firms, family offices, foundations, holding companies, academies, and trust companies. To organize these contributions and chart the next wave of research, we draw on and extend the entrepreneurial family galaxy perspective, combining its five dimensions (shape, mass, luminosity, distance from the center, and regeneration rate) with the input-process-outcome framework.

keywords: Labor Market Efficiency JEL codes: D82

detail.abstract: We examine whether state laws restricting employers' use of non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) improve labor-market efficiency. Employers use NDAs to suppress negative workplace information to appear more attractive to job seekers. However, widespread suppression degrades the labor-market information environment, potentially creating a market failure that disincentivizes workplace improvements and worsens firms' recruiting outcomes. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design around the enactment of state NDA restriction laws, we find that firms fill job vacancies more quickly, workplace conditions improve, employee turnover declines, and firm performance improves. These results indicate that restricting firms' ability to suppress workplace information improves labor-market efficiency and helps correct a market failure created by widespread NDA use. Our findings extend the accounting literature on labor-market information frictions by suggesting that firms' strategic suppression of employee disclosures can create market externalities with real consequences for workers and firms.

detail.abstract: Extreme left-tail market shocks present persistent threats to modern equity portfolio management, often resulting in severe drawdowns that erode long-term capital accumulation. This paper evaluates the structural performance, cost-effectiveness, and payoff profiles of static out-of-the-money (OTM) put option strategies versus dynamic tail-risk mitigation strategies (such as trend-following overlays and volatility-managed asset allocations) during high-volatility market regimes. Using historical simulations of an S&P 500 benchmarked portfolio (2006-2026) with stress periods including 2008, 2020, and 2022, incorporating public market data and calibrated option pricing models, we find that while static OTM put options provide instantaneous convexity and high execution reliability during abrupt crashes, their persistent negative carry severely drags cumulative long-term returns. Conversely, dynamic tail-risk mitigation frameworks minimize negative drag during benign market environments by adapting exposure through multi-asset momentum and volatility scaling, offering superior risk-adjusted returns (Sharpe and Sortino ratios) across complete market cycles.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: A large body of literature studies the fundamental trade-offs of product information provision. However, much of this work treats prices as non-informative: prices affect demand, but are not modeled as a signal about quality. To fill this gap, we study the joint design of information and pricing in markets for vertically differentiated products whose quality is privately observed by sellers. Each seller commits ex ante to a joint information–pricing mechanism that maps quality into a distribution over signal–price pairs, allowing the posted price itself to also convey information. We begin with a monopoly setting. We show that information design is payoff-irrelevant for the seller: any information structure attains the optimal revenue when paired with prices proportional to the induced posterior-mean qualities. We then turn to oligopoly competition in which sellers simultaneously choose such joint information–pricing mechanisms. We establish that the family of transparent contingent-pricing mechanisms is best-response-closed: against any profile of rival mechanisms, each seller has a best response that fully reveals qualities and posts deterministic, quality-dependent prices. In the resulting symmetric equilibrium, the pricing rule, which may not be monotone, coincides with the bid-shading function in a private-values first-price auction. When the quality distribution is log-concave, this pricing rule is strictly increasing, and the price alone reveals quality: the market needs no disclosure beyond the price tag. This equilibrium outcome is efficient: the buyer purchases the highest-quality product almost surely, and social welfare is first-best. Compared with fixed-price benchmarks with restricted disclosure, pricing flexibility triggers over-competition: each seller adopts transparent contingent pricing willingly, yet in thick markets every seller earns less than under a fixed-price regime, while buyers gain and social welfare rises. Finally, we discuss extensions with ex ante asymmetric sellers and with privately informed buyers.

detail.abstract: U.S. patent litigation has come to rely on third-party litigation funding (TPLF), which involves an external investor providing funds to pay for a lawsuit or a law firm in return for its share of any recovery. This paper uses a litigation dataset spanning January 2010 through June 2026 to examine the growth of identified TPLF, its concentration across federal patent venues, the role of non-practicing entities, and the policy implications of uneven disclosure requirements. The data show a long-run increase in identified funding, with TPLF reaching roughly one quarter of filings in the most recent period, alongside a renewed concentration of patent litigation in the Eastern District of Texas and a decline in Delaware following the adoption of heightened disclosure requirements. The paper also examines how changes in inter partes review practice alter the litigation environment in which patent owners, defendants, and funders operate, and evaluates competing approaches to TPLF regulation, including case-by-case disclosure, a uniform federal disclosure rule, targeted legislation, and prohibition. It concludes that a uniform disclosure framework is preferable to the current court-by-court patchwork, while distinguishing disclosure of funder identity and control rights from automatic production of all economically sensitive funding terms.

detail.abstract: Estimates of how much school principals matter differ by an order of magnitude, in part because conventional estimators require principal identifiers and absorb sampling noise into the estimated dispersion. We identify the variance of principal-by-school effects without identifiers, using successions dated by principals' reported tenure in Brazil's 2011 national assessment, which imply known probabilities of a change between consecutive tests. The standard deviation is 0.05 student standard deviations in grade 5 and indistinguishable from zero in grade 9, against 0.18 for plug-in estimates on the same data. Dispersion is concentrated in networks where principals are appointed rather than competitively selected. These estimates imply that principal replacement can explain only a small share of the learning losses that prior work attributes to mayoral party turnover. In close elections, a change in the ruling party replaces municipal principals and, where these posts are discretionary, also disrupts the teaching staff and worsens grade progression. The rules by which principals are chosen matter more than the identity of any individual principal.

detail.abstract: Six filings from five operators with the US Federal Communications Commission propose about 1.16 million satellites for AI computing in orbit, including SpaceX's January 2026 plan for up to one million satellites and 100 GW of compute. This paper examines those proposals at three scales. The case for orbit is real: sunlight is continuous in a dawn-dusk orbit and no land or water is needed. But the fleet must be rebuilt in full every five years, cost does not fall with scale, and the required launch rate does not yet exist. Collision risk, upper-atmosphere loading, loss of astronomical observing time, and conflicts with crewed flight and military orbits fall on parties who have not consented and are not compensated. Current laser links cannot provide the tightly coupled network that frontier model training needs, although satellites that each serve their own inference users remain plausible. The paper concludes that at any useful scale orbital data centers cost more than terrestrial ones and push their largest costs onto others. It proposes a terrestrial alternative: a dry-cooled, solar-and-storage-powered park in Chile's Atacama Desert, where sodium-ion storage provides continuous power for about 4.4% of capital cost. detail.abstract: Does constraining shareholder power turn managers into self-serving agents or committed stewards? Agency theory and stewardship theory give opposite answers. We reconcile them with a tale-of-two-effects framework that separates differences between firms from changes within a firm. We test it on a panel of the 1,500 U.S. firms across 20 years. We measure managers' organizational identification (OI) and analyst inquiry from earnings call transcripts with transformer-based language models. We estimate Mundlak and fixed-effects models with heteroskedasticity-based instruments. Firms with more constitutional constraints show higher average OI (the stewardship effect). However, an increase in constraints within a firm is followed by lower OI (the entrenchment effect). Positive media coverage strengthens this decline (the hubris effect), and intense analyst inquiry weakens it (the vulnerability effect). Our findings suggest that whether insulated managers act as agents or stewards depends on the stability of their insulation and the scrutiny that surrounds it. We discuss implications for boards and shareholders who debate the adoption of new governance provisions.

detail.abstract: Sellers of scarce goods often keep the price below the market-clearing level and let buyers earn the right to buy through purchases of their other products. Luxury brands allocate handbags, watches, and cars to established clients, and underwriters have allocated hot IPO shares to clients who generate commissions. We develop a theory of this practice, earned access, built on four features. Capacity is scarce at the posted price, buyers can resell, buyers pay partly in a second currency that they value in part and on which the seller earns a margin, and the seller cannot commit to rewarding currency already paid. Resale makes the right to buy worth the same to every buyer, so access goes to buyers for whom the second currency is cheapest. Earned access beats market-clearing pricing if and only if the seller's margin exceeds the marginal buyer's cost per unit of the second currency, and it then leaves no consumer worse off than market-clearing pricing, though buyers lose relative to a lottery. The optimal mechanism sells part of capacity for money when such buyers are few and makes random offers among more qualifiers than units when they are many. Because the second currency is paid before the offer, the mechanism needs commitment; relationships supply it if and only if the seller is patient relative to the buyer's cost of the currency, which explains why the rules are opaque. A calibration to Hermès illustrates the magnitudes.

detail.abstract: Creativity research often treats divergent thinking, creative production, and recognized achievement as interchangeable outcomes. The Divergent Conduit Model separates them. Its minimal empirical architecture distinguishes creative search (𝐶 𝑆), expressed creative production (𝐶 𝐸), and recognized creative achievement (𝐶 𝑅); latent creative capacity (𝐶 𝐿) is retained only as an optional latent construct and is not required to test the model. Within search, perspectival divergence (𝑃) and ideational proliferation (𝐼 𝑑) describe search structure, while closure resistance (𝑅 𝑐) is proposed as the model's principal novel mechanism: continuation of search after a viable candidate has already appeared. Search becomes production through conversion dispositions (𝐾), execution resources (𝑋), and domain expertise (𝐷 𝑒). Failure integration (𝐹 𝑖) is specified as a facet of 𝐾, describing whether candidate failure is used as information for revision, restart, or strategy change. Expressed work then encounters a separate recognition environment (𝑂 𝑟) shaped by exposure, gatekeepers, networks, status, capital, timing, and institutional access. The model is positioned against BVSR, associative and conceptual-blending theories, satisficing, need for closure, maximization, explorationexploitation, personality, intelligence, executive-control, motivational, Four-C, and systems approaches. It makes several risky predictions: post-viability search should show an interior optimum under finite budgets; failure integration should help principally when failure contains usable information; expanding candidate supply without expanding evaluation capacity should eventually reduce realized quality; and recognition opportunity should predict social uptake beyond blinded artifact quality. The stage sequence itself is treated as scaffolding rather than the model's principal novelty. The framework survives as a distinctive theory only if closure resistance, information-sensitive failure integration, and recognition opportunity add explanatory value beyond established constructs. Psychopathology, neurodevelopmental difference, and adversity are treated as applications and possible antecedents rather than as the theory's defining variables.

detail.abstract: This structured integrative review examines cybersecurity risks that arise when AI agents support operational supply-chain decisions through machine-learning models and data in distributed multi-cloud environments. The review brings together five related research streams: AI agents in operational supply chains; security of AI agents; machine-learning and data integrity; multi-cloud security and identity; and cybersecurity risk management in supply chains. The reviewed literature shows that these streams are established to different degrees. Combined, these streams point to several supply-chain-relevant risk conditions, supported by direct supply-chain evidence for some and transferred evidence for others: manipulated demand forecasts that can resemble a genuine demand shock; delegated non-human identities that can complicate decision provenance (a derived concern); exposure of procurement and negotiation agents to manipulation; operational consequences that differ by supply-chain function; and multi-cloud deployment as a condition that adds identity, API, configuration, policy, and telemetry boundaries. An initial coding of 12 studies in which AI agents perform or support operational supply-chain tasks found seven with no substantive security treatment, three with security mentioned in passing, one with qualitative security discussion, and one with dedicated conceptual threat analysis; none reported an empirical security evaluation or addressed multi-cloud deployment. This result does not indicate that security research is absent; the documented literature instead shows limited integration across agent security, ML/data integrity, multi-cloud identity, and operational supply-chain consequences, and direct empirical evidence for a complete cross-layer relationship remains sparse. The review distinguishes reported findings from derived connections and unsupported links, and it reports database and access limitations explicitly.

detail.abstract: Guidance on generative AI is written sector by sector, yet the tools employees and students reach for are the same everywhere. We formalise fifteen sector profiles, from K-12 schools to defense, as layered decision rules over a functional taxonomy of AI tools, and apply every profile to the same register of 11,890 active AI tools. The share of tools a profile blocks ranges from 10.0% for marketing and creative agencies to 81.6% for defense and critical infrastructure. "Allow with controls" is the most common verdict in ten of fifteen sectors, so the practical question is rarely a choice between banning and permitting AI. Two sectors picked at random disagree on 41.3% of tools on average; only 13.4% of tools receive the same verdict everywhere, while 51.9% are blocked in one sector and allowed in another. Profiles cluster: healthcare and insurance differ on 3.2% of tools, K-12 schools and universities on 76.0%. We present the complete policy matrix for one sector, K-12 schools, with a rationale for each of the 18 categories and all 165 subcategories. Under this profile 71.5% of tools are blocked, and 35.4% of verdicts are set by a subcategory rule rather than a category default. We argue that sector policies should be published as explicit, testable rules at the subcategory level, and we release the aggregate statistics as open data.

detail.abstract: Smart infrastructure, meaning the transportation networks, power systems, industrial facilities, and digital platforms that are instrumented with sensors and coordinated through software, is generating data at a scale that conventional rule-based management cannot absorb. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are widely proposed as the analytical layer that converts this data into forecasts, control actions, and security decisions. This paper reviews peer-reviewed literature on ML and deep learning for infrastructure management across four domains: urban traffic, smart grids, industrial process and maintenance, and cybersecurity. The review shows that deep spatio-temporal models and reinforcement learning have advanced traffic forecasting and signal control, that supervised and deep classifiers dominate intrusion detection for grid and enterprise networks, and that predictive analytics is the most mature application in industrial settings. It also shows that evidence is uneven: results are usually obtained on benchmark or simulated data, evaluation protocols differ across studies, and deployment considerations such as interpretability, data governance, and lifecycle monitoring receive far less attention than model accuracy. Building on these observations, the paper proposes a conceptual, layered framework that couples edge and cloud analytics with a structured, Six Sigma-inspired improvement loop and an explicit trust and governance layer. The framework is offered as a research agenda, not as a validated system; no new experiments are reported. The paper closes with practical implications for infrastructure operators and priorities for future empirical work.

title: The New Sovereignist Order: How AI and Autonomous Systems Are Rewriting the Economics of National Sovereignty

detail.title: The New Sovereignist Order: How AI and Autonomous Systems Are Rewriting the Economics of National Sovereignty

detail.abstract:
The international economic order of recent decades has relied on specialization, cross-border production, and access to global technology markets. These arrangements expanded national capability while creating dependencies whose consequences become visible during supply disruption, export restrictions, or commercial withdrawal. AI and autonomous systems can change the resources required to maintain selected capabilities, including the labor, expertise, coordination, and organizational scale involved.

This paper develops a qualitative framework for examining how those changes affect sovereignty. The dependency premium describes the additional economic and strategic exposure associated with reliance on a capability once interruption and replacement are considered. The autonomy dividend describes an improvement in the relative practical or economic feasibility of maintaining a capability under domestic, regional, or trusted control attributable to AI and autonomous systems. Foreign suppliers also automate, and gains depend on complementary infrastructure, institutional competence, and implementation.

A Sovereign Capability Stack maps the physical, digital, and institutional dependencies supporting an essential function. It reveals a sovereignty paradox: measures that improve control at one layer can create new dependencies elsewhere. The resulting policy choices can support selective interdependence, combining international exchange with stronger continuity and credible alternatives around consequential functions. Shared capability can improve access where national replication is impractical, although its value depends on arrangements that remain usable under stress. Productive gains can coexist with unequal control over the infrastructure and conditions through which they are obtained.

The paper calls the possible international configuration arising from these interactions the New Sovereignist Order. Its emergence requires evidence that changes in productive feasibility influence state and firm decisions and become embedded in durable international practices. The analysis separates this order-level hypothesis from the practical usefulness of dependency assessment. It preserves the distinction between technological capacity and accountable exercise of that capacity, and identifies foundations for subsequent empirical assessment without proposing a country ranking or numerical sovereignty score.

detail.abstract: Estimating travel behavior parameters is essential for understanding current travel patterns and for forecasting how travelers may respond to future changes in transportation systems. However, reliable estimation remains difficult when behavior must be inferred from sparse and aggregate observations, especially when jointly recovering several behavioral components. In this paper, we develop a bi-level estimation program for a combined destination, mode and route choice model with congestion. The inner level is a convex program at given scale parameters, and returns the taste coefficients as its dual variables together with the equilibrium travel pattern. The outer level selects the scale parameters by out-of-sample prediction, measured by how well the modeled travel pattern predicts observations withheld from estimation. To solve the bi-level problem at scale, we propose a matrix-free Hierarchical Lagrangian Dual algorithm as the inner solver and an outer search by implicit differentiation, which uses the sensitivities of the inner solution to enable efficient search over the scale parameters and reaches the calibrated scales in a handful of iterations. We validate the approach on Los Angeles County using public origin-destination, mode-share and traffic-count data. Our approach scales to a county-level problem with 2.7 million variables and substantially improves computational efficiency over a general-purpose conic solver. Compared with the fixed-scale benchmark, the calibrated model improves predictive performance at the destination and mode levels, with consistent gains across complementary goodness-of-fit measures.

detail.abstract: This monograph examines a recurrent theological inference: because Scripture anticipates worsening evil, deception, lawlessness, apostasy, and moral disorder, attempts at spiritual formation must ultimately be fruitless. The argument is shown to depend on a category error. Biblical texts that warn of intensified evil do not constitute a universal prophecy that every person, every community, or every period of Christian history will become progressively worse. At the same time, the New Testament explicitly expects conversion, renewal, maturation, perseverance, love, holiness, and the fruit of the Spirit. The biblical canon therefore presents simultaneous trajectories: persistent and sometimes intensifying rebellion, and genuine Spirit-enabled transformation. These trajectories are not mutually exclusive because they concern different persons, responses, communities, stages of formation, and dimensions of eschatological history. The study develops a framework for distinguishing prophecy from description, universal claims from bounded claims, religious activity from spiritual transformation, spiritual experience from spiritual maturity, church growth from spiritual growth, and imperfect sanctification from total spiritual failure. It also analyzes a recurring evaluative problem: a judgment becomes unfalsifiable when visible virtue is dismissed as pretense while visible failure is treated as decisive evidence that the gospel, the Church, or the Holy Spirit is ineffective. Such a framework is inconsistent with the New Testament's own practice of evaluating fruit, testing claims, acknowledging hypocrisy, correcting failure, and nevertheless affirming real transformation. The paper concludes that the biblical expectation of continuing or increasing evil cannot coherently be used as a defeater for the biblical doctrine of sanctification. Christian theology must preserve both eschatological realism about sin and evidential openness to genuine moral and spiritual change.

detail.abstract: Advanced nanomaterials can manipulate heat, charge, fields, photons, ions, and chemical intermediates at length scales where interfaces and boundaries dominate. This capability supports four distinct but connected functions: rapid thermal transport, thermoelectric heat-to-electricity conversion, electron field emission, and clean energy generation and storage. The required properties are not universally compatible. Thermal spreaders favor continuous high-conductivity pathways, thermoelectrics require high electronic performance with suppressed heat conduction, field emitters favor sharp geometries and controlled surface barriers, and electrochemical or solar systems require charge transfer, accessible reactive sites, and long-term chemical stability. This critical technical review compares graphene and other two-dimensional materials, carbon nanotubes, nanowires, quantum dots, MXenes, nanostructured chalcogenides, half-Heuslers, skutterudites, nanodiamond, and hybrid porous architectures. Evidence shows that record nanoscale properties often diminish in devices because of boundary resistance, carrier depletion, contact loss, field screening, Joule heating, oxidation, coarsening, mechanical damage, and package-level heat leakage. The paper proposes the NEXUS framework: Name the system function; Establish coupled transport targets; eXamine structure and interfaces across scales; Unite material, contact, and thermal architecture; and Screen reliability, scalability, safety, and lifecycle value. NEXUS is an evidence-derived design and reporting framework rather than an experimentally validated model. Its purpose is to prevent isolated material metrics from being mistaken for sustainable device performance.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the safe-haven properties of the Japanese yen (JPY), Bitcoin (BTC), gold, and the 10-year U.S. Treasury (UST10Y) under comparable tail-risk conditions. We integrate Granger causality in risk, a VAR-for-VaR model, and the cross-quantilogram into a quantilebased "triple-check" framework to jointly assess risk spillovers, dynamic tail-risk transmission, and contemporaneous tail dependence. Our contribution lies in integrating these three existing tools into a unified, definition-aligned, and structured triangulation exercise for classifying and ranking safe-haven assets. Using daily data from 2012 to 2025, we consider three sources of market stress: equity market downturns (S&P 500), volatility spikes (VIX), and surges in economic policy uncertainty (EPU). The results show that safe-haven performance is shockspecific and timing-specific. Gold consistently exhibits the strongest safe-haven properties across stress scenarios, while the Japanese yen provides limited and context-dependent protection, and Bitcoin displays only weak or conditional safe-haven behavior and never ranks as the most reliable safe-haven. The 10-year Treasury provides strong contemporaneous protection against equity downturns but only weak or conditional protection otherwise.

detail.abstract: Catastrophe bonds have become a central instrument for transferring catastrophic risk to capital markets, yet their payout structures are typically specified exogenously rather than optimized. In this paper, we treat the indemnity function as the decision variable and study the optimal design of CAT bonds from the sponsor's perspective. We establish the optimality of a piecewise linear indemnity function under both expected-disutility and spectral-risk-measure frameworks and thereby reduce an infinite-dimensional design problem to a one-dimensional optimization over the attachment point. The optimal design also eliminates the potential moral hazard associated with the discontinuity of threshold payout structures. We characterize the optimal attachment point under six risk criteria and obtain explicit or semi-explicit solutions. We further derive bounds for the optimal attachment point and develop comparative statics that provide practical design insights. Using U.S. severe storm losses from NOAA's Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters database for calibration, we show that the optimal CAT bond designs achieve substantial risk reductions across most risk criteria.

detail.abstract: How does foreign direct investment affect domestic product quality? Exploiting FDI liberalization across Indian manufacturing industries, we find that domestic product quality declines on average, but this masks sharply heterogeneous responses. Domestic firms substantially below the quality of foreign competitors upgrade following liberalization, while those near or above foreign quality downgrade. Uncovering a novel mechanism supporting the competition channel, we show that foreign firms occupy an intermediate position on the quality ladder and charge prices comparable to high-quality domestic producers. Greater exposure to such competitors may therefore reduce the returns to maintaining quality substantially above the foreign benchmark, reinforcing competitive pressures to downgrade. Our findings show that domestic firms’ quality responses to foreign entry depend critically on their position relative to foreign competitors.

title: On the Regularization of Inverse Price Impact Metrics in Discrete-Tick Markets

detail.abstract: Inverse price impact metrics of the form |∆V t |/(|∆P t | + ε) are increasingly used to measure passive liquidity absorption in high-frequency data. These metrics are ill-posed: when ∆P t = 0, the value is determined entirely by the arbitrary regularization constant ε, and cross-asset comparisons become meaningless. We show that in a market with discrete tick size δ, the choice of ε is not free. Using the standard rounding-to-nearest convention, we prove that when the observed displacement between two consecutive observations is zero, the latent displacement is bounded above by δ. We propose the Regularized Inverse Metric (RIM), with canonical regularization ε = δ, and show that after normalizing volume by average daily volume and price by mid-price, the metric becomes dimensionless and cross-asset comparable. On 30.7 million BTCUSDT 1-second bars, the Spearman rank correlation between the naive metric and RIM is only 0.62, indicating that the choice of regularization constant substantially changes the ranking of observations. A controlled cross-market comparison confirms that RIM is invariant to tick size while the naive metric is not. Our result applies to any metric of the form |∆V |/(|∆P | + ε), including the reciprocal of Amihud illiquidity.

detail.abstract: When the U.S. dollar appreciated significantly beginning around 2021, exports in Korea did not improve as predicted by conventional trade channel through price competitiveness. This paper examines whether dollar credit conditions, via the financial channel, help explain this pattern using firm-product-level data for Korean exporting firms. Estimation results show that a strong dollar is associated with tighter financial conditions and weaker exports, indicating the presence of a financial channel. The role of the financial channel is more pronounced for firms with positive dollar debt exposure. When we consider both channels, the traditional trade channel dominates the financial channel's effects on exports. However, the effects of both trade and financial channels become less pronounced during periods of sustained dollar strength. These findings suggest that the relationship between exchange rate and exports in Korea cannot be understood through price competitiveness alone and that financial conditions may also be relevant to explaining this relationship.

detail.abstract: American adolescent suicide stopped falling in 2007 and rose by more than half over the next decade. The increase was largest at the youngest ages, while adult suicide showed no comparable turn. We develop a coordination model in which the exposure is the peer network, not an adolescent's own technology use. As reaching one another became cheaper, adolescents coordinated on meeting through the phone, and the least sociable left in-person contact first. School surveys show contact thinning from the bottom of its distribution and loneliness rising among adolescents who still met, in the years suicide turned and then accelerated. The 2007 turn is concentrated among non-Hispanic white adolescents; suicide rose later among Hispanic adolescents and the youngest Black adolescents. Clinical records associate peer isolation with about twice the documented suicidal ideation; at that relative risk, shift-share arithmetic gives the mechanism up to a third of the rise.

detail.abstract: Statistical Process Control (SPC) is an important quality management approach for controlling process variation, improving product quality, and enhancing customer satisfaction in manufacturing organizations. This study examines the adoption and significance of SPC practices within Malaysia’s Electrical and Electronics (E&E) manufacturing sector, with particular emphasis on their contribution to continuous improvement and organizational competitiveness. A questionnaire-based survey was conducted among 260 companies operating in the Malaysian E&E sector to investigate the role of SPC in supporting quality-oriented manufacturing practices. The findings indicate that SPC represents an important component of effective quality management and provides organizations with a systematic approach to monitoring process performance, identifying variation, and supporting data-driven improvement initiatives. The study further highlights that achieving world-class manufacturing performance requires organizations to integrate advanced manufacturing management practices with technological innovation. Engineering innovation, therefore, should extend beyond the adoption of physical or “hard” technologies to include sophisticated quality management and process improvement techniques. The study contributes to the existing literature by highlighting the relevance of SPC within Malaysia’s E&E manufacturing environment and by providing a basis for developing a more comprehensive SPC framework for the sector. Future research could examine SPC implementation across other Malaysian manufacturing industries and investigate sector-specific factors influencing its successful adoption, thereby supporting the development of an integrated framework for total quality and operational excellence.

title: Income distribution, international competitiveness and land use in a peripheral economy: a post- Keynesian model

detail.title: Income distribution, international competitiveness and land use in a peripheral economy: a post- Keynesian model
detail.abstract: This paper develops a post-Keynesian–Structuralist model that discusses the interactions between income distribution, international competitiveness, and environmental sustainability in a peripheral economy. The economy exports land-intensive commodities and industrial goods, while industrial production relies on imported carbon-intensive energy. In the short run, commodity exports relax the balance-of-payments constraint and stimulate aggregate demand and capital accumulation, but the use of land for commodity production increases emissions and reduces carbon-sink capacity. In the long run, directed technical change can alleviate these tensions. Public R&D that increases energy efficiency and systemic competitiveness allows the periphery to reduce deforestation and the dependence on imported fossil fuels, and to diversify towards more technology-intensive industrial exports. These changes also favor a higher wage share, creating potential complementarities between environmental and distributive objectives. The results suggest that a just green transition in peripheral economies requires structural change and the endogenous development of technological capabilities capable of transforming the basis of international competitiveness.

detail.abstract: We study how banks adjust mortgage and small business lending growth in response to policy uncertainty arising from gubernatorial elections in their headquarters states. Using a bank-county-year panel from 1994 to 2016 that integrates HMDA, CRA, and Call Report data, we exploit variation across on-cycle incumbent elections (held concurrently with presidential contests), off-cycle incumbent elections, and term-limited elections to capture different levels of expected policy continuity. Banks respond systematically: during on-cycle incumbent elections, when expected continuity is highest, they expand small business lending growth and contract mortgage lending growth; during off-cycle incumbent elections, they reduce small business lending growth; and during term-limited elections, they reallocate toward safer mortgage lending, a progression from risk-taking to risk-avoidance as expected continuity declines. These patterns mask substantial institutional heterogeneity. The term-limited reallocation is driven primarily by large national banks, while large state-chartered banks move in the opposite direction, expanding small business lending growth in peripheral markets, consistent with capturing market share as national competitors retreat, and small banks adopt a wait-and-see stance. Banks also differentiate between headquarters and peripheral markets during incumbent elections, but this geographic selectivity disappears under term-limited elections. Close-election effects depend on bank type: close term-limited elections generally push banks toward a wait-and-see stance, whereas close off-cycle incumbent elections produce deeper cuts in small business lending growth among state-chartered banks.

detail.abstract: The pursuit of excellence represents one of humanity's most enduring and defining endeavors, shaping individuals, organizations, and civilizations across millennia. This comprehensive paper examines the multifaceted construct of excellence through an interdisciplinary lens, integrating philosophical, psychological, neurobiological, and practical perspectives. Drawing upon classical philosophical foundations from Aristotle's virtue ethics to Confucian principles of selfcultivation, alongside contemporary research in positive psychology, neuroscience, and organizational behavior, this analysis synthesizes current knowledge on the development, manifestation, and sustainability of excellence across diverse domains. Key findings reveal that excellence is not an innate trait but a dynamic process cultivated through deliberate practice, growth mindset, emotional intelligence, and supportive environments. The paper explores the neuroscience of peak performance, including neuroplasticity and flow states, and examines psychological factors such as grit, self-determination, and resilience that predict exceptional achievement. Practical applications encompass goal setting, habit formation, deep work, mentorship, and collaborative excellence. Domain-specific analyses address excellence in arts, sciences, sports, business, education, and healthcare. The paper also considers ethical dimensions, the relationship between excellence and well-being, and emerging challenges in an era of rapid technological change. This synthesis provides researchers, practitioners, educators, and leaders with a comprehensive framework for understanding and cultivating excellence in themselves and others.

detail.abstract: Is loss aversion a trait, or a state? We report a preregistered test: Japanese financial-group employees completed a two-state task (Kawakami and Fujitani, 2026) in one sitting, under a normal and then a crisis frame. Because selected stress items offer strictly better odds, a monotone choice model with unchanged preferences and reference points and no position effects predicts nondecreasing expected participation. It fell, significantly; a matched control pair did not. Loss aversion rises under stress. Three of four registered hypotheses are supported; the attribute bound is falsified for probability weighting alone. Normal-state rank predicts stress-state rank only in part, so single-state measurement misses a state component that the attribute set does not reach.

detail.abstract: This paper seeks to disentangle two justifications for state power over land and environment in Kenya that courts and commentators routinely conflate: the public trust doctrine and the public purpose doctrine. It argues that public trust, rooted in Articles 62, 69 and 70 of the Constitution, and public purpose, rooted in Article 40's eminent domain power, rest on different logics, serve different ends, and generate different obligations, yet Kenyan jurisprudence since 2010 has treated them as functionally interchangeable. Drawing on Peter Waweru v Republic, Mitu-Bell Welfare Society v Kenya Airports Authority, Patrick Musimba v National Land Commission, and William Musembi v Moi Educational Centre, the paper traces how this conflation has permitted public purpose reasoning to erode trust obligations, particularly in infrastructure-driven evictions and compulsory acquisition. It builds critically on Kenyan scholarship, including Okoth-Ogendo, Kameri-Mbote, Odote and Manji, before proposing a layered doctrine in which trust operates as a threshold constraint that purpose-based justifications cannot extinguish, only limit. The paper closes with legislative, judicial and institutional recommendations for restoring that hierarchy in Kenyan land law. provided the deprivation serves a public purpose or is in the public interest. 2 The first article restrains state power. The second article authorises it. Kenya's courts have not always kept these logics separate. In case after case, the language of trust is invoked to justify acquisitions, and the language of purpose is invoked to excuse the erosion of trust. Mitu-Bell Welfare Society v Kenya Airports Authority illustrates the confusion starkly, distinguishing squatters on public land from squatters on private land in a manner this paper will argue borrows uneasily from both doctrines at once. 3 This paper's thesis is that the two doctrines are conceptually distinct and must be kept so. Public trust asks what the state may do with land it holds for the people. Public purpose asks when the state may take land the people already hold privately. Confusing the two allows purpose-based reasoning, calibrated for exceptional deprivation, to colonize trust-based reasoning, which was calibrated for permanent stewardship. The paper proceeds in three sections. Section one excavates each doctrine's separate genealogy within Kenyan law, before situating the paper within existing scholarship. Section two tests the distinction against four leading cases, showing where the rivalry surfaces and who wins. Section three reconstructs a layered doctrine, in which trust functions as a threshold that purpose can limit but never extinguish, and proposes concrete legislative, judicial, and institutional reforms. The stakes are not academic. Every eviction from public land, every compulsory acquisition for a railway or a road, every forest degazettement, turns on which doctrine a court reaches for first. Kenyan land law has spent fifteen years reaching for both at once. This paper argues that it is time to choose, deliberately, which comes first.

detail.abstract: Through this study, I examine how artificial intelligence (AI) demand forecasting models and automated inventory management algorithms can optimize perishable stock control and minimize waste in small and medium-sized hospitality and retail enterprises (SMEs). Traditional inventory control in SMEs is characterized by manual, rule-based reorder points and periodic stock reviews that lead to substantial food spoilages, stockouts, and inflated working capital requirements. I operated two inventory tracking systems in parallel during a three-month comparative case study with a cluster of regional food service and grocery SMEs: a traditional periodic reorder system and an AI-powered demand forecasting platform utilizing timeseries machine learning algorithms. I analyzed five key performance indicators across 15,000 inventory stock-keeping unit (SKU) transaction records: monthly inventory waste rate, stockout frequency, inventory turnover ratio, demand forecast error (MAPE), and monthly inventory carrying overhead cost. The results indicate a remarkable operational improvement in the AI-enabled environment. The monthly waste rate was reduced by 77.2%, stockout events decreased by 80.7%, inventory turnover velocity increased by 116.1%, forecast error dropped by 77.3%, and monthly inventory overhead costs were reduced by 45.8%. The practical implications demonstrate that integrating predictive AI algorithms directly into supply chain workflows substantially advances circular economy goals and operational profitability for resourceconstrained SMEs.

title: DermStack: A Heterogeneous CNN–Transformer Ensemble with Grad-CAM++ Explainability for Five-Class Skin Disease Image Classification

detail.title: DermStack: A Heterogeneous CNN–Transformer Ensemble with Grad-CAM++ Explainability for Five-Class Skin Disease Image Classification
detail.abstract: Multi-class skin-disease image classification remains challenging due to intra-class variation, visual overlap between disease categories, uneven class frequencies, and the computational requirements of high-capacity deep-learning models. This study evaluates DermStack, a heterogeneous logit-level stacking configuration that combines GhostNet, MobileNetV3-Small, Swin Transformer-T, and a multilayer-perceptron meta-learner. The objective was to compare the practical performance of heterogeneous stacking with alternative CNN, Transformer, hybrid, and ensemble configurations under a shared experimental setting. A total of nine configurations, including four individual/hybrid models and five ensemble strategies, were evaluated on a five-class dataset containing 9,548 images using stratified training, validation, and held-out test partitions. Weighted random sampling and class-weighted cross-entropy were applied as baseline measures to mitigate the observed class imbalance. Performance was assessed using accuracy, macro precision, macro recall, macro F1-score, AUC-ROC, confusion matrices, inference efficiency, and McNemar testing. On the held-out test set of 955 images, DermStack obtained 98.53% accuracy, 0.9853 macro F1-score, and 0.9995 macro AUC-ROC, exceeding the compared configurations within this experimental setting. Grad-CAM++ was used for qualitative inspection of salient image regions, while t-SNE and K-means analyses were used to inspect feature-space separation. The findings indicate that nonlinear logit-level integration of heterogeneous CNN and Transformer predictions can improve discrimination on the evaluated dataset.
