detail.abstract: Mexico is often presented as a successful case of liberalization, as the country managed to sustain a significant manufacturing base after its openness in the mid-1980s. This paper introduces a new dimension to the analysis of manufacturing performance in the country by assessing the role of industrial policy implemented during the preliberalization period, known as the import substitution industrialization (ISI) era, in shaping post-liberalization labor productivity. This paper makes two main contributions. First, it constructs industry-level measures of industrial policy, including import licenses, tax subsidies and public credit support, based on primary sources, mainly historical government documents, and develops a harmonized industry classification using data from the Censos Econ ómicos spanning 1970 to 2019. Second, leveraging the vertical and temporal nature of ISI-era industrial policies, it examines their long-term effects in a quasi-experimental setting. The analysis shows that the gains from liberalization were larger in industries that had been more intensively promoted through fiscal subsidies and public credit during the ISI period, while no differential effects are found for industries protected through import licenses. Evidence on employment and investment suggests that these productivity gains reflect a combination of firm selection and capability building. Overall, this paper provides new evidence on the long-term effects of industrial policy and contributes to the still limited empirical literature on ISI in Latin America.

detail.abstract: Using jointly held granted invention patents in clean-energy technologies from IncoPat for 2000–2024, this study uses 89,125 institution-level records for descriptive statistics and 84,407 retained records after group consolidation to construct undirected weighted networks for eight time windows. Social network analysis, sensitivity analysis and quadratic assignment procedure (QAP) correlations examine full-network size, Top 200 subnetwork structure and the evolution of core actors. The full network expanded from 7,828 to 12,606 nodes. The core of the selected subnetworks broadened beyond Japanese manufacturing firms to include universities, research institutes, and Chinese energy and materials firms, with differentiated roles in collaboration intensity and brokerage. Removing single-record co-patenting ties leaves the identification of high-strength core actors relatively stable. Weighted QAP correlations of 0.647–0.728 between adjacent equal-length windows support tie persistence among common actors. Aggregate trends remain sensitive to actor selection, weight transformation and window duration. Additional dyadic models associate technological similarity with tie formation and recurrence. Degree-matched single-record ties connect more distant technological portfolios, but their deletion does not consistently cause greater reachability loss than deleting repeated ties. By distinguishing collaboration intensity, structural brokerage and tie persistence, the study informs differentiated partner selection, the organisation of joint R&D and collaborative innovation policy design.

title: Long-Term Population Health And Economic Effects Of Alcohol Consumption And Preventive Interventions In England: A Microsimulation Modelling Study
affiliations: University of Toronto, University of Toronto and University of Toronto

detail.title: Long-Term Population Health And Economic Effects Of Alcohol Consumption And Preventive Interventions In England: A Microsimulation Modelling Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
Background: Alcohol causes a large and unequally distributed burden of disease in England, which applies fewer population-level alcohol control measures than the other UK nations. We aimed to compare the long-term health, economic, and equity effects of four preventive interventions.

Methods: In this microsimulation modelling study, we simulated 1 000 000 individuals representing the adult population of England annually from 2025 to 2040, using openly available national data. Four interventions were compared with continued 2024 consumption: minimum unit pricing (MUP) at £0·50 and at £0·65, a duty increase raising retail prices by 10%, and expansion of structured treatment coverage from 18% to 40% of dependent drinkers. Outcomes were alcohol-related and alcohol-specific deaths, premature deaths, years of life lost, hospital admissions, alcohol-related cancers, and admission costs, by sex, age, deprivation quintile, and region. Inequality was summarised with the slope index of inequality and relative index of inequality (RII).

Findings: Against a baseline of 311 800 alcohol-related deaths and £8·56 billion in admission costs, the duty increase averted the most deaths (15 007 [4·8%]), followed by MUP at £0·65 (13 014 [4·2%]), expanded treatment (10 845 [3·5%]), and MUP at £0·50 (4807 [1·5%]). MUP at £0·65 averted the most alcohol-specific deaths (6214 [6·7%]) and alcoholic liver disease admissions (7·5%), directed 57·0% of its benefit to the most deprived fifth of the population, and reduced the RII from 7·01 to 5·87. The duty increase distributed benefit evenly and left relative inequality unchanged (RII 7·04); expanded treatment slightly widened it (RII 7·33).

Interpretation: The intervention that averts the most deaths is not the intervention that most reduces inequality. MUP at a level comparable with Scotland is the most effective option for the heaviest drinkers and the most equitable, whereas duty increases deliver a larger but evenly distributed gain. Policy choices should be judged on both criteria.

detail.abstract: A generalization of the widely applied regime switching autoregressive (RS-AR) model by Hamilton (1989) is proposed. It can be interpreted both as an approximation to the standard RS-AR model when the state variable follows an infinite-order Markov chain and as a scoredriven dynamic mixture model. We analyze the stochastic properties of the new model and establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator for it, providing the basis for formal testing against the standard model. To demonstrate its practical advantages, we conduct an empirical comparison across a variety of time series and find that the new model delivers improved estimation and predictive performance relative to the standard model.

title: Beyond Delta-Gamma: Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall for Intrinsically Quadratic Portfolios under Elliptical Risk

detail.title: Beyond Delta-Gamma: Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall for Intrinsically Quadratic Portfolios under Elliptical Risk

detail.abstract: We revisit and substantially extend an early framework for Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES) of intrinsically quadratic portfolios of securities under multivariate elliptical and mixture-of-elliptical risk factors. The quadraticity considered here is conceptually different from the usual delta-gamma approximation of derivative portfolios: it arises directly from the second-order expansion of the exponential map linking log returns to security prices. This distinction yields a structured quadratic loss whose coefficients are determined by portfolio holdings rather than option Greeks. The revised analysis makes four substantive improvements. First, it separates the exact security loss, its linear approximation, and its quadratic approximation, and derives an explicit third-order remainder bound. Second, for long-only portfolios it identifies a canonical noncentral quadratic form and shows that the quadratic loss is bounded above by one half of initial portfolio value, thereby clarifying the local nature of the approximation and the origin of the classical restriction that the quadratic VaR remain below that bound. Third, it gives a clean joint characterization of VaR and ES through the distribution and lower partial first moment of a positive quadratic form. This yields transparent extensions to finite mixtures and precise existence conditions. Fourth, it develops modern computational routes for Gaussian and Student-t factors, combining generalized noncentral chi-square methods, scale-mixture representations, and Monte Carlo validation. A reproducible simulation study compares exact revaluation, linear approximation, and quadratic approximation under Gaussian, Student-t, and mixture risks. We then apply the framework to an equally weighted portfolio of eleven French equities observed weekly from September 2019 to September 2026. On the historical sample, the quadratic approximation is nearly indistinguishable from exact revaluation at the 95%, 97.5%, and 99% levels, while the linear approximation materially overstates tail risk. A fitted multivariate Studentt model yields an estimated degree of freedom close to 5.1, confirming substantial tail thickness. We further conduct an out-of-sample-style horizon validation using daily and directly observed weekly S&P 500, NASDAQ Composite, and CAC 40 returns from September 1 2016 to September 2026, together with an equally weighted three-index portfolio. Across all markets and confidence levels, the quadratic approximation remains extremely close to exact exponential revaluation; its relative error increases from daily to weekly horizons but stays below 0.4% even for weekly 99% ES, whereas the linear approximation can overstate weekly 99% ES by about 7%. We additionally compare directly observed weekly VaR and ES with the conventional √ 5 scaling of daily measures. The scaling rule is not uniformly accurate: it generally overstates weekly tail risk for the S&P 500, NASDAQ, and the equally weighted portfolio, while it can understate some CAC 40 weekly risks. The analysis therefore separates Taylor-approximation error from temporal-scaling error. The resulting framework preserves the original contribution while providing a more rigorous, transparent, and computationally modern treatment of quadratic portfolio tail risk.

title: Compensation or Subsidy? Welfare and Political Support for Reform

detail.title: Compensation or Subsidy? Welfare and Political Support for Reform

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: A welfare-improving reform may fail to obtain majority support. We compare balanced-budget compensation to individuals who do not adapt to a reform with subsidies to those who do. Both policies affect subsequent adaptation decisions. When adaptation costs have a symmetric, weakly single-peaked distribution, and provided that at least one politically feasible transfer exists, the median individual's efficient action identifies the welfare-preferred direction of redistribution: subsidy is preferred if the median should adapt, and compensation if she should not. The same characterization determines whether economic efficiency and broad political support are aligned. Politically feasible compensation is a Pareto improvement and generates unanimous weak support, whereas a politically feasible subsidy necessarily leaves some individuals worse off and the minimum implementing subsidy obtains exactly the required majority. We extend the welfare characterization to some asymmetric distributions and provide an example showing why the distributional conditions matter.

title: Temporal Patterns And Projections Of Firearm Suicide And Homicide Mortality Among US Youth In 1999-2030
affiliations: Wuhan University - School of Health Sciences, Wuhan University - School of Health Sciences, Wuhan University - School of Health Sciences, Wuhan University - School of Health Sciences, Wuhan University - School of Health Sciences, Zhengzhou University, Xuzhou Medical University - School of Public Health and Wuhan University - School of Health Sciences

detail.title: Temporal Patterns And Projections Of Firearm Suicide And Homicide Mortality Among US Youth In 1999-2030

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This study was partially supported by the Hubei Provincial Outstanding Young Talent Project for Public Health (Principal Investigator: Bin Yu).

detail.abstract:
Background: Firearm suicide and homicide remain major public health concerns among adolescents and young adults in the United States. We aimed to disentangle age, period, and birth-cohort effects on firearm suicide and homicide mortality and to project mortality through 2030.

Method: In this population-based repeated cross-sectional study, we analyzed firearm suicide and homicide mortality among US individuals aged 15–24 years from 1999 to 2024 using CDC WONDER data. Age, period, and cohort effects were estimated using age–period–cohort models with the intrinsic estimator method. Bayesian age–period–cohort models were used to project mortality from 2025 to 2030.

Findings: The age effects of firearm suicide and homicide increased rapidly during adolescence and attenuated in early adulthood. Firearm suicide showed a V-shaped period pattern, with the lowest level around 2007, whereas firearm homicide showed a more fluctuating M-shaped pattern, with increases during 2000–2006 and 2015–2021 and declines thereafter. Cohort effects for both outcomes declined after earlier increases and rose again among more recent birth cohorts. Bayesian projections suggested that firearm homicide mortality would decline from its recent peak, whereas firearm suicide mortality would remain relatively stable at an elevated level through 2030.

Interpretation : Firearm suicide and homicide remain substantial public health burdens among US adolescents and young adults, with persistent demographic and geographic disparities. Their differing projected trajectories support sustained and targeted prevention strategies.

title: Weight of the Debt: A Selection-Adjusted Microsimulation of the Break-Even Price for GLP-1 Coverage Under Medicare and Medicaid

detail.title: Weight of the Debt: A Selection-Adjusted Microsimulation of the Break-Even Price for GLP-1 Coverage Under Medicare and Medicaid

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any people or organizations that could be perceived to have influenced this study. The author has no financial ties to, and has received no consulting fees or other compensation from, any pharmaceutical manufacturer, insurer, or other entity with a commercial interest in the outcomes discussed in this paper, including manufacturers of GLP-1 receptor agonists.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or primary data collection. It used publicly available, de-identified, aggregate survey data from the Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey, the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, and the American Community Survey to construct a synthetic simulated population for modeling purposes. No individually identifiable data were accessed, and no interaction with human subjects occurred.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or non-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
This paper estimates the price at which Medicare and Medicaid coverage of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) for obesity would pay for its own cost through medical savings. We define this price as the point at which medical savings fully offset the cost of the drug. We built a microsimulation model using two national surveys, the Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey and the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, each adjusted to match Census population totals. The model projects outcomes from 2026 to 2035.

Two features distinguish this model from prior work. First, the probability that an individual begins the drug depends on that individual's cardiovascular, kidney, and diabetes risk rather than on a single rate applied to the whole population. Second, the probability that an individual remains on the drug depends on treatment duration and out-of-pocket cost rather than on a fixed rate.

We average central-case results across 100 simulation runs. These results show that GLP-1RAs do not generate enough savings to cover their cost at current prices. In the central case, the break-even price is $820.84 per person-year for Medicare and $371.11 for Medicaid. Both figures fall well below the observed price of $2,940 to $4,478. Over ten years, this produces $215.0 billion in drug costs for Medicare and $12.6 billion for Medicaid. Savings over the same period reach only $13.3 billion and $1.1 billion.

The break-even price falls substantially under proportional coinsurance compared with a fixed copay. Coinsurance ties a patient's out-of-pocket cost directly to the price of the drug, so a higher price leads more patients to stop treatment. This finding held across an extensive set of parameter, structural, and imputation-based sensitivity tests.

We conclude that current GLP-1RA pricing does not pay for itself through medical savings alone. Changing how patients share costs would narrow this gap more than negotiating a lower price.

title: Rebuilding The Climate Code For The Digital Age Coordinating The Reformation Of Carbon Accounting And Environmental Markets To Scale The Transition Economy Common Ground Requires A Common Language, Common Instrument, And Common System Of Record

detail.title: Rebuilding The Climate Code For The Digital Age Coordinating The Reformation Of Carbon Accounting And Environmental Markets To Scale The Transition Economy Common Ground Requires A Common Language, Common Instrument, And Common System Of Record

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: No studies, just research
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract: Corporate carbon accounting and the verified carbon market ("VCM") were built by different climate action communities, for different purposes, on incompatible logics. The dominant carbon accounting framework, the Greenhouse Gas Protocol ("GHGP"), treats greenhouse gas ("GHG") emissions as information, as a company's subjective view of its direct and indirect impact, not as a transactable legal object capable of embodying or representing the environmental performance of a company project or product in commerce. Environmental attribute certificate ("EAC") markets like the VCM do the opposite. The VCM treats verified GHG reductions and removals as transferable intangible property, assets that are generated through a constitutive process that distinguishes and decouples the right to own and convey a defined environmental achievement from the measurement, reporting and verification ("MRV") information evidencing it. The net result is carbon accounting that produces MRV data with no concept of property or transactability, and the VCM that produces transactable intangible property that is disconnected from its MRV data. Neither domain, as architected, connects and integrates climate action with business decision-making, and the friction between the two stunts demand for low-carbon investment. A new coordination architecture is needed to enable markets to scale the transition, one that connects property to environmental achievements with their evidentiary records, using an authoritative system of record.

detail.abstract: NGOs and political parties publish case studies accusing multinational enterprises (MNEs) of systematic tax avoidance. We analyze three such case studies on German MNEs (BASF SE, Bayer AG, and Fresenius SE & Co. KGaA). We replicate the quantitative results presented in these studies to the extent possible and assess whether they can be considered methodologically sound. Our analysis reveals methodological weaknesses and one-sided argumentation. We therefore offer suggestions for improving the quality of future case studies from a scientific perspective. Our results also show that tax avoidance can hardly be reliably demonstrated on the basis of financial statement data.

detail.abstract: Access to the Raudhah, the sacred chamber beside the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, is officially free. Yet in 2026, thousands of Indonesian pilgrims reported paying Rp 3-5 million for "guaranteed" entry, with touts operating openly around the mosque. This chapter argues that the root cause is a four-layered systemic failure. First, the malfunctioning Nusuk app structurally excludes elderly and non-digital pilgrims through complex password requirements, an Arabic interface, and quota systems with no offline fallback. "Red card" errors, caused by duplicate data entries, turned pilgrims away at the door despite months of waiting. Second, rampant touting fills the resulting access vacuum, with intermediaries selling navigational competence at extortionate prices. Third, unauthorized levies are de facto legitimized by the absence of official alternatives. Fourth, the Indonesian Ministry of Hajj and Umrah, through PPIH, responded with empty warnings and a "barcode charity" scheme asking pilgrims to solve institutional failure themselves. This chapter terms this response procedural abdication: acknowledging app failure while refusing structural remedies such as mandatory offline pathways, expanded tasreh coverage, or bilateral engagement with Saudi authorities. Drawing on ministry statements, Ombudsman reports, Nusuk documentation, and media coverage, the study develops a Pilgrimage Access Governance Framework comprising digital accessibility assessment, offline fallback adequacy, intermediary accountability, and bilateral regulatory coordination. The chapter concludes that the Raudhah crisis is a global warning: digitizing pilgrimage governance without protecting the vulnerable invites exploitation, and weak bureaucracies become part of the crime they fail to prevent.

title: Restart Economics for AI Agents: Cutoffs, Retries, and Cost per Resolved Task

detail.title: Restart Economics for AI Agents: Cutoffs, Retries, and Cost per Resolved Task

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This work received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Repeated runs of the same AI coding agent on the same task differ widely in what they cost and whether they succeed, so an operator runs a policy rather than a single attempt: cap each attempt, retry, and hand the task to an engineer when the attempts are spent. Most work on stopping agents early asks how much compute a stopping rule saves for a given loss in success. This paper asks the operator's question instead: once every lost success has to be bought from a fallback that costs money, does stopping still save anything? It replays four logged OpenHands runs on each of the 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks for seven model configurations, 13,681 attempts in all, and scores every policy on expected cost per task, which charges agent spend, verification of what the agent submits, and a task-specific outside option priced from the benchmark's annotated engineer time at a swept wage. Because the outside option resolves every task, no policy can look cheap by abandoning hard ones. Policies are chosen on training folds and scored on held-out folds, under an analysis plan frozen and registered before any result existed.

Three things follow. When verification is automated and the fallback is an engineer, retrying is the lever: at $100 to $300 an hour it cuts expected cost by 13 to 21 percent for six configurations and 4 to 8 percent for the seventh, and raises the share of tasks the agent resolves itself from 58 to 69 percent to 69 to 78 percent. Choosing a cap on attempt length from these data adds nothing at any human wage, because attempts that have run long still succeed a third to a half of the time, and each success cut off costs tens of dollars against the few dollars of tokens a cutoff saves; a cap pays only while the fallback is worth fewer than two to four attempts, which is a few dollars an hour here, and in an unregistered check even the best cap chosen with hindsight saves at most three cents per task at $100 an hour. When each submitted patch must be reviewed at a large share of the fallback's cost, the economics reverse: retrying stops paying, the cap saves in point estimate at every wage, distinctly from zero below about $10 to $50 an hour, by keeping long attempts out of review, and, in an unregistered comparison, the best capped policy costs about what sending every task straight to the engineer costs, so the question becomes whether to run the agent at all. The registered low-complexity state rule adds little beyond a fixed cap, and switching configurations after a failure saves about 9 percent in point estimate, with an interval that includes zero.

title: Agentic Sales and Distribution in ERP: Valuing Autonomous Order-to-Cash Decisions

detail.title: Agentic Sales and Distribution in ERP: Valuing Autonomous Order-to-Cash Decisions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The sales and distribution (S&D) process inside enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems executes order capture, pricing, availability checks, credit release, and billing through deterministic rules, and routes every exception those rules did not anticipate to a person. This paper presents research and development on converting the S&D order-to-cash cycle into an agentic process, in which specialized AI agents reason over exceptions while the ERP core remains the auditable system of record. To decide which exceptions agents should handle, and with how much autonomy, the paper introduces a Total Cost of Intelligence (TCI) framework that counts every cost of machine reasoning (build, run, governance, error, and maintenance) and compares it, decision class by decision class, with the cost of the same decision made by a person. The framework draws on the hybrid deterministic-plus-agentic designs of Dharankar and Datta for pricing engines and supply chain risk mitigation. We describe the framework and its autonomy rule, illustrate it through a running example drawn from a mid-size industrial manufacturer, and detail a system architecture expressed as a directed graph with conditional routing and a humanapproval cycle. The illustrative model shows that inference tokens are about 2% of TCI while governance and residual error account for about 45%, and that most of the value comes from better pricing and substitution decisions rather than from fewer manual touches. We close with governance considerations and a key performance indicator (KPI) set for evaluating the framework's business impact.

title: Technically Ready, Operationally Defeated: Information Manipulation as a Health and Biosecurity Threat
affiliations: University Duisburg-Essen - University of Duisburg Essen, George Washington University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Cambridge - Department of Psychology and University of Duisburg-Essen

detail.title: Technically Ready, Operationally Defeated: Information Manipulation as a Health and Biosecurity Threat

declarations.declarationOfInterest: DP is the director of Novantu Ltd. He received no funding or payment for this work and contributed in his personal capacity as a researcher. All other authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Health and biosecurity preparedness focuses on pathogen detection, laboratory security and countermeasure development, yet these capabilities depend on information environments that can be manipulated. Adversaries can undermine a biological response without ever touching a pathogen: distorting how health information is produced, authenticated or circulated can reduce reporting and countermeasure uptake, endanger health workers and disrupt coordination. In this Health Policy paper, we describe a four stage pathway through which scientific uncertainty, social memory, data voids and borrowed authority are turned into operational harm, and show that generative AI accelerates each stage. We argue that digital surveillance should track loss of response function rather than volume of misleading content. Because evidence is split across health agencies, platforms, AI providers and publishers, we propose a two stage threshold: corroborated manipulation with credible effects on the response opens a time limited assessment and evidence preservation, whereas coercive measures require evidence of intent and independent authorisation.

title: Worker Type Selection in AWS Glue: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-and Memory-Optimized Resources

detail.title: Worker Type Selection in AWS Glue: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-and Memory-Optimized Resources

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: No external fund is used.

detail.abstract: AWS Glue's worker type selection determines the vCPU, memory, and disk allocated to a Spark job, and since July 2025 spans two distinct families: general-purpose G-series workers (G.025X through the newly introduced G.12X and G.16X) billed at $0.44 per DPU-hour, and memory-optimized R-series workers (R.1X through R.8X), billed at $0.52 per DPU-hour and built on a Memory-Optimized DPU that delivers exactly twice the memory per unit as a standard DPU. This paper analyzes the specific economic trade-off this pricing structure creates, computed directly from AWS's own published specifications and rates rather than assumed proportionally from the DPU-hour price alone. We show that despite carrying an 18.2% higher headline DPU-hour rate, R-series workers deliver memory 41% cheaper per gigabyte-hour than G-series workers ($0.0163 versus $0.0275 per GB-hour), while simultaneously costing 18.2% more per vCPU-hour, since vCPU count does not double alongside memory in the R-series design. We situate this finding within AWS's own official guidance for choosing between worker families, document the startup-latency trade-off AWS's own documentation attaches to the newer G.12X, G.16X, and full R-series lineup, and propose a workload-characteristic-based selection framework together with an evaluation methodology for teams validating this paper's cost analysis against their own AWS Glue jobs.

title: Deleted but Retained: What Counts as a Deletion Unit in AI Services

detail.title: Deleted but Retained: What Counts as a Deletion Unit in AI Services

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was entirely self-funded by the author. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract: AI service providers commonly state that deleted user data is removed from their systems within a fixed period, typically thirty days. This paper examines what such statements cover. Drawing on records collected by a single user across several services in 2025 and 2026, it argues that the weakness of the right to be forgotten in AI services lies less in the length of retention periods than in which stores are counted as objects of deletion at all. The paper introduces the notion of a deletion unit, the set of objects that a user's deletion action actually reaches, and shows how account-bound derivatives, configuration objects, and legally held copies can remain outside it. The analysis is placed within the lineage of zero trust, from its computational formulation to recent vendor frameworks that extend it to AI workloads, and contrasts those frameworks with an approach that directs verification at vendor claims about data collection and deletion. Verification of such claims, the paper argues, can only be established through records held outside the vendor.

title: Long-Horizon Compatibility Contracts for AI Audit Trails

detail.title: Long-Horizon Compatibility Contracts for AI Audit Trails

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Quantamix Solutions B.V., which develops AI governance software and holds pending European patent applications related to the subject of this paper; the author therefore has a commercial interest in it. Drafting and source verification were assisted by an AI system (Claude, Anthropic); the author reviewed the text and is responsible for all content.

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors. It was carried out by the author at Quantamix Solutions B.V.

detail.abstract:
The EU Artificial Intelligence Act obliges providers of high-risk AI systems to build logging into their systems "over the lifetime of the system" (Article 12), to keep the resulting logs for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months unless other Union or national law provides otherwise (Article 19; Article 26(6) for deployers), and to keep technical and quality-management documentation at the disposal of authorities for ten years after the system is placed on the market (Article 18). Following the 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI, these obligations apply to Annex III systems from 2 December 2027 and to Annex I systems from 2 August 2028. The Act says what must be kept and for how long. It is silent on a question that every long-lived digital record eventually faces: will anyone still be able to check it?

This paper argues that the evidentiary value of an AI audit record is a function of two things, not one: the record, and the continued existence of a verifier that can interpret it and reach the same verdict that would have been reached on the day the record was made. Record formats are revised, cryptographic algorithms are retired on published timetables that fall inside the Act's retention window, vendors exit markets, and verification software stops being maintained. None of these events deletes a record; each can silently turn it into bytes that prove nothing. The digital-preservation and long-term-signature communities have understood this for three decades, and EU law already recognises it for electronic signatures. We argue that the practice of AI audit logging has yet to absorb the lesson.

We propose that any party producing AI audit records for regulatory purposes publish a compatibility contract comprising four commitments: (C1) an explicitly versioned proof format, (C2) a stated negotiation rule that determines what a verifier does when it meets a record version other than its own, including refusal on unknown versions, (C3) a published long-term-support window tied to the retention horizon rather than to the vendor's release cadence, and (C4) a governed procedure for the rare cases in which compatibility must be broken. We state each commitment normatively, derive a checklist that a market-surveillance authority, notified body or procurement officer could apply without access to source code, and relate the proposal to ISO/IEC 42001, the OAIS reference model, ETSI long-term signature preservation standards and the eIDAS Regulation. This is a position paper. It reports no measurements, and its limitations, including its single-vendor perspective, are set out explicitly.

title: The Enterprise Data Access Architecture: A Decoupled Approach to Real-Time, Conversational Access to Enterprise Systems

detail.title: The Enterprise Data Access Architecture: A Decoupled Approach to Real-Time, Conversational Access to Enterprise Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any organization that could be perceived to have influenced this research. This work was conducted independently, outside of and unaffiliated with any employer.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper describes the author's independent engineering work and an illustrative case study; it does not involve human research participants, patient data, or personally identifiable information, and no third-party consent is required.

detail.abstract: Enterprise software increasingly promises conversational, natural-language access to operational data-spend records, order status, procurement history-as an alternative to navigating traditional reporting interfaces. This promise is harder to deliver than it first appears: many enterprise backends expose their most useful data only through asynchronous, rate-limited application programming interfaces (APIs) that were never designed with a conversational, near-instant user experience in mind. This paper describes the Enterprise Data Access Architecture, a practitioner's architectural view on reconciling these two worlds. By decoupling the natural-language understanding, backend integration, and result-delivery functions-conventionally bundled into a single tightly coupled request-response cycle-into independent layers, conversational interfaces can be made to feel responsive even when the underlying infrastructure is not. An illustrative implementation of this architecture, referred to here as the Enterprise Data Access Assistant, was deployed against a commercial enterprise procurement platform to validate the approach. With this backdrop, this paper discusses the concrete failure modes that motivated this separation, explores the high-level design philosophy, and addresses the broader implications for enterprises looking to enable conversational and AI-assisted access to legacy and third-party enterprise systems. This paper is meant to provide a conceptual and business-focused companion piece to a more detailed technical treatment maintained separately by the author.

title: Proof-Carrying Data Obligations for AI Audit Trails: Implementation Lessons toward the PCT Open Specification

detail.title: Proof-Carrying Data Obligations for AI Audit Trails: Implementation Lessons toward the PCT Open Specification

Drafting and source verification were assisted by an AI system (Claude, Anthropic); the author reviewed the text and is responsible for all content.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The paper involves no human participants, patient data or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors. It was carried out by the author at Quantamix Solutions B.V.

detail.abstract:
The European Union AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) requires, in Article 12, that high-risk AI systems "technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system", in order to ensure "a level of traceability of the functioning" of the system. The Act prescribes the property, not the mechanism; in practice the requirement is met by vendor-specific log formats whose semantics are not portable and whose integrity protection is procedural rather than cryptographic. The OPSF draft Proof Claims Token (PCT) specification defines a portable, signed, JWT-inspired token in which data carries its obligations with it: before any action - an AI model call, a cross-border transfer, a processing operation - the token is verified, the action is allowed or blocked, and an audit record is generated.

This working paper reports what one implementer learned while building a publicly available PCT v0.1 issuer and validator in the GraQle SDK, alongside a separate RFC 6962 Merkle-commitment layer for audit records in the same SDK. We ask two questions: (RQ1) how should a PCT deployment commit its audit records to an external transparency log without anchoring every record individually? and (RQ2) which EU AI Act obligations can be carried inside the PCT extension mechanism beyond the five fields of the core specification's x-ai-act namespace?

We make four contributions. First, we describe the reference issuer/validator (graqle.pct) and state precisely what it does and does not yet implement. Second, we offer two additive proposals to the specification - batch-mode commitment of audit records with a published deadline and pinning of the governing constraint version inside the signed or hashed content. Third, we document the x-ai-eu extension namespace, an eleven-field binding to EU AI Act articles that we filed publicly with OPSF on 27 June 2026 , and map each field to the article it serves. Fourth, we give an analytical (not measured) account of the anchoring cost that batch-mode removes.

Evidence status. This paper contains no measured performance results. The reference implementation has unit tests but has not been benchmarked, and we know of no production deployment of it. Where quantities appear they are either public facts with a citation, configuration defaults readable in the public repository, or arithmetic consequences of stated parameters. The paper is offered to the OPSF technical committee as implementer input; it is not an OPSF document and implies no endorsement.

title: Catchy or Sketchy? How Thumbnail-Title Congruence Shapes Curiosity and Video Viewership
affiliations: University of Georgia, University of Connecticut - Department of Operations & Information Management, Yonsei University and College of Business, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)

detail.title: Catchy or Sketchy? How Thumbnail-Title Congruence Shapes Curiosity and Video Viewership

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations about this paper
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding

detail.abstract: On video-sharing platforms, where countless videos compete for attention, users decide what to watch based on a small set of cues jointly signaling a video's content. We examine how the title's semantic congruence with each thumbnail component-its image and overlaid text-shapes viewership. A field study of 10,098 YouTube videos from 233 creators reveals a modality asymmetry: image-title congruence is positively associated with subsequent views, whereas text-title congruence is negatively associated with them. Drawing on information-gap theory, we propose that congruence shapes both the perceived information gap between the cues and its expected resolvability through viewing. A preregistered experiment with 996 participants, using generative AI to manipulate both forms of congruence, supports this account. Increasing image-title congruence enhanced curiosity and video choice, whereas increasing text-title congruence did not. Image-title congruence also more strongly affected perceived information gap and expected resolvability. Moreover, the association between information gap and curiosity became more positive as expected resolvability increased and was positive at high levels of resolvability. These findings suggest that curiosity depends not only on the discrepancy conveyed by a preview but also on its expected resolution, and multimodal preview components are not interchangeable.

title: Passport of Verified Anthropogenic Information as the Basis for an Exit from Epistemic Resonance in the Era of AI

detail.title: Passport of Verified Anthropogenic Information as the Basis for an Exit from Epistemic Resonance in the Era of AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
This work conceptualizes "Epistemic Resonance" — the synchronous, convergent demand of the human, large language models (LLMs), and the AI industry for verified Anthropogenic Information. This resonance arises as a coincidence of extreme structural crises, provoked by autonomous yet interdependent interactions among these actors. 

The work formalizes and delineates the conceptual apparatus. The anthropogenicity index Ia is introduced as an ontological characteristic of the origin of information. It is demonstrated that in an AI-centric reality, the verifiability and factual reliability of data are necessary but insufficient conditions for the emergence of trust.

The mechanisms of the destructive feedback loop are investigated, in which the delegation of creation to AI forces the contamination of training corpora, accelerates model collapse, and destroys the epistemic barriers to further delegation. The neurocognitive and evolutionary foundations of the human demand for an anthropogenic trace are analyzed, as well as the architectural dependence of the LLM on verified anthropogenic raw material and the systemic crisis of the AI industry, expressed in the scaling impasse, the decline of trust, and the insolvency of a posteriori solutions. 
 
As a systemic exit from this resonance, the author proposes the "Passport of Verified Anthropogenic Information" (PVAI) — an open standard for the a priori verification of information origin that captures the cognitive signature of live creation during human mental inference. The architecture of the PVAI software core and its global verification registry infrastructure (pvai.app) are described. The study concludes that Epistemic Resonance can trigger a structural shift toward the a priori affirmation of human agency, shaping the future of the global information ecosystem.

The conclusion is drawn that the recorded Epistemic Resonance is capable of acting as a trigger of a structural shift toward the a priori affirmation of human agency, and thereby of defining the contours of the next turn of development of the global information ecosystem.

title: A Payment and Entitlement Gate for Self-Serve Agentic Expert-Access: Architecture and a Formal Admission Model

detail.title: A Payment and Entitlement Gate for Self-Serve Agentic Expert-Access: Architecture and a Formal Admission Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of True Primary, the firm whose practice and target architecture this paper describes. The paper makes no claim of deployed product capability.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
A software agent buying expert work for a principal needs an answer, inside one request, to whether a purchase may start. This paper gives an architecture and a formal model for that decision. One gate state separates quotation and authority checks from fulfilment and admits a quote on one of two branches: a payment credential presented against the operator’s internal payment requirement, or a plan check against an entitlement the client already holds.
Four structural facts and one invariant theorem are established over the task model: fulfilment starts only after admission; a request key yields at most one activation; a task consumes at most one admission token; a delivered artefact carries an operator-signed receipt that verifies against the operator’s own records, with no independent party attesting it; and gross committed spend under a mandate stays within its cap when purchases run concurrently, under a per-mandate serialised reserve-and-commit. A corollary adds the entitlement side: a prepaid balance never goes negative under concurrent draws. A validation supplement, identified in the paper by its hash, checks the results on fulfilment, token consumption and spend, and the corollary by exhaustive search of five bounded instances of a Python encoding of the model. The Machine Payments Protocol (MPP) is the candidate wire protocol for the payment branch, and the paper fixes how an adapter binds MPP challenges to the internal requirement, what each response carries and how a refused credential leaves the task at the gate.
The model departs from the author’s Internet-Draft of July 2026: it adds a separate entitlement branch and the concurrent budget result, and it differs from the draft on the timing of the payment challenge, gate refusals, deadlines and mandate revocation. Admission records an accepted credential, a billing receivable or a consumed allowance; collection of funds, provider behaviour and any deployed implementation lie outside the results.
AI use. The author conceived this paper and its argument, directed its development, verified its content, and takes full responsibility for it. AI tools assisted with drafting, editing, code and typesetting. AI was not used to generate scientific content, analyses, interpretations, or conclusions.

title: Open Source as Regulatory Infrastructure: Where the Open/Closed Line Should Sit for AI Governance Tooling

detail.title: Open Source as Regulatory Infrastructure: Where the Open/Closed Line Should Sit for AI Governance Tooling

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Quantamix Solutions B.V., which develops AI governance software and holds pending European patent applications related to the subject of this paper; the author therefore has a commercial interest in it. Drafting and source verification were assisted by an AI system (Claude, Anthropic); the author reviewed the text and is responsible for all content.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The paper involves no human participants, patient data or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors. It was carried out by the author at Quantamix Solutions B.V.

detail.abstract:
The EU Artificial Intelligence Act obliges providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems to generate, keep and hand over records: automatically generated logs, technical documentation, and information supplied to authorities on request. A market of "AI governance tooling" is forming to produce those records. This paper asks a narrow question that the Act does not answer: who can check such a record, and with what? If the only software able to read and verify an evidence record is sold by the party whose customer produced it, then regulators, notified bodies and affected persons depend on that vendor's goodwill, pricing and survival. We call this the verification asymmetry.

We first set out, cautiously and from the primary texts, how EU law treats open source today: the AI Act's exclusions and carve-outs (Article 2(12), Article 25(4) as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, Article 53(2), recitals 89 and 102-104); the Cyber Resilience Act's definition of free and open-source software and its "open-source software steward" regime (Articles 3(14), 3(48), 24, 25 and 64(10)); and the one place we found where Union law requires open-source licensing of trust-critical software, the European Digital Identity Wallet (Article 5a(3) of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 as amended). We then examine four precedents in which open verification became shared infrastructure - Certificate Transparency, ACME and Let's Encrypt, Sigstore, and reproducible builds - and identify what made them work, including the parts that have nothing to do with licensing.

We compare three places a vendor could draw the line - everything open; open verification with commercial operation; closed with escrow and authority access - and their consequences for regulators, deployers, affected persons and vendors. We argue that the verification side (format specifications, verifier implementations, test vectors) has the economic character of infrastructure and should be open, while value-added operation can remain commercial, and we make recommendations to policymakers and standardisation bodies. The paper is conceptual: it reports no measurements and takes no position on any particular company's licensing decisions.

title: The Global Hyperscale Dilemma: A Unified Engineering, Political Economy, and Policy Framework for Water-Efficient, Grid-Sovereign, and Chemically Safe AI Data Centres

detail.title: The Global Hyperscale Dilemma: A Unified Engineering, Political Economy, and Policy Framework for Water-Efficient, Grid-Sovereign, and Chemically Safe AI Data Centres

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study as it did not involve human participants or live animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or external funding from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors

detail.abstract: The rapid structural proliferation of high-density Artificial Intelligence (AI) workloads including large-scale transformer model training and continuously executing agentic computing architectures has driven rack-level power densities from 5-15 kW to 40-60+ kW, concentrating unprecedented resource stress on civilian electricity grids, hydrological aquifers, and global chemical ecosystems. This paper presents the first integrated global framework that simultaneously addresses the technical, political economy, and institutional dimensions of this crisis. We make three original contributions. First, we document and analyse the political economy of inaction: why existing regulatory models have systematically failed despite the availability of proven technical solutions, mapping the stakeholder conflicts among hyperscale corporations, sovereign grid operators, municipal water authorities, and affected local communities. Second, we address the fluorinated dielectric fluid toxicity trilemma: the dangerous paradox whereby liquid immersion cooling-the leading technical solution for water conservation-introduces irreversible per-and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) contamination into soil and groundwater systems if not governed by chemical containment mandates. Third, we propose three binding institutional mechanisms-a G20 Data Infrastructure Sustainability Compact modelled on cap-and-trade architecture, an IEA Tier-1 Hardware Certification Matrix with mandatory Chemical Passports, and a UNEP Fluid Governance Framework operating under Stockholm Convention precedent-each with explicit enforcement mechanisms, funding structures, and stakeholder incentive designs. Drawing on comparative case analysis of the Dublin EirGrid moratorium, Singapore's compute migration crisis, and the Northern Virginia PJM grid emergency, this paper argues that the failure of data centre governance is not primarily a technical failure but a political economy failure requiring institutional architecture capable of overcoming the collective action problem of the global commons.

title: Claim Limits in AI Audit Records: Naming What a Record Cannot Prove

detail.title: Claim Limits in AI Audit Records: Naming What a Record Cannot Prove

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Quantamix Solutions B.V., which develops AI governance software and holds pending European patent applications related to the subject of this paper; the author therefore has a commercial interest in it. Drafting and source verification were assisted by an AI system (Claude, Anthropic); the author reviewed the text and is responsible for all content.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The paper involves no human participants, patient data or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors. It was carried out by the author at Quantamix Solutions B.V.

detail.abstract:
The EU Artificial Intelligence Act requires high-risk AI systems to record events automatically, requires providers and deployers to keep those logs, and gives authorities access to them. The Act says what logs are for - traceability, monitoring, post-market surveillance - but it does not say what a log proves. That silence matters. A well-made audit record is good evidence of a small number of things: that an event was recorded, by which system or party, at what time, and that the record has not been altered since. It is not evidence that the decision was correct, that the inputs were true, that the model was unbiased, that a human reviewer exercised real judgement, or that the law was satisfied. Yet a record that is tidy, signed and complete-looking invites exactly those inferences. We call this the over-reading problem, and its institutional consequence the "auditable-but-wrong" moral hazard: an organisation that can produce an impeccable record of a bad decision is better placed to defend that decision than one that kept no record at all.

This position paper argues that AI audit records should carry an explicit claim-limit declaration: a short statement, readable by people and processable by machines, of what the record attests and what it does not. We (i) read Article 12, Article 13, Article 14, Article 19 and Article 26 of the Act for what they ask of records; (ii) offer a vendor-neutral taxonomy that separates four things a record can attest (occurrence, integrity, origin, time) from eight things it cannot attest on its own (completeness, input veracity, output correctness, fairness, explanatory fidelity, quality of human oversight, legality, and generalisation); (iii) show that declared limits are an established practice in neighbouring fields - the auditor's opinion under the International Standards on Auditing, the rules of evidence on electronic records, the eIDAS presumptions, content-provenance and software-supply-chain specifications, and model cards and datasheets; and (iv) state normative requirements for the content, placement, language and stability of such a declaration, with two plain-language illustrations (a credit assessment record and a remote biometric identification record) and a worked application of the taxonomy to the published evaluation record of the author's own system. We also examine how the idea can fail: as boilerplate, as a liability shield, and through limit inflation. The paper is conceptual. It reports no empirical results, and its taxonomy has not been tested with auditors, courts or regulators.

title: Industrial Expansion: The Absorption Constraint

detail.title: Industrial Expansion: The Absorption Constraint

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Industrial development is often analysed through the question of how productive capacity is created. Capital accumulation, technological acquisition, infrastructure construction, and organisational improvement expand the ability of an economy to produce. However, the expansion of productive capacity creates a further analytical problem: whether the surrounding economic system can absorb, circulate, and reproduce the additional output generated by that capacity.

This paper develops the concept of the absorption constraint. The absorption constraint is not equivalent to insufficient consumption alone. It refers to the wider capacity of an economic system to incorporate additional output through household demand, productive investment, intermediate demand, public provisioning, and external markets.

The framework distinguishes the absorption constraint from general theories of demand deficiency and from the broader concept of constraint migration. Constraint migration describes the movement of binding constraints after successful development; the absorption constraint describes a specific case in which expanding productive capability exceeds the adjustment speed of the systems required to realise and reproduce that output.

Keywords absorption constraint; industrial expansion; productive capacity; demand absorption; productive organisation; development economics

detail.abstract: Recommendation systems are becoming vital for enabling users to find useful materials in the rapidly growing world of digital and hybrid library collections. However, they face problems of data sparseness, cold starts, anonymous users, heterogeneous metadata, privacy, and low diversity. This paper shows the development of recommendation systems from collaborative filtering and content-based methods to hybrid, semantic, knowledge-based, context-aware, and AI approaches in terms of their applicability in libraries. The analysis demonstrates perspectives of hybrid recommendation systems, which combine bibliographical, behavioural, semantic, and contextual evidence. One of the main focuses is on the use of semantic representations and transformer-based methods, which allow establishing connections between different resources in libraries without using mere keywords. The article discusses problems of privacy, algorithmic biases, explainability, quality of metadata, interoperability, and evaluation issues. The synthesis reveals knowledge gaps in the areas of anonymity, regular users and cold users, behavioural and semantic evidence, diversity, user power, and privacypreserving personalisation. Therefore, the identified issues show the importance of adaptive and responsible recommendation systems that focus on more than just accuracy.

detail.abstract: E-hailing services, connecting passengers with vehicles via apps, are widespread. However, street-hailing taxis retain a significant market share, especially where regulations protect traditional taxis or internet access is limited. Robotaxis (shared autonomous vehicles) are emerging as a new taxi service mode. As robotaxis are unsuited for street-hailing, understanding operations where human-driven taxis (both hailing modes) coexist with e-hailing-only robotaxis is crucial. While prior studies examined mixed-hailing, few considered its interplay with heterogeneous fleet compositions, especially robotaxis' inability to serve street-hailing. This study introduces "mixed-hailing" and "heterogeneous fleet" concepts, presenting an analytical model to understand their serviceability impact, validated by simulation with real-world Daejeon data. Analysis confirms that higher e-hailing and autonomous taxi proportions reduce costs, guiding efficient service management. Conversely, dominant street-hailing requires larger fleets and higher costs to maintain service levels, increasing user waiting times and vehicle idle times-undesirable for all stakeholders.

title: Financial Access and the Returns to Digital Infrastructure: Evidence from Broadband Upgrades and Firm Exports
affiliations: Universitat Barcelona, Universitat de Barcelona, Ministerio de Comercio, Industria y Turismo, Colombia and The World Bank

detail.title: Financial Access and the Returns to Digital Infrastructure: Evidence from Broadband Upgrades and Firm Exports

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: We gratefully acknowledge financial from the Spanish Ministerio de Ciencia e Innovación (MCI), Agencia Estatal de Investigación (AEI) and the Fondo Europeo de Desarrollo Regional (FEDER) (Grants: PID2022-139468NB-I00, PID2024-158983OB-I00).

detail.abstract: We study whether access to finance shapes firms' ability to benefit from digital technologies. Exploiting the staggered rollout of fiber broadband (FTTX) across Peru between 2014 and 2020, we show that improved internet quality increases exports, primarily by strengthening existing trade relationships rather than inducing exporter entry or product diversification. The gains vary substantially with firms' pre-existing access to bank credit. Firms with intermittent credit access experience the largest export gains, while those with no pre-existing credit access experience smaller gains and those with stable credit access exhibit no significant response. Alongside these export gains, firms with intermittent credit access also experience the largest increase in borrowing after FTTX arrives. These findings point to a non-monotonic relationship between pre-existing financial access and the returns to digital infrastructure. Our interpretation is that the returns to digital technologies depend not only on access to infrastructure but also on firms' financial capacity to exploit new opportunities.

detail.abstract: This study develops and evaluates a circular supplier-selection framework for Vietnam's electronics industry by identifying criteria relevant to strategic sourcing, determining their relative priorities and examining the influence structure connecting supplier capabilities with operational outcomes. A two-round modified Delphi process involving ten experts validated 29 criteria across six dimensions. The Analytic Hierarchy Process was subsequently applied to 20 consistent expert responses to determine the relative weights, while DEMATEL was used to distinguish the netinfluencing dimensions from those primarily influenced within the system. The results identify Product Quality, Cost and Service Performance, and Environmental Management as the highest-priority dimensions. However, Environmental Management and Technological Capability and Innovation emerge as the principal net-influencing dimensions, whereas Product Quality and Cost and Service Performance are positioned primarily as system outcomes. Circularity serves as a connecting mechanism through which enabling capabilities contribute to operational performance. These findings suggest that firms should retain quality and cost as supplier-screening conditions while directing supplier-development efforts towards environmental management, technological innovation and circular capabilities. By distinguishing the criteria prioritised in supplier evaluation from the capabilities exerting the greatest systemic influence, the study extends circular supplier selection from an operational purchasing decision towards a strategic sourcing process. The expert-based, singlecountry design nevertheless limits generalisability; future research should validate the framework using supplier performance data and applications across different industries and countries.

detail.abstract: In a world of increasing civilization, innovation, and inventive voyages, technology has transformed the way we interact with one another, although the pace of technological growth varies across different continents. Theologically, technology can be traced back to ancient Babylon. Technology plays a crucial role in various aspects of daily life, including communication, education, household chores, healthcare, and transportation. Technology law is one of the emerging and most in-demand fields of the legal profession today. You may not have heard about it, but technology law helps keep you and your information safe. It also ensures a fair and competitive marketplace for sellers and buyers and may provide answers to some of modern society's most complex questions, particularly those relating to robotics and artificial intelligence. Technology law is important because technology increasingly shapes how we live, work, communicate, conduct business, and exercise our rights. As innovation develops faster than traditional legal frameworks, technology law provides the rules necessary to ensure that technological advancement remains responsible, secure, and respectful of fundamental rights. The emergence of rules and regulations governing the development, deployment, and use of technology is broadly referred to as technology law. There is, however, no single definition that exhaustively captures its scope. Technology law encompasses, inter alia, areas such as data protection and privacy, Finance, cyber security, intellectual property, telecommunications, competition law, Environmental law (climate law) and human rights law. It is therefore noteworthy to draw a distinction between technology law and other branches of law, even though it often intersects with them.

title: Sacred Steinkerns: Shaligram Shilas as a Living Geomyth, and the Palaeontological Consequences of Devotional Custody

detail.abstract: Shaligram shilas are Late Jurassic ammonoid internal moulds and concretions that weather out of the Spiti Shale Formation in the Kali Gandaki valley of Mustang District, Nepal. They are venerated across South Asia as aniconic, self-manifest forms of Vishnu, one of the longest continuously documented engagements between a religious tradition and a specific fossil assemblage. Part I reconstructs the object: its Tethyan setting on the northern Gondwanan margin, its low-diversity, perisphinctoid-dominated ammonoid fauna, and the taphonomic pathway from anoxic to dysoxic organic-rich muds, early concretionary cementation, internalmould preservation and fluvial rounding in a gorge incised during Himalayan uplift, that yields the black, smooth, spirally-marked object ritual practice requires. Part II places the tradition within geomythology, arguing that Shaligrams fit Vitaliano's etiological class poorly and are better read as a custodial geomyth: one in which the myth attaches to a portable object rather than a fixed feature, and in which ritual demands the object's removal and circulation. An interview study of 35 Hindu households in Hyderabad (analytic n = 31), coded on six dimensions, yields three findings. There is no cross-generational gradient in fossil awareness; grandparents scored marginally highest. What differs by generation is not the level of naturalorigin knowledge but the route to it: elders held it as pre-existing traditional transmission, whereas young respondents more often reached it through their own online research. And fossil recognition does not erode reverence: 90.3% reported coexistence or deepening, and awareness and reverence were weakly positively associated. Custodial disposition was near-uniform (93.5% scoring 2 or 3 of 3; none willing to sell), which we read as an informal conservation mechanism but qualify against evidence that formal geoheritage protection in Mustang is now in tension with the ritual mobility the tradition requires.

title: The Balance Sheet Illusion: Why Traditional Credit Metrics Penalize Private Manufacturing SMEs and Family Businesses

detail.title: The Balance Sheet Illusion: Why Traditional Credit Metrics Penalize Private Manufacturing SMEs and Family Businesses
detail.abstract: This article challenges traditional financial ratios as definitive measures of organizational health, exposing a ’Balance Sheet Illusion.’ Drawing on senior-level executive experience, this qualitative multiple-case study (N = 7) analyzes manufacturing SMEs to demonstrate that unadjusted financial statements function strictly as trailing indicators of an underlying corporate culture. For instance, mechanical credit underwriting templates frequently misclassify an intentional corporate net loss as operational failure, blind to strategic capital extractions engineered precisely to satisfy strict bank covenants. Findings indicate that enterprise recovery requires a dynamic turnaround loop transitioning from financial diagnostics to qualitative cultural alignment and strategic leadership execution. Ultimately, sustainable profitability occurs indirectly through core purpose alignment, or obliquity.

title: The Architecture Of Theft

detail.title: The Architecture Of Theft

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing personal, financial, or institutional interests that could have influenced this study.

detail.abstract:
This article develops a conceptual model of extraction as an architecture rather than a single act. Its starting question is why sophisticated exploitation can proceed without overtly defeating resistance. The proposed answer is that extraction may be enabled through a sequence of conversions: asymmetric power creates access; access borrows trust from institutions, professions, communities, or recognized positions; borrowed trust can reduce consequential verification; a decision environment can make transfer appear reasonable; protected or dormant resources can be converted into extractable forms; and extracted value can be recycled into protection, influence, and renewed access. Exposure does not necessarily terminate the architecture. If the conversion functions remain intact, a depleted legitimating story may be replaced by another and the cycle can restart. The paper integrates research on trust and affinity, fraud and victim decision-making, organizational corruption and normalization, corruption networks, accountability, and legitimacy repair. It formulates six propositions: trust-verification substitution, impunity learning, engineered consent, resource mobilization into extractability, protective architecture, and recurrent re-legitimation. Each proposition is paired with an observable implication and a mechanism-breaking condition. A short decoder then translates the model into comparative questions without treating loss, persuasion, trust, delay, or institutional complexity as proof of wrongdoing. The model is conceptual. It does not establish empirical causality, collapse distinct legal categories, or function as a forensic diagnostic.

detail.abstract: This article examines the organisation of French online content creation through an analysis of the business models of creators active either on YouTube or Twitch. Our findings highlight similarities with the traditional creative activity, as there are disparities in the audience and revenue among content creators. Through a Hierarchical Clustering on Principal Components, we identify three distinct models of production and monetisation strategies (also referred to as creative models): amateur production, commercial activity in an indirect partnership with brands and advertisers, and commercial one in a direct partnership with brands. Moreover, we find that the adoption of a creative model depends on the platform chosen by the creator to publish his production, his videos' genre and his audience size. Some characteristics are key eligibility criteria in a platform's monetisation policy. Our results shed additional light on the dependence relation between content creators and platforms, and in some extend between producers and advertisers.

detail.abstract:
This paper is written by Jiawei Wang (Warwick Business School, University of Warwick).

Large language models lower the cost of reading corporate disclosures, but reliance on common models can also make investors’ interpretations more similar. I study this trade-off using the public launch of ChatGPT and three pre-launch properties of corporate filings: readability, length, and uncertainty. AI can help decode difficult prose, but it cannot resolve uncertainty about outcomes that the disclosure leaves unaddressed. After the launch, order flow becomes more one-sided in hard-to-read firms. The effect grows as frontier models accumulate and appears in both retail and non-retail trading. This greater synchronization also carries information. In these firms, weekly return reversal falls by about half, earnings news is incorporated faster, and synchronized order flow predicts returns at longer horizons. The effect also extends across stocks: non-retail order flow comoves more across hard-to-read stocks. Length has little stable relation with these outcomes, while uncertainty weakens synchronization without improving price discovery. To rationalize these patterns, I develop a Kyle-style model in which delegation improves decoding but introduces shared error. Because trading on information held by others is less profitable, delegation is a strategic substitute and crowding limits adoption. The model explains how greater synchronization can coexist with better price discovery.

detail.abstract: Many adult professionals who use English at work are grammatically accurate yet still hesitate, tire quickly and are judged as less fluent than their knowledge would predict. This conceptual paper proposes a pedagogical framework that treats fluency as two distinct teaching targets, defined by whose experience they describe. Internal fluency is the speaker's side: the cognitive effort, confidence and fatigue involved in producing speech. Perceived fluency is the listener's side: speed, pausing, recovery from breakdowns, and recognisable first-language (L1) patterns that make speech harder to process. The framework is a deliberate pedagogical simplification of Segalowitz's distinction between cognitive, utterance and perceived fluency, and the paper states what that simplification gains and loses. It then describes a five-stage instructional sequence developed over a decade of one-to-one teaching with executives in Brazil, the three ordering principles behind it (simplicity, foundation, socialisation), a delayedfeedback format for advanced learners, the use of L1 transfer from Portuguese ("lusophonisms") as a diagnostic category, and a between-session feedback loop based on recorded lessons. The paper closes with seven falsifiable propositions, with the controls each one needs. It reports no outcome data and makes no claim of effectiveness; its aim is to make the approach explicit enough to be tested and, where the evidence goes against it, revised.
