detail.abstract: This essay proposes a unified theoretical framework for the macroeconomics of monetary capitalism. Its starting point is a methodological distinction between accounting identities-income and output, saving and investment, the quantity identity MV ≡ PQ, the zero sum of world trade balances-which always hold ex post, and adjustment laws, which describe how agents decide and determine which variable of each identity actually moves. On this basis, the essay builds a system governed by the maximization of the mass of profit on committed capital, own and borrowed, and by six laws of behavior: diminishing marginal social returns to labor, nominal wages rising with employment, a declining marginal propensity to consume, a net-worth constraint on credit, price adjustment according to the scope of market signals, and asset prices driven by expected profit and a speculative factor. The normal price is anchored in the rate of interest, which thereby regulates the rate of profit and the real wage. Persistent inflation is derived as distributive conflict financed by endogenous bank money, so that the quantity identity is read in reverse. It is shown that private expansion meets an endogenous limit before full employment, because realization is exhausted before profitability. Once that limit is reached, the State is the only agent able to expand effective demand autonomously, through the inflation of private portfolios validated by the central bank. The contradiction of the system is thereby displaced to the balance-sheet plane, measured by the gap between market prices and the simultaneous realization price of assets. The framework is extended to open economies with a floating exchange rate and a central bank balance sheet, and to currency-taking economies, which face a second, external limit to growth imposed by the availability of foreign exchange within an international monetary hierarchy headed by the reserve-currency issuer.

title: Optical Fiber in the AI Era: Korea’s Position and Challenges Ahead
affiliations: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade

detail.title: Optical Fiber in the AI Era: Korea’s Position and Challenges Ahead
detail.abstract:
Demand from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers for submarine cables is expanding, and optical fiber is emerging as a core material of digital infrastructure; cable demand for AI applications rose 77 percent in 2025 over the previous year (CRU).

South Korea leads the OECD in the share of fixed lines carried on optical cable, at 90.5 percent, yet its materials base is thin: only one domestic company produces preform, the stage at which value is concentrated. China, the United States, Japan, and India have each cultivated a domestic optical fiber industry, through subsidies and procurement preferences, domestic content requirements, state-funded research and development, and production linked incentives respectively, whereas Korea has no policy tailored to optical fiber materials.

This study compares demand and price trends in the global optical fiber market, the competitiveness of the major producers, and policy at home and abroad, and on that basis sets out directions for developing Korea’s optical fiber materials industry: securing high-value preform manufacturing capability, developing next-generation fiber technologies such as multi-core fiber (MCF) and hollow-core fiber (HCF), and broadening the demand base through national infrastructure projects.

detail.abstract: This paper seeks to interrogate a paradox at the centre of Kenya's post-2010 constitutional order: a jurisprudence, and an accompanying body of scholarship, that describes itself almost without exception as progressive, transformative and generous, while consistently producing outcomes that leave the distribution of public power and public resources substantially undisturbed. Drawing on Karl Klare's theory of transformative constitutionalism and H.W.O. Okoth-Ogendo's earlier, sterner warning against constitutions without constitutionalism, the paper traces how Kenyan courts and commentators have constructed an interpretive vocabulary broad enough to describe every outcome, including its own retreats, as an instalment of progress. Through close analysis of the two-thirds gender rule advisory opinions, the Building Bridges Initiative litigation, and the Mitu-Bell socioeconomic rights retrenchment, read against South African jurisprudence in Grootboom, Doctors for Life and Glenister, the paper identifies three doctrinal techniques progressive realisation, advisory containment and remedial minimalism that together produce this outcome, and proposes a reoriented jurisprudence of consequence.

detail.abstract: Nepal is a developing country that continues to face challenges in organizing, accessing, and formalizing national statistics and public data. Nepal's economic data, at both aggregate and disaggregated levels, remain distributed across multiple institutions, formats, and data systems. Although Nepal has an established national statistical system, challenges remain in the integration, accessibility, and dissemination of statistical information. Usually, the dataset is not easily accessible; either it is distributed across multiple platforms or trapped in messy Excel files, PDF reports, or fragmented or inaccessible web sources. Such fragmentation can constrain policy and empirical research, and the reproducibility of analyses. Limited country-specific research may increase reliance on economic concepts and policy frameworks developed in other contexts, raising questions about their applicability to Nepal. The concern may also shift from context and structure research to following powerful economic models. Such approaches may overlook differences in institutional, geographic, environmental, historical, and structural constraints across economies. Atlasonomics aims to set up an organized database for socioeconomic research in Nepal. The objective includes working on macro and disaggregated data, the informal sector, inequality, the history of economic thought, and the economics of minorities, where all the aforementioned areas of interest are bounded by data. detail.abstract: We study the effects of direct consumption of professional news in a randomized experiment with 1,658 voters during Brazil's 2022 elections. Participants interested in subscriptions chose among five newspapers. Offering three-month free subscriptions and reading incentives shifted consumption from social media to newspapers without increasing total news consumption. Treatment improved news knowledge and trust in professional media, with evidence of stronger support for democratic norms and no effect on affective polarization. Effects on trust and democratic attitudes were concentrated among non-left-wing participants. Despite the positive overall effects of consumption, only three participants subscribed to newspapers after the intervention.

detail.abstract: AI-enabled smart education combines connected learning devices, behavioral data, and machine-learning models to adapt instruction at increasing levels of granularity. The same connectivity that enables personalization also expands the attack surface and concentrates sensitive information about learners. This critical review examines the relationship between cybersecurity and personalization in connected learning environments and asks how both can be governed as interdependent design requirements. Evidence is synthesized from intelligent tutoring, learning analytics, smart-classroom architecture, educational privacy, IoT security, intrusion detection, and AI risk-management research. The literature indicates that personalization depends on trustworthy identity, accurate provenance, secure availability, and valid learner models; cybersecurity controls can protect these foundations but may also cause surveillance, exclusion, or learning disruption when deployed without pedagogical constraints. The paper introduces BALANCE, a seven-stage machine-learning framework: Bound purpose, Authenticate, Limit data, Assess dual outcomes, Notify stakeholders, Control decisions, and Evaluate continuously. The framework separates learning and security data while permitting controlled exchange of device-trust and service-risk signals. It further links model evaluation to educational benefit, cyber resilience, privacy, equity, explainability, and human authority. The contribution is a systems framework for schools, universities, and vendors seeking to personalize learning without treating security as an afterthought or learners as unrestricted sources of behavioral intelligence.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether firms with low performance are more engaged in earnings management practices than firms with high performance in an emerging market; namely, Egypt. We estimate a model of the relationship between earnings and cash flows from operations with a dummy variable that allows parameter shifts for cash flows of low performance firms. Thus, the model captures whether the strength of the relationship between earnings and cash flows differs between low and high performance firms. The results show that, compared to firms with high performance, firms with low performance have a smaller regression coefficient of earnings on cash flows. These results can be interpreted as indicating that low performance firms engage in more earnings management (increase their earnings management practices) than high performance firms. Overall, these results suggest that firm performance is a critical determinant of earnings management. Given the current weakness of shareholder protection and regulatory enforcement in Egypt, these results encourage policymakers to improve considerably corporate-governance mechanisms in Egypt. This study contributes not only to the limited research on earnings management in the emerging market of Egypt, but also in other emerging economies.

detail.abstract: Shared resource limits can make a player’s admissible responses depend on the correlation recommended by a mediator. We show that this dependence remains computationally tractable when decisions generate few independent resource variations. In rational polymatrix games with common additive expected-resource constraints, we compute a sparse rational correlation that is exactly feasible and approximately obedient against every safe stochastic recommendation-dependent response. For resource variation dimension r, the bit running time is (L + 1/ε)^(O(r+1)), where L is input length and ε is the incentive tolerance. Both the player population and the number of nonredundant resource inequalities may grow. No strict-feasibility margin is required. The construction combines common prices, exact facial reduction, multiplicative interpolation of taxed equilibria, and exact resource clearing. Polynomial-size rational certificates permit independent verification of the output.

detail.abstract: A portfolio of fallback measurement designs can reduce operating risk, but sharing physical measurements also couples the designs' failures. We study how this sharing changes both exact rank failure and the probability of simultaneous near failure. Under pairwise sharing, the failure codimensions of all subportfolios form a representable polymatroid with an exact graphic-matroid formula. Each sharing edge saves one physical measurement, while the first-order reliability exponent loses exactly the nullity of a union of graphic matroids; sharing under an integer reliability-loss budget is therefore a weighted matroid optimization problem. For Gaussian measurements, the joint failure exponent is the Lovász extension of the same codimension function. A logarithmic correction can still separate portfolios that are tied at every first-order scale. With three-way sharing, submodularity can already fail, and locally small designs can realize arbitrary finite-type local singularities. Thus pairwise sharing marks a structural boundary between a uniform polymatroid description and substantially richer failure geometry.

detail.abstract:
Most procurement professionals working on critical mineral supply chains, advanced technology, energy storage, or data center infrastructure know this exact sinking feeling: a supplier clears every single stage of qualification—the financials check out, the manufacturing facility has open capacity, the quality record is completely clean—and everyone happily moves on to award the contract. Then, eight months down the road, a single upstream refinery, chemical processor, or component fabrication node suffers a disruption, gets acquired, or stops taking new orders. Suddenly, your fully qualified, fully compliant supplier cannot get you the critical battery-grade lithium, rare-earth permanent magnets, advanced logic chips, or high-purity polysilicon required for your buildout. Nobody did anything technically wrong; the standard qualification process simply was not built to catch that specific kind of upstream risk.

That is the exact gap I want to address in this piece.

Standard supplier qualification answers whether a vendor can perform on paper. It rarely answers what has to keep flowing upstream—from mineral extraction and chemical refining to advanced component manufacturing and energy grid elements—for that performance to actually hold up. When you are building capital-intensive assets around energy storage, solar cells, data centers, and battery supply chains, that second question is usually the one that determines whether your project hits its commercial operation date or stalls out entirely.

title: Persuading the Supplier with Imperfect Forecast Capability

detail.abstract: We consider a canonical supply chain in which a retailer shares its market-state forecast with an upstream supplier, who chooses production before demand realization. Because the supplier bears all overproduction costs, the retailer designs an information-sharing policy to persuade the supplier to produce more. The extant literature shows that full disclosure is optimal when state-dependent demand distributions differ only by a location shift, assuming that the retailer can perfectly predict the market state. In contrast, we focus on the same demand setting but allow for imperfect forecast capability, and show that partial or no disclosure can be optimal. When the supplier faces a high overproduction cost relative to underproduction, full disclosure is optimal at very low or high forecast capability, whereas partial disclosure can be optimal at intermediate capability. When the relative overproduction cost is low, the optimal policy progresses from no disclosure to partial disclosure and then to full disclosure as forecast capability improves. Thus, our results uncover how a retailer's forecast capability shapes its information sharing incentives. Fully sharing an imperfect forecast may be less effective than partially sharing it or not at all. The supplier can sometimes benefit from wider demand ranges associated with each state because it can induce the retailer to disclose more information.

detail.abstract: Nalla (2026a) introduced Generative Brand Narrative Intelligence (g-bni) as a formal construct for the autonomous, continuous generation and governance of outbound brand narratives, and presented the Emotionally Adaptive Brand Narrative (eabn) framework as its first architectural instantiation, satisfying five qualifying properties — Operational Continuity, Emotional Adaptivity, State-Aware Lifecycle, Governed Autonomy, and Closed-Loop Analytics — through a seven-agent, LangGraph-orchestrated pipeline. That paper's own limitations section identified five structural gaps left open by the v1 design: the absence of any quantitative check that generated content remains consistent with institutional identity prior to human review; a Closed-Loop Analytics property that collects engagement data without a mechanism for distinguishing a theme's causal effect from confounding by publication-time context; a single-tenant, single-brand deployment model with no isolation mechanism for serving multiple institutions; an approval pipeline with no defined recovery behavior under mid-cycle computing failure; and a governance model calibrated for general commercial marketing with no configuration path for regulated domains such as healthcare or financial services, where reviewer credentialing and disclosure obligations are not optional. This paper presents g-bni v2, which closes each of these five gaps through four new architectural mechanisms layered onto the unchanged v1 core. A Consistency Scoring Module computes a composite consistency index for every candidate artifact, prior to human review, as a weighted geometric mean of five component measures evaluated against a canonical knowledge representation of the institution, with weights fit by a calibration procedure against human-rated exemplars rather than fixed a priori. A Causal Attribution Module exploits the independence, by construction, of the v1 theme-rotation schedule from publication-time context to produce a back-door-adjusted, sensitivity-bounded estimate of a theme's causal effect on outcome, replacing the correlational engagement tracking of v1. A Domain-Configurable Governance layer substitutes reviewer-credential requirements, theme sets, and mandatory lifecycle states through a declarative configuration record, extending the framework from a single commercial-marketing embodiment to regulated healthcare and financial-services deployments without modifying the underlying pipeline. A Multi-Tenant Execution Architecture, paired with a failure-recovery and state-resumption mechanism, extends the v1 single-brand deployment to concurrently served, isolated institutional tenants with recorded resilience to mid-cycle interruption. We formalize four new qualifying properties extending the original five, enumerate seven new contributions, present worked operational examples in healthcare and financial-services configurations and under concurrent multi-tenant load, and extend the v1 evaluation framework with v1 itself as an explicit comparison baseline for the empirical study this paper proposes. Two further, previously open validation gaps — an unvalidated emotional taxonomy and unaudited rater independence — are additionally closed by a Taxonomy Validation Module and an Independent Rater Governance extension, both built entirely from infrastructure this paper already introduces.

detail.abstract:
As artificial intelligence reduces the time required to perform research, drafting, analysis, and other legal work, traditional relationships between time, efficiency, and professional performance are beginning to change. This article argues for a shift from time-based performance to capability-based performance—measuring professional value less by time spent producing legal work and more by the strategic human capabilities professionals bring to AI-assisted work, including the ability to evaluate, direct, and apply AI-generated outputs through sound legal and strategic judgment. This shift requires firms to rethink how judgment is developed and distributed across the workforce, including how junior and senior lawyers share responsibility, how quality control is embedded in AI-assisted workflows, and how pricing models respond to reduced execution time.

The article also proposes a broader framework of AI-complementary strategic human capabilities for judgment-centered performance, treating these capabilities as teachable and scalable across the legal workforce rather than concentrating strategic judgment at senior levels. Within this framework, it presents work-life harmony as a fundamental judgment-centered performance capability, defined as the sustained ability to self-regulate mental, emotional, and physical states in ways that support mental clarity, emotional regulation, and consistent judgment, and proposes a concrete approach to strengthening this capability through structured self-regulation. The article thus connects AI-enabled efficiency with the development of the strategic human capabilities required to work effectively with AI and argues that the quality of collective legal and strategic judgment across the legal workforce can become a central source of competitive advantage in AI-accelerated legal practice.

detail.abstract: Purpose: Brand management literature has evolved from mechanical metaphors toward human-centric approaches; however, there remains a lack of an integrated framework that organizes scattered stakeholder perceptions into a coherent "perceptual reality." This study aims to move beyond personality-centric theories by proposing the "Biological Brand Anatomy Model," termed Brandiatry; a metaphorical-physiological framework that conceptualizes brands not as static objects, but as living organisms amenable to clinical diagnosis. Methodology: Adopting an interpretivist-constructivist paradigm, this exploratory qualitative research employed an exploratory multiple case study design. Data were collected through semi-structured in-depth interviews with 50 senior brand strategy experts (selected via criterion-based purposive sampling across five distinct industrial poles), utilizing the novel "Function-to-Metaphor Elicitation" technique to prevent metaphor induction bias. Data analysis was conducted based on the principles of Constructivist Grounded Theory (CGT), aided by MAXQDA software, involving three stages of initial, focused, and theoretical coding. Findings: Results led to the emergence of six biological systems: Skeletal (identity and values), Muscular (agency and execution), Nervous (cognitive processing), Circulatory (resource flow and emotional bonds), Immune (resilience), and Integumentary/Sensory (interface and experience). Cross-case analysis revealed that while these systems are universal, their weight and function undergo "functional morphing" depending on the industry context. Furthermore, the novel concept of "Strategic Autoimmunity" was identified, wherein brand defense mechanisms attack healthy internal tissues (e.g., innovation and trust). To ensure clinical validity, a Brand Pathology Operationalization Matrix was developed, translating biological metaphors into measurable managerial indicators (e.g., Value Osteoporosis, Informational Stroke). Originality/Value: By elevating anthropomorphism theory from "personality" to "organizational physiology," this research bridges the gap between static semiotic models and dynamic brand realities, offering a diagnostic tool for moving beyond superficial symptom treatment to root-cause pathology. Finally, testing the extracted hypotheses via consumer neuroscience tools (EEG and Eye-tracking) is suggested for future neurological validation of the model.

detail.abstract: This paper measures how exposed workers are to generative AI in three Sub-Saharan African economies, using household surveys that reach agricultural and own-account workers and the own-use producers outside the employment boundary. Across 24,838 workers in Nigeria, Tanzania and Uganda the mean task-exposure score is 0.072, and 0.090 weighted, on the moderate 2030 Qwen 2.5 ratings, and runs 0.045 to 0.489 across nine versions. Agricultural workers average 0.029 against 0.134 for non-agricultural own-account workers and 0.150 for non-agricultural wage employees. detail.abstract: Employee productivity is a key component of organizational effectiveness, particularly in the public sector, where employees deliver government programs and services. This study examined the relationship between working environment and perceived employee productivity among employees of a selected national government agency (NGA) in Makati City, Philippines. Specifically, it assessed the working environment in terms of workplace facilities, ergonomic conditions, equipment and resources, and organizational and social environment. It determined perceived employee productivity in terms of work efficiency, timeliness and task completion, quality and accuracy of work, and accomplishment of work responsibilities. The study employed a quantitative descriptive-correlational research design involving 98 employees selected through simple random sampling. The study analyzed data using frequency and percentage distributions, weighted mean, and Spearman's rank-order correlation. Results showed that respondents rated the overall working environment moderately, while they rated perceived employee productivity highly. Significant positive relationships were found between all dimensions of the working environment and perceived employee productivity, with equipment and resources demonstrating the strongest relationship. Based on these findings, a workplace and service improvement plan was developed to improve the working environment and enhance employee productivity in the NGA. This study highlights the importance of strengthening workplace resources, facilities, and organizational support systems to enhance employee productivity and improve organizational effectiveness in government agencies. The results also provide empirical support for Social Exchange Theory.

detail.abstract: Generative AI broke the zero-marginal-cost model of software: every prompt consumes GPU time, and the heaviest users can cost far more than they pay. As a result, the leading AI companies practise demarketing at scale while investing record sums in capacity. This paper maps AI access levers (waitlists, invite codes, usage caps, premium tiers, partneronly models) onto Kotler and Levy's (1971) typology of general, selective, ostensible and unintentional demarketing. A review of eight documented access decisions between December 2024 and May 2026 shows that all four types coexist in one industry and that selective demarketing dominates. The analysis finds that scarcity raises perceived value before users hold access, and triggers reactance once they do. The paper proposes the Scarcity-Trust framework, six testable propositions, a playbook with metrics for product teams, and a three-study validation protocol. Version note. detail.abstract: Mastery in professional fields has traditionally been built through years of repetitive, ground-level work performed by junior staff at the base of the organizational work pyramid. Artificial intelligence increasingly performs many of these technical tasks, raising the question of whether the pipeline that produces experts is at risk. This paper distinguishes technical knowledge from expertise, drawing on the concept of tacit knowledge and Klein's Recognition-Primed Decision model, and introduces a knowledge-to-expertise ratio describing how the balance between technical execution and expertise shifts across levels of the work pyramid. Situating the discussion within human capital theory, the paper treats enterprise AI as a form of capital that competes with human capital in technically weighted roles and complements it in expertise-weighted roles. Evidence from entry-level job posting data, audit automation, software development productivity studies, and workplace AI adoption surveys suggests that automation pressure is concentrated at the base of the pyramid, while augmentation is more common at managerial and executive levels. The paper argues that AI is unlikely to eliminate experts but is shifting demand toward behavioral and judgment-based skills earlier in careers, moving expectations traditionally associated with senior roles down the work pyramid.

While archival studies document a relative prevalence of expensing development costs, this study explores the views of preparers and auditors on the accounting for the capitalisation of development costs under IAS 38. Design/methodology/approach Semi-structured interviews were held with 11 preparers and 10 auditors as key actors in the supply of financial reporting information. All had substantial experience in accounting for R&D. Interviewees were drawn from a range of countries reporting under IFRS, which could help minimise potential bias arising from country specific factors. An iterative interpretative thematic approach was followed for the analysis of the interview data employing ambiguity aversion. Findings Preparers and auditors portray a tendency to expensing. This finding is consistent with ambiguity aversion where individuals act as if they take a worst-case outcome, and a fear of negative evaluation regarding future impairments. Moreover, this sheds light on the findings of archival studies as to a relative lack of capitalisation. Further, the findings show that the accounting treatment of development costs can be viewed as being a dialogic social construction between preparers and auditors. Originality The findings advance the financial accounting literature in relation to R&D and the consideration of ambiguity and ambiguity aversion in accounting practice. Prior accountingrelated studies considering ambiguity have primarily adopted an experimental design often in a training environment with students. In contrast, this research directly reports the views of highly experienced auditors and preparers regarding a key, and highly topical, accounting issue. detail.abstract: Can paid consumer AI services identify the eligible five-star hotels in Greater London and rank the Top 25 using guest-review evidence from one specified year? IA vs AI compared five independent runs each of ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity (20 primary runs), plus one separate, context-informed ChatGPT run, with a HotScore benchmark locked before AI testing. The original benchmark contained 167 eligible hotels and 148,167 verified guest reviews from five platforms. A later audit identified four additional eligible hotels missing from the locked reference, giving a corrected count of 171 without changing the original file. Claude presented five ranked Top 25 lists and Gemini three. ChatGPT's fifth primary run presented an alphabetical 25-hotel candidate list, not a ranked Top 25; the other primary ChatGPT and Perplexity runs likewise did not deliver a ranked Top 25. Gemini's three ranked lists shared 8, 9 and 7 hotels respectively with the locked HotScore Top 25. Across the 20 primary responses, 24 of the locked HotScore Top 25 hotels were named at least once; the separate informed ChatGPT response named the remaining hotel. This aggregate identification is not a reproduced ranking. The outputs that ranked hotels did not demonstrate a complete and consistently applied five-platform assessment restricted to 31 July 2025–31 July 2026. Six distinct ineligible AI candidates were identified in the examined outputs, appearing 15 times. The findings concern these particular consumer services, prompts and recorded settings, not every possible AI workflow. They show that an answer that looks complete is not necessarily a verified annual market ranking, while also showing how AI can help find gaps in a specialist database. AI assistance disclosure. detail.abstract: Generative AI chatbots have become a revolutionary technology in customer service, they have progressed way beyond the functionalities of traditional rule-based systems. Initially, chatbots were heavily reliant on execution scripts and inflexible pattern-matching techniques, they usually were not capable of understanding the complexity of natural language and customer intent to large language models, generative AI chatbots can create context-aware, adaptable, and humanlike responses, thus, they are more engaging and interaction quality has improved dramatically. This study explores the architecture, classification, machine-learning methods, and communication abilities of generative AI chatbots, their advantages, disadvantages, and the potential of the new use cases in customer service.

detail.abstract: Enterprise data migration remains one of the most consistently failure-prone categories of IT project: Gartner reports that 83% of data migration projects either fail outright or exceed their budget and schedule, a figure broadly consistent with Bloor Research's finding of 60%-plus overrun rates and McKinsey's 2021 survey finding only 15% of cloud migrations complete on time and within budget. Bloor Research further finds that 75% of data migration projects rely on in-house, ad-hoc methodology rather than a reusable, standardized approach-a gap this paper addresses directly. We present a case study of a production data conversion framework built for an enterprise property and casualty insurance claims migration, in which approximately 49,000 insurance claims were migrated from a legacy platform to Guidewire ClaimCenter in a single production cutover with zero rollback events. We describe the framework's architecture-extraction, configurable mapping, a standing reconciliation engine, repeated dry-run/parallel validation cycles, and a monitored cutover with a defined rollback path-and report that its mapping and reconciliation components were subsequently reused, largely unmodified, across approximately 80% of later migrations on the same program. We situate this case study against Guidewire's own reported track record of more than 100 completed core system replacement projects industry-wide, and propose a generalized reusable conversion architecture, together with an evaluation methodology, for teams undertaking similar enterprise system migrations. We are explicit throughout that the case-specific figures in this paper are self-reported from the author's own production experience as the migration's technical lead and are not independently audited, a limitation we distinguish clearly from the externally published industry statistics also cited.

detail.abstract: Effective decision-making does not stop at generating ideas; it requires a systematic process for developing and evaluating alternatives. This article examines the development of alternatives through brainstorming and their evaluation through criteria setting, scoring, weighting, trade-offs, and final selection within decision-making theory. This study uses a literature review of four journal articles related to multi-criteria decision-making, team collaboration, and critical thinking, analyzed descriptively and qualitatively. The results indicate that brainstorming can generate a broad range of candidate alternatives; evaluation criteria should be relevant and measurable; scoring and weighting can be supported by methods such as the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), Weighted Sum, and Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS); and trade-offs can be addressed through outranking methods such as PROMETHEE. The final choice depends on the evaluation method, criteria, and assigned weights, and can be strengthened through collective decision mechanisms and sensitivity analysis. Overall, the five stages are interrelated and form a structured process for alternative evaluation in managerial decision-making.

detail.abstract:
Because the sustainability criterion is stated in terms of wealth, wealth is the right ledger for the AI transformation, but current wealth accounts do not identify it. The paper's one substantive claim is an accounting identity, the AIW identity, equation (1), which states where the new terms enter an existing ledger. National wealth accounting records, as far as the corpus swept for this paper reaches, neither data and AI capital as a separately identified asset nor AI-induced depreciation of human capital. AI systems and databases enter produced capital, where they enter at all, inside software, valued at cost rather than at an accounting price. Neither of the two frontier human capital accounts separates technology-induced obsolescence: one carries no depreciation term, the other names obsolescence without isolating it. Two rules govern the identity's use: the AIW compilation triple (v, B, π), which comprises the compilation vintage, the asset boundary and the accounting-price convention and without which no term has a determinate meaning; and the two-branch rule, under which the elasticity of substitution governs the magnitude of the adjustment but not its sign. Three disciplines, D1-D3, constrain how δ_AI, the AI-induced rate of human capital depreciation, may be defined: separability from attrition that is already booked, a net rate, and parallel life-year and monetary reporting. Proposition 1 gives provisional conditions, with known gaps stated in the paper, under which the four added terms are additive to inclusive wealth as currently compiled; Proposition 2 gives the unit convention that separates the fourth term from the fifth; without it the two cannot be told apart from data. Two testable propositions and one internal check are stated with provisional failure conditions, each of which will be registered before its test is run. A descriptive Japan skeleton reports an employment-weighted mean task-share exposure of 0.31. A cancellation threshold of 0.2-1.3 percent a year, the uniform net rate of human capital depreciation that would cancel measured growth in wealth per capita, is reported as a sensitivity value. No term of the identity is estimated.

detail.abstract: HYROX, a globally franchised and standardised functional-fitness race that involves running and completing eight resistance-based workout stations, has scaled from its initial 650 participating athletes in Germany in 2018 to over a million athletes per annum worldwide, and recently arrived in India, where reported participation increased from an estimated 1,650 athletes in the inaugural Mumbai event in May 2019 to 8,200 athletes in a two-day Bengaluru event in April 2020-an approximate five-fold increase in just twelve months. Such a steep upward trajectory raises two related but still analytically distinct questions that we aim to empirically test: 1) why would Indian consumer-athletes choose, and keep participating in, HYROX as a new sport format, from a psychological and social standpoint; and 2) does and how would the adoption/continued participation in HYROX translate into commercial potential for gyms, organisers and sponsors? Based on Rogers' (2003) diffusion of innovation (DOI) theory, selfdetermination theory (SDT) explanations of functional-fitness sport motivation, and a Chinese Cross Fit study that found that community-belongingness and sport-commitment mediated the relationship between intrinsic motivation and an intention to continue participating, we thus develop and defend an integrated model where perceived innovation attributes and intrinsic motivation predict adoption/continued participation intention, sport commitment mediates the motivation/adoption relation, community-belongingness moderates the innovation-attributes/adoption relation, and adoption intention predicts commercial potential. Empirically, a quantitative, cross-sectional survey of participants of Indian HYROX and functional-fitness gym members will be used, with a condensed yet validated set of scales, analysed via partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM)-a justified approach given the model's predictive-exploratory orientation and the combination of an earlystage market with established psychological dimensions. Consistent with registered-report norms, no primary survey data are reported here, instead presenting the analytical plan-a transparent templateup front. We thus propose India-specific, theory-based guidelines for contextually appropriate premium-participatory-sport adoption at a juncture of exponential category growth, which have potential implications for gyms, event operators, sponsors, and policymakers who seek to promote the commercialisation of functional-fitness racing in emerging markets.

detail.abstract:
An iPhone retail price ratio is not a foreign-exchange rate. The study shows materially different posted prices for the same nominal iPhone 18 Pro 256GB configuration across markets when expressed at market FX. In the frozen 21 September 2026 snapshot, the median headline wedge relative to the US pre-tax list price is 33.9%; removing identified consumption taxes lowers the median residual to 13.3%.

The decomposition illustrates why the headline number should not be assigned to one economic mechanism. India provides the clearest example: the ₹137.53 price-equivalent rate falls to ₹116.55 after removing 18% GST, leaving a residual that can include duty, distribution and pricing effects that the cross-section cannot separately identify. Türkiye shows a complementary tax-stack effect: a VAT-only treatment leaves a very large residual, while the stated four-layer scenario reduces it to 15.6%.

The launch-window design is deliberately narrow. It measures contemporary retail-price architecture rather than long-run PPP, law-of-one-price convergence or causal tax incidence. The euro-area analysis is consistent with less-than-proportional VAT pass-through, but the eight-market sample and confidence interval that includes full pass-through prevent a causal interpretation. The headline statistic is also sensitive to sample composition and US sales-tax treatment; the residual is comparatively less sensitive under the specifications examined.

The study's contribution is methodological. It applies the Big Mac calculation architecture to a highly tradable manufactured product while keeping market FX, the price-equivalent retail ratio, identifiable tax wedges and an unassigned residual as separate quantities. The replication workbook preserves the calculations, assumptions, sources and QA checks needed to rerun the analysis. A longitudinal panel, direct tariff observations, independent FX quotes and store-level tax verification are the natural next step.

detail.abstract: This study examines how differentiation of self (DoS), a psychological construct associated with relational and spiritual maturity, relates to spiritual joy and preferences for mission service. Data were collected from 450 adults who had participated in or intended to participate in service projects. An integrated mixed-membership model jointly analyzes open-ended text, DoS scale responses, MaxDiff measures of spiritual joy, and conjoint choices among mission opportunities, identifying five latent archetypes. Respondents characterized by stronger differentiation exhibit more clearly defined, but distinctly different, patterns of spiritual joy and mission preferences. One archetype emphasizes relationship with God and faith-oriented outcomes, whereas another emphasizes relationships with others, community support, and tangible service. These findings suggest that differentiation may produce clarity rather than uniformity in spiritual orientation. A relational-spiritual pathway is proposed through which serving and sustained relational presence can generate relational joy that may subsequently be interpreted as participation in God's mission. Mission experiences may therefore provide contexts in which relationships with others and relationship with God become meaningfully connected. detail.title: Learning to Price in Feature-Based Pool Markets under Censored Feedback

detail.abstract: In this work, we study dynamic pricing in a market with a fixed population of customers who check posted prices intermittently, purchase at most once, and leave the market immediately after purchasing. We assume that customer valuations depend on observable features through an unknown parameter. The seller knows the population distribution of these features but observes an individual customer’s features only upon purchase. This creates a fundamental challenge for learning: the seller must estimate the valuation parameter from censored transaction data generated by a customer pool whose composition evolves endogenously as purchases occur. Thus, unlike standard pricing models with independent arrivals, exploration not only incurs a direct revenue cost but also changes the composition of the population available for future learning and sales. We address this issue by studying markdown policies over a finite price ladder. When the valuation parameter is known, we show that the population markdown problem can be formulated as a finite-dimensional concave optimization problem. When the valuation parameter is unknown, we derive a censored likelihood that accounts for latent valuations, prior price exposure, and the endogenous evolution of the customer pool. Building on this likelihood, we develop a markdown-preserving learn-then-optimize policy that screens prices from high to low, collects transactions at the first active price to estimate the valuation parameter, and then optimizes the remaining markdown schedule for the residual customer pool. We show that the resulting estimator achieves a mean-square error of $O(1/m)$ after observing $m$ transactions. By exploiting the strong concavity of the residual markdown schedule problem, we bound the revenue loss from estimation by $O(n/m)$, while the cost of data collection is $O(m)$. Balancing these two terms yields $O(\sqrt{n})$ expected regret relative to the hindsight-optimal schedule for the realized customer pool. We further identify a free-learning regime in which population regret improves to $O(\log n)$. By contrast, near the boundary at which a high price changes from being skipped to being used, we prove a local $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ regret lower bound.

detail.abstract:
The reforms of 1974–1978 vested in the economic organization the right to dispose of the foreign exchange it had earned, while the duty to balance the foreign exchange account and to answer for the external debt was placed on the republics and provinces. As long as the inflow of new external credit covered the payments, the gap between the duty assigned and the capacity to bear it did not become visible. The crisis of 1982 was the first to test it. The subject of this paper is the fate of a duty already assigned, not the origin of the debt.

Drawing on primary legal, statistical, and banking sources, the paper traces the whole chain along which assigned liability was to become a recovered debt. The enterprise's right to the foreign exchange it had earned is reconstructed from the constitution and the foreign exchange laws; the duty to surrender the prescribed share and the reliance on common reserves are measured across the eight regions whose accounts the system kept separately; the debtor's solvency and interbank recovery are not measurable in the same way — for these, the surviving evidence consists of legal texts, court decisions, and the minutes of Party leadership sessions and of meetings between bankers and the federal authorities.

The assigned liability could not be discharged. Recovery requires three conditions, and the documents below are examined under these three; all three failed, and the sources do not allow their working to be told apart. Knowledge: the debtor's solvency could neither be established nor ruled out — no market set a price for the bank's assets, and it was checked by audit, extensive but answering a different question. Will: a claim in foreign exchange against a debtor in another region was not recovered — though on debt in dinars inside the region itself the system knew how, and did. Enforcement: no federal rule established in advance saying who was to reimburse a bank, and from which source, for a payment it had already made abroad is found in the norms and cases examined, and no body would recover across the boundary of a region — though the courts worked, a court order could reach a foreign exchange account and enterprise bankruptcy was used. The soft budget constraint explains why the debtor survived, but not to whom the claim is attributed or out of what source it is met.

The bank's claim on a debtor in another region was one in foreign currency, and that is why it fell outside the machinery that did work: domestic obligations were to be discharged in dinars, and foreign exchange could not be bought at the official rate, the market having run on the National Bank's own supply, which ceased in February 1980.

The rule naming the source of funds and the order of reimbursement came only after the payments themselves. The statutory provision that required those sources to be settled came into force on 1 January 1983, and at first it did no more than direct the banks to agree among themselves; the reimbursement procedure itself took effect on 8 January 1984 and covered only payments made up to the end of 1982.

Within eighteen months the federation dismantled the foreign exchange part of the regional regime of 1977–1978 — the law of 1977 itself remained the foundation — and in the summer of 1983 it brought all external credits contracted up to the end of 1982 under a state guarantee: the share of debt under guarantee rose from 35 to 50.8 percent. The federation did not become the principal debtor: the debtors remained the banks and the enterprises. For payment abroad the law of July 1983 built a ladder for collecting funds down to its last link — reaching every socially owned legal entity in the country; for settlement between the banks at home, a law of the same day gave no more than a power to make a rule. Abroad the account was closed in the way debt crises usually are. At home it was not reconciled: how much fell to each side depended on which rule of attribution was applied, and no rule was accepted by all of them. It was a costly arrangement, and those who paid for it were not those who had borrowed: the missing foreign exchange came out of common funds, and in the end it was the holders of dinars and the country's enterprises who covered it. Hence the conclusion drawn from this case: devolving liability upon the republics and provinces did not ensure that they would actually bear it.

title: The Algorithmic Crowd: Artificial Intelligence, Correlated Trading and the Limits of Institution-Level Regulation

detail.title: The Algorithmic Crowd: Artificial Intelligence, Correlated Trading and the Limits of Institution-Level Regulation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This research did not involve human participants, patients, personal data collection or experimental procedures requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Separately controlled trading systems can behave lawfully and still create market-wide risk when they rely on common models, signals or constraints. This article examines how UK and EU law allocate responsibility for that problem, which predates AI and may be amplified by more advanced automated trading. Existing law reaches much of the conduct. Firm-level duties can extend to foreseeable market interactions, venues can respond once trading effects appear, and article 42 of UK MiFIR can reach defined practices firms can identify in advance. It does not clearly reach an emergent crowd visible only after lawful decisions combine. The remaining gaps concern cross-firm information, limited scope and early detection. Responsibility should sit where aggregate risk can be seen and coordinated control can be exercised.

title: How Competitive Are Regional Universities in Developing Talent? The Current Picture and Policy Directions
affiliations: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade

detail.title: How Competitive Are Regional Universities in Developing Talent? The Current Picture and Policy Directions

keywords: Plan for Training Local Talent Linked to Growth Engines

detail.abstract:
A shrinking school-age population and the preference for universities in the Seoul Capital Area (SCA) are together rapidly weakening the ability of regional universities to fill their places and the foundations for developing local talent. The study warns that this could set off a vicious cycle in which a shrinking talent pool weakens industrial competitiveness and reduces jobs, job losses drive people out of the regions, and population outflow further erodes the competitiveness of regional universities. Workforce development outcomes also vary among regional universities. Until fairly recently, flagship national universities achieved outcomes broadly similar to those of SCA universities and had accumulated foundations for teaching and research. Recently, however, signs of weakening competitiveness have emerged, including declining admission competition ratios and employer reputation, which call for a preemptive response before those foundations erode further.

Completing the hub development strategy of balanced development policy depends above all on building a system, centered on flagship national universities, that develops talent in the regions to meet the needs of growth industries and keeps that talent there. Each region’s flagship national university should be developed into a core hub for talent development, research and development, and industry-academia collaboration, and should spread its results across the wider region through links with non-flagship universities, firms, and research institutes. Support for regional universities, likewise, needs to move away from scattered support for individual institutions toward a system that extends the capabilities of flagship national universities across the wider region.

Existing university support programs and R&D programs should also be linked and reorganized to fit talent development systems for each wider region, centered on flagship national universities, and tied to the workforce needs of each region’s growth industries.

title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Higher Education: Transformations, Challenges and Opportunities
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Higher Education: Transformations, Challenges and Opportunities
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being increasingly incorporated in all spheres of the society. It is poised to fundamentally upend workplaces and daily lives. Concerns over this looming shift are widespread, especially in the labor market. The deployment of AI in the workplace could eliminate more jobs than it could create and change the nature of work. As a result, workers may need to develop new skills.  Higher education has a salient role to play in preparing future workers for these new skills.  However, it appears that there is a mismatch between the degrees - or skills - people study for and what is needed. It is therefore crucial to rethink higher education system to enable individuals keep up with the development of AI. Our article explores these challenges and transformations faced by higher education. It also proposes possible solutions to gradually transform educational programs to cope with AI development and harness the full potential of human-machine collaboration.

title: Learning from Peers' Private Information: Evidence from Failed Mergers & Acquisitions
affiliations: California State University, Fullerton - Department of Accounting

detail.title: Learning from Peers' Private Information: Evidence from Failed Mergers & Acquisitions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not any
declarations.funderStatement: Boston College and California State University Fullerton

detail.abstract: I investigate the effects of private information acquisition from Mergers and Acquisitions (M&A) due diligence on bidders' subsequent innovation activities. Using a sample of negotiated and announced M&A deals that fail to close, I find that following the failed transactions, bidders file significantly more patents and produce higher-quality innovations relative to propensity-scorematched control firms. Moreover, I show that the bidders' post-failure patents become technologically more similar to the target's pre-bid patent portfolio, linking the innovation gains to the information acquired during due diligence. I also find that the effects are concentrated among bidders with pre-bid patenting experience, low agency costs, and when they operate within the same industry. In falsification tests using hostile bids, where due diligence is absent, I find no comparable effects on innovation. A placebo test that assigns each bidder a pseudo-event date before its actual failed bid likewise yields no evidence of an effect, which mitigates the concern that the results reflect a pre-existing trend or mean reversion. Finally, using termination fee provisions from merger filings, I find that the post-failure gains are larger for deals with high termination fees, suggesting that targets anticipate and price in the bidder's learning. Overall, my study contributes to the understanding of the real effects of learning from peers' proprietary information.

title: Institutional Capital Readiness: A Transaction-Level Framework for Institutional Evaluation

detail.title: Institutional Capital Readiness: A Transaction-Level Framework for Institutional Evaluation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Managing Principal of Changoo & Associates, an independent advisory firm whose work includes institutional capital readiness, transaction structuring, governance, and execution planning. The framework presented in this paper draws in part on the author's professional experience. No external organization or financial sponsor influenced the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper presents a conceptual and practitioner framework and does not involve human participants, patient data, or identifiable case-study subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Institutional financing is often framed as a capital-access problem: a sponsor has an economically credible opportunity and seeks an investor or lender capable of funding it. This framing can obscure a prior question. Before institutional capital can determine whether it should commit, the underlying opportunity must be translated into a transaction that can be evaluated. 

This paper develops a transaction-level framework for institutional capital readiness. It distinguishes commercial viability from transaction readiness and positions readiness as a precursor to, rather than a substitute for, underwriting. The framework proposes that institutional evaluation progresses through four connected states: readiness, underwriting, structuring, and execution. At the readiness stage, the relevant question is whether the transaction is sufficiently defined, evidenced, governed, capitalized, and sequenced to permit serious evaluation. Underwriting then tests the resulting proposition by tracing specific claims through risk, risk ownership, capital consequences, protection or compensation, capital-stack interaction, repayment or realization, downside performance, and closing dependencies.

Structuring translates those findings into an architecture of capital, priority, control, risk allocation, conditions, and timing. Execution determines whether that architecture can be converted into commitment, drawdown, deployment, monitoring, and completion or exit. The framework is offered as a practitioner synthesis rather than an empirically validated universal model. Its purpose is diagnostic: to identify where a transaction has failed to progress and what type of change is required before further institutional evaluation is productive.

title: The Contribution of International Master Students to Entrepreneurship in the World
affiliations: University of Luxemburg, University of California, Davis - Department of Economics, Aix-Marseille University - Aix-Marseille School of Economics and Independent

detail.title: The Contribution of International Master Students to Entrepreneurship in the World
detail.abstract: We provide the first global empirical evidence on the relationship between international master’s education and entrepreneurship. Using large-scale longitudinal data from LinkedIn/Revelio, we document that international master’s graduates are systematically more likely than domestic graduates to create firms across the world’s leading destinations for international students. We further show how this entrepreneurial advantage varies across fields of study, gender, origin and destination countries. In addition, we document the geography of post-graduation firm creation, highlighting the international mobility of entrepreneurial activity among former international students. Taken together, the results offer a new global perspective on the economic impact of international student mobility and the contribution of international master’s graduates to entrepreneurship, innovation, and business dynamism worldwide.

title: Capital-Skill Complementarity Beyond Firm Boundaries
affiliations: National Bank of Belgium, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and KU Leuven

detail.title: Capital-Skill Complementarity Beyond Firm Boundaries
detail.abstract: New machinery has long been argued to raise the relative demand for skilled labor, yet firm-level evidence finds no such shift at investing firms. We resolve this puzzle by looking beyond firm boundaries. Linking Belgian data on capital investments, buyer–supplier transactions, and worker skills, we show that the skill bias of new machinery arises entirely at external suppliers. Following machinery investment spikes, purchases from suppliers raise firms’ total demand for high-STEM workers by 45%, three times the rise for other skill groups, while in-house hiring raises it by less than 5%, evenly across skill groups. This external demand comes first from machine integrators and later from complementary services such as software, and is stronger for smaller firms, lumpier investments, and rapidly advancing capital, consistent with fixed and adjustment costs of hiring high-STEM workers in-house. In a general-equilibrium model estimated on our event studies, the rise in machinery per worker from 2003 to 2021 raises relative demand for high-STEM workers by 8.8 log points and their wage premium by 3.1. Measured on payrolls alone, both would fall.
